text: Aiscellaneous Repository. From the Albany Register, WAR, OR A PROSPECT OF IT, From recent instances of British Outrage. BY: WILLIAM RAY, Author of the contemplated publication, entitled, “Horrors of Slavery, or the American Turf in Tripoli,” VOTARIES of Freedom, arm! The British Lion roars! Legions of Valor, take th’ alarm—; Rash, rush to guard our shores! Behold the horrid deed— Your brethren gasping lie! Beneath a tyrant’s hand they bleed— They groan—they faint—they die. Veterans of seventy-six, Awake the slumbering sword;— Hearts of your murderous foes transfix— 'Tis vengeance gives the word. Remember Lexington, And Bunker’s tragic hill; “The same who spilt your blood thereon, Your blood again would spill. Ye who have seen your wives, Your children, and your fires, Too British ruffians yield their lives, And roast in savage fires;— Our cities lost in flames,— Your mothers captive led; Rise and avenge their injured names, Ye kindred of the dead. But not Revenge alone, Should urge you to the field; Let Duty lead you firmly on, And justice be your shield. Sure as we fail to join And crush our impious foes, War, fire and sword, and death combine, And woes succeed to woes.

The Portsmouthaathinna in the Miscellaneous Repository. & @i ienngnninn i@ The following patristic ODE was composed for the celebration of American Independence, July 4, 1806, and sung by the Republicans of Portsmouth on the late joyful occasion. 1. LET all the nations' Anthems sing, And praise to our Almighty King, Swell high the choral lay! This day his fiat gave us birth, Among the nations of the earth, Hail to the glorious day! CHORUS, Let us loud hosannas raise, Let us sing his constant praise, Let us praise our God above, The God of glory and of love. II. When first this happy infant land, Heard of oppression’s stern command, Trusting, O Lord! to thee, Her sons with justice for their shield, Rushed forth indignant to the field, To die, or to be free. CHORUS, Let us, &c. III. When hostile troops in torrents poured, And war through all the country roared With havoc and her spoils, Then didst thou, Lord, thy power display, And strike our foes with dire dismay, Till victory crowned our toils. CHORUS, Let us, &c. IV. Now let the people Anthems sing, Loud thanks to our Almighty King, For his divine decree; Which gave, this day, a nation birth And loud proclaimed to all the earth, Columbia shall be free! CHORUS, &.

From the above data, it is evident that the ideas of delicacy entertained by British ladies are approximating in a certain ratio to that of the females of ancient Sparta, or perhaps indeed, to their own ancestors, the Britons; and from these premises, it may be no unwarrantable assertion that in ninety years there will be little smuggling of Flanders lace or other frippery, but their beautiful skins may again be dyed with wood and have the figures of the heavenly bodies cut or tattooed upon them. From Archbishop Herring’s Sermon on Riches. "How imprudently do we act, and against all experience, in imagining we make our children happy by leaving them very rich. Alas! If you have made no other provision for their happiness, and have not sown the seeds of virtue in their minds, cultivated their understandings, and brought their passions to the command of reason in giving them riches, you have only put instruments of mischief into the hands of madmen; and your friends will live to see it when you do."

To the Honorable the officers of the Superior Court of Judicature sitting at Dover, in and for the county of Strafford February term one thousand eight hundred and six. SHEWS, the petition of William BREWSTER, of Portsmouth, in the county of Rockingham and State of New-Hampshire, esquire, that your petitioner is testamentary guardian of the persons and estates of John Gerrish and Alphonzo Gerrish, minors and children of Samuel Gerrish, jun’r, late of said Dover, merchant, deceased—that the said minors are seized in equal undivided moieties, in fee simple, of a certain Farm or tract of land lying in Moultonborough, in said county containing fifty acres; with the dwelling house standing thereon, and is the same farm formerly owned by and now in the possession of Joab Harriman and which said Harriman sold and conveyed to the said Samuel Gerrish, by deed dated the twenty eighth day of March one thousand seven hundred and ninety nine.—And the said minors, are also seized of the one quarter part of a certain oil Mill and mill privilege at Waldrop’s Falls so called in Dover aforesaid, which they hold in equal undivided moieties.

Tuesday, September 15, 1807. Trial of Aaron Burr. Richmond [Vir.] Friday, August 28. The court sat at 9 o’clock in the morning.—Mr. Martin continued the argument on the great question concerning the admissibility of evidence.—His speech was remarkably zealous and animated, and replete with law-learning. It commenced immediately after the meeting of the court, and was not finished when they adjourned about five o'clock in the afternoon. Saturday, August 29.—On this day Mr. Martin spoke again from 9 in the morning until nearly 3 o’clock in the afternoon. He was followed by Mr. Randolph on the same side, who closed the debate. Monday, August 31.—A numerous audience assembled for the purpose of hearing the truly important opinion about to be pronounced by the Chief Justice of the U.S. About 40 minutes after 11 o’clock, the Judges took their seats. The Chief Justice delivered in writing the opinion of the court which was uncommonly lengthy, learned and argumentative. Two hours and a half were consumed in reading it. The result was in favor of the motion made by Col. Burr and his counsel, to exclude the evidence.

Such parts of the opinion of the Supreme Court in the case of Bollman and Swartwout, as appeared to convey an opposite doctrine, were explained and declared to have been misunderstood by the counsel for the U.S. though the language of that opinion was acknowledged to have been equivocal and inaccurate in some respects. Whether the evidence was sufficient to charge the persons who were present at Blannerhassett's island with an overt act of treason, was not expressly decided; but the contrary was strongly insinuated. Although all evidence was proclaimed to be irrelevant and inadmissible upon the indictment which had been filed against Aaron Burr, the jury were informed that the court by no means intended to interfere with their rights, and, if they chose to find him guilty upon the testimony which had been introduced, they had a right to do so. The joy and exultation visible on the faces of Burr and his friends, was such as might have been expected. Hay observed that the opinion he had heard furnished a variety of matter of consideration; that he could not immediately determine upon the course which ought to be pursued on the part of the U.S.

After some conversation his motion was acceded to, and the session suspended till 6 P.M. at which time the counsel for the U.S. not being yet satisfied as to the measures to be taken, a further indulgence was granted to them, and the court adjourned until Tuesday 10 o’clock. R O H N E Tuesday, Sept. 1.—The court sat at ten o’clock. Present the Chief Justice only. M's Hay informed the court the opinion delivered yesterday had been maturely considered by the Council for the U. States the result of which was that he had nothing farther to offer, of evidence, or argument, to Wixiary. The jury then withdrew; and, after an absence of twenty minutes, returned into court, and Col. Carrington their foreman offered their verdict, in the following words indorsed on the bill of indictment: "We of the jury find that Aaron Burr is not proved to be guilty under this indictment by any evidence submitted to us... We therefore find him not guilty."

Unfortunately, Capt. C. brought no papers; and we lament it the more, as had he brought any we should have been in possession of very late news from the Continent of Europe. Capt. C. informs that a report had just been received of an attack upon Stralsund, and its capture, by the French; that previous to the attack, the English had joined the Swedes; that the battle was very severe, and that the loss of the French was very great. Off the Naze, Capt. C. saw 27 sail of British vessels, 27 of them ships of the line. (Ibid. - LATEST FROM EUROPE. The President Adams, Capt. Wood, arrived at Boston on Saturday last, in 32 days from Liverpool. Capt. W. informs that two days before he sailed, a letter was received there from London, by Messrs. Rathbone, Hughes & Duncan, advising them of the improbability of an accommodation taking place between England and this country; and recommending the American Captains under their charge, to leave port as soon as possible, whether freighted or not. The pilot boat was ordered by the commander of the Columbine to weigh anchor and remove farther off, or he would compel her.

To this order no attention was paid; she continued where she was, and no violence was immediately offered. But on Saturday morning, under pretence of having missed a hand, the pilot boat was boarded from the Columbine by men armed with pistols, cutlasses, and blunderbusses, who swore that the man was concealed on board; and that they would search every nook and corner for him—Accordingly the Revenue Cutter was searched, but not finding the hand whom they pretended they had lost, the searchers averred that he was concealed among the ballast, and threatened to tear up the planks which covered it! They were told that they could do so if they pleased; but that if the ballast was disturbed the Cutter would instantly upset; at length, having exhausted their vocabulary of insolence the searchers desisted and returned to the Columbine. * * LE N On Saturday a man was detected in supplying the British ships at the Hook with provisions, and was very improperly suffered to go home. It is understood that his name is Eldridge, from Staten Island, and that he pretended ignorance of the Proclamation. We are informed that the crew of the Jason mutinied on Saturday night—which was quelled by the officers, and 60 of the principals put in irons. Sep. 9.—Yesterday a boat from the Columbine, with an officer and five men, went.

Is very prevalent throughout the country. The best remedies that have yet been applied for it, when people are seized violently, is to take a large dose of Tartar Emetic, the operation of which, take a pint of Tea, made of catnip, sage, and balm of Gilead, a small glass of spirit, and if you have them, 3 teaspoonsful of Bateman’s drops; drink it as warm as possible, after you are in bed; cover yourself up warm, and take a decent sweat. Keep house the next day, and you will soon get better.

The two thirds of that valuable Farm of Land and Buildings that Joseph Weather span, late of Chester, died seized of, containing about fifty acres of good mowing, tillage, pasturing and woodland, with a sufficiency of orcharding, one third part of a Cider-mill with four wells of good lasting water on the farm, and otherwise well supplied with water. At the same time will be sold two young cows, one pair of new cart wheels, two new ploughs, three new chains, one horse sleigh, and good new harness, some articles of household furniture. Said farm will be sold altogether or in separate lots, as may best suit the purchaser or purchasers, with two thirds of one ground pew in the Rev. Mr. Bradstreet's meeting house.

Accounts from Hayti, [St. Domingo] state that a battle was expected about the beginning of April, between the forces of the rival Presidents of that island, Christophe, who commands the blacks, and Petion, who commands the men of colour. In the town and neighbourhood of Waterford, (Ireland) no less than fifty thousand Hogs were killed and salted for bacon for exportation to England, in the year 1806, in addition to the usual large quantity annually taken for the navy and army. Remarkable Whirlwind - On Wednesday last, about three o'clock took place the most tremendous hurricane or whirlwind ever experienced in this county. At the Fork Meeting-house, called Methodist Meeting, near the dwelling of Aquilla Hally Esq. were swept away seventeen houses and several large trees and fences were swept off - in fact, not a single vestige left in that thriving place except the meeting-house and dwelling house of C. Gorsuch. The hurricane continued its course from thence northerly across the falls of gunpowder to Harford county; and, lamentable to tell! the devastation committed in blowing down trees and fences, and entirely destroying the property of David Lee, junr. living near the Friends’ meeting-house, in said county, &c. [Balt. dmer. Six bridges, a sawmill, and other property, have been destroyed by the late Freshets near Windsor, (Va.)

The Richmond Enquirer, on the subject of a new President says, “It is now almost reduced to a certainty, that Mr. Jefferson will retire from the Presidential chair, at the expiration of his present term. The first wish of our hearts must necessarily be, that his successor may be not less able and virtuous than himself.” After a discussion of the circumstances of another choice, it adds: “Let no man be supported who is not a most decided opponent of Federal principles. He must be one that has been tried by the unerring test of experience; bleached by the hoary hand of time, and his principles attested by many winters of federal persecution.” The treaty is now a subject of speculation. What has become of it? Upon what terms have the negotiations been continued, or for what object? When we recollect what has been said in past times on the same subject, and know how severe would be the censures on the government should any embarrassments arise to Commerce from hasty and indiscreet measures, and therefore how much depends upon these treaties for our national quiet, we feel a just acquiescence in every measure which tends to gain the fullest information, at least, on the subject of all our claims.

Thursday arrived, the Three Friends, Capt. Trefethen, in 14 days from St. Thomas—cargo, Coffee, Sugar, and Molasses. A Plymouth schr. supposed to be bound to Kennebunk, with flour, corn, &c. has been wrecked on Seguin. - It is thought the people were saved, as she appeared to be stripped of her rigging, &c. Capt. Wm. Chale, arrived at Boston in the Midas, from Saco, informs, that on the 7th May inst. at 9 A.M. he discovered a light schr. of about 130 tons, standing on the same course with him; and that at 9 P.M. the schr. came up abreast of him, distant about half a mile, when she upset. That he immediately hove to, and sent the boat to her assistance, but could only save one man, John Simonds, who reported, that the vessel was the schr. William, John Anderson, master, from Portland, for Beverly, and that the names of the persons drowned from her, were, Capt. John Anderson, John Staples, and Robert Carter; these being all the people on board, excepting himself, when she upset. The brig Rambler, Pope, sailed from Tobago, April 15 for Wells; and Olive Branch, for this port, the 12th April. The schr. Jones Eddy, Harrold, from Trinidad for this port, is at anchor on Plum Island; the vessel will be got off without much injury, and the cargo saved.

——— THE BEATS . ORDAINED— At Dover, on Wednesday last, the Rev. Mr. C. H. SHERMAN, to the pastoral charge of the church and congregation of the first parish in that town. The prayer, introductory to the solemn exercises of the day, was made by the Rev. Abiel Abbot of Beverly. The Rev. Thaddeus M. Harris of Dorchester, delivered a sermon, from 1 Timothy, iv. 12, "Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in faith, in purity."—The consecrating prayer was made by the Rev. John Thompson of Berwick.—The charge was delivered by the Rev. Benjamin Balch of Barrington,—The fellowship of the churches was conferred by the Rev. Samuel Chandler of Kittery; and the concluding prayer was made by the Rev. Dr. Buckminster, of Portsmouth. The exercises of the day, generally, were appropriate, solemn and impressive. The sermon which we fondly hope will be shortly presented to the public, was in itself truly evangelical, and exhibited specimens of pulpit oratory, which must be read with pleasure, by the votaries of true religion, and the judges of erudition and taste. The music was observed by the lovers of harmony, to have been extremely fine.

Of the Kentucky Conspiracy much is said, but our 'acts will not admit all the communications on the subject. The Palladium of Frankfort, Kentucky, represents that the discoveries of the Conspiracy have taken full liberty to abuse and vilify any person who comes in their way. They think such insolence ought to be chastised, and they think to do it soon would bring the shameful affair to a crisis. The Editor scruples not to give his opinion. He believes the charges audacious falsehoods, and as far as they relate to himself as employed by conspirators, malicious. That the whole is the work of a party. But as many things are insinuated and not said; as many things do not admit of evidence directly, the publishers of the conspiracy are called upon for proofs against Gen. Wilkinson, for proofs of letters said to be written, for proofs of journeys and conversation referred to in the charges, or of the presence of Gen. Bowles, at the time mentioned. Till these important questions are answered, the conspiracy is to be reckoned among the many artifices adopted under the cover of secret design, to alarm and perplex the public mind. And till the proper evidence is produced, we shall feel ourselves at liberty to treat it as other former conspiracies, which have ended in delusion, and have no existence but in the designs of party. (Salem Register.)

You cannot fail to have heard before this hour of the great work of God in the great meeting held in, and about the middle of June last, there were 165 souls converted at the meeting held since that time, there were 1120 converted in all, and many besides multitude uninified we fear, for the Lord is on our found of many waters going through the land, and it seems that the glory day is coming. In the late election for Members of Congress in this state, the Republican Ticket has prevailed by a great majority, although the meetings were in general, but thinly attended. The following is a correct statement of the number of votes (exclusive of the scattering) that each candidate received—as taken from the records of the Secretary of the State. The stern of a brig having "Polly of Portsmouth" painted on it, has drifted ashore at the southward. The southern papers are filled with disastrous narratives of shipwrecks, and sufferings by the late storms. The Jamaica fleet, of 150 sail, convoyed by one 74 and two frigates, experienced a gale on 25th Aug. in lat. 29, long. 80. The persons saved in the boat of the Jamaican Frances, report that while in the boat they saw five vessels bottom upwards; and they suppose that one half of the Jamaica fleet must have foundered. MARRIAGES: In Amherst, (N.H.) the Hon. Benjamin West of Charleston, to Mrs. Frances Gordon. In Newmarket, Mr. Henry Wiggins to Miss Arunia Hill. In this town, Capt. Richard Salter to Miss Elizabeth Trusell. DEATHS: In Albany (N.Y.) the Hon. William Patterson, one of the associate judges of the Supreme Court of the United States.

I Geo. 48 847 46. 80 48 31 47 13 60 John Reiley, 70 50 36 55 157 NATHANIEL W. CARR, ESQ., Near Forge-Gore, September 1, 1805 Mr. TURNER’S Ordinary Ball, will take place this evening, at the Assembly Room, to commence at half past 6 o'clock, after the Ball the room will be appropriated for the use of the ladies and gentlemen who may honor Mr. T. with their company. Tickets may be had at Col. Woodward's. Portsmouth, Springs. Valuable Real Estate, THIS DAY At 12 o'clock, M. will positively be sold at Public Auction, at the Bell Tavern in this town, THAT Valuable and elegantly situated FARM, lately owned by Col. I wish since he is irrevocably gone, his mantle had been left among us; but knowing, as I do, what he was, and feeling, as I do, what I am, I will yet go forth armed with but my scrip and sling; and knowing that my cause is righteous, I will not fear for my weakness, though a host of Goliaths be brought against me. Before, however, I enter the lists, I would wish to propose some preliminaries, as I am warranted in doing by the usage in all such feats of chivalry. I would beg leave then, in the first instance to prescribe, that the right honorable gentlemen would upon the present question, be more sparing of their reflections upon me as the uniform advocate for our enemies, and against England. These gentlemen have been too liberal in dealing out such reflections against me; in any question where England is right, I will support her, where she is wrong, I will oppose her injustice and in advocating the just cause of America, or of any other power against the injustice of England, I am advocating the cause of my country. I am not an advocate of America—I am not the advocate of France but the advocate of my country, because I am the advocate of justice—( Hear! hear! )

Addressed to that right honorable gentleman himself, did on the part of the American government, strongly remonstrate against the injustice of these very orders. I say, that at the moment he thus informed this house he was conscious that he had excited a flame in America, to which he has since added such a portion of fuel as is calculated to blow up every interest Great Britain has in America, if any such interest remains. Yet we are told, as I well recollect, by the chancellor of the exchequer, that America would see no source of discontent; that she would feel no grievance, unless from the re-echo of the speeches made at this side of the house.

Although, for, were even such a consequence justified by the sac, I would by no means surrender the right of full and free discussion in this house; still I must tell the right honorable gentleman, that he has miscalculated dates and distance, and that he was not justified in the inference he drew; I told him that we have now before us vouchers which show that both dates and distance, fully refute the observations he had made. Another prediction on the benefits arising from those orders has also falsified itself. The prospect was held out of a consequent increase of exports and imports; without attempting to grovel into custom house details, and well knowing that such accounts have been swelled out into an artificial magnitude, for the purpose of public delusion. I am still ready to prove that even from the returns thus made up, there has been a considerable diminution in your imports and your exports, I will say to the amount of 11 millions. But suppose such a diminution did not amount to more than 7, 8, or 9 millions, still, it is sufficient to prove that the effect has completely contradicted every boasted promise with which the right honorable gentleman opposite deluded the house and the country.

Equally futile and inefficient was the hope of an unlimited supply of raw materials for our manufacture; From America, previous to these orders, Great Britain imported of cotton wool from America, thirty-two millions of pounds. Since that part of the world was closed against our commerce, what was our supply of that article? Why, sir, from Asia, and the Portuguese settlements in South America, we imported five millions. Thus the illustration which this system affords of the total command of the raw materials for our manufactures is by furnishing us with a deficiency of twenty-seven millions of pounds, in an article essential to their prosperity. But then it is affirmed that all such effects are attributable to the Berlin decree. Really it is inconsistent with every principle of common reasoning, to find men laying such a stress upon a measure which never had, and scarce ever could have operation. To see the best interests of the empire dissipated and overturned by the influence of an idle phantom; of what I must call a Castle Otranto, scaring by its imaginary terrors, an administration out of their senses. But what, I ask, was the effect of this terrific decree issued at Berlin on your imports and exports! Why, the effect was this, that they were greater in the year of its full operation, than in the preceding year.

The advocates of corruption—who have gone so far as to write, print and circulate a book to defend England for the outrage on the Chesapeake! who have abused our own government for it. [See "The Honest Politician" written by Luther Martin, Esq. of Baltimore]--Now the truth is, the American federalists have outpaced the British ministerial printers in defending the most iniquitous acts of England: this ought to be a humiliating and impressive lesson to men who plume themselves on being "native and enlightened Americans". It is irresistible proof of early corruption. "There are a set of Renegade Americans, who side with England, as the Christian Renegades take part with the Turks against the Christians; and in all cases, 'one renegade is worse than ten Turks'." Facts are stubborn things; and the following show that the federalists in the late congress refused to resist foreign aggression; and voted against putting the country in a state of defense. "On the passing of the non-intercourse law which repealed the embargo, except as to France and England, the following persons voted in the NEGATIVE; from which it will be seen that all of that party in the house of representing, excepting Culpeper, Key and. Davis, voted AGAINST THE REPEAL OF THE EMBARGO, NEGATIVE." Messrs. J. Campbell, Champion, Chittenden, Clay, Dana, Davenport, Elliot, Ely, Gardiner, Hoge, R. S.

Jackson, Kellogg, Minor, Morley, Sturges, Tallmadge, Upham, Van Dyke, Van Rensselaer. “Federalists have also pretended to be warm advocates for the ample defence of the country. Yet caution to expunge the clause in a bill, which appropriated a million of dollars for the defense of our seaports; the following persons in the Senate of the United States voted to expunge the clause: Messrs. Bayard, Goodrich, Hillhouse, Lloyd, Pickering, and White.” I will leave the reader to judge of federal modesty after this exhibition of their regard for the honor and safety of the country! There are two ways of making peace; one is by submitting quietly to the enemy’s demands. This was the Federal mode of adjusting matters with England. Every outrage and innovation of Britain, on the persons of our citizens, and the laws of nations was vindicated by renegade Americans! The Republicans took the right way of producing peace, by resisting the claims of the pirates. No man of sound mind or honest heart can withhold his execrations from the vile hirelings of Britain in America. May we soon be purged of these vipers! [Whig. SEPARATION OF THE STATES!? The Federalists not only deny that they wish for a separation of the union; but they go so far as to impute a wish so treasonable to the Republicans.

We never supposed for a moment that the federal party at large would advocate so wicked and ruinous a measure; but unfortunately the federalists at large know no more of the designs of their leaders than they do of the secret views of Bonaparte, or the Turkish Divan of Constantinople. When Pickering drank his late toast, at New York, he did not explain to his gaping auditory the allusion it evidently contained, to a separation. He did not tell them that what he said about "no dimits 3o affection" between New York and New England had a squinting at an alliance between this state and those of New England, to oppose the southern states, upon some plausible, but unfounded pretext of opposite interests; nor did Mr. Hillhouse, when he toasted, at the late federal feast in New Haven, "The state of New York; when she looks to her compass Joe will see that the needle points to the north! undertake to declare his meaning unequivocally to his deluded followers. But what man of discernment will be at a loss for the meaning of these dark and jesuitical hints at an object, which those who cherish the hope of affecting it, dare not openly avow.

To accurate observers, it is clear, as the handwriting on the wall, that some of the federal leaders, and more particularly those of the Essex Junto, aimed “at a federation of the union, and an alliance between the northern states, Canada, and Great Britain. A federal hand-bill recommending this system, has been recently published at New Haven. Independent of this fact, and the numerous proofs hostile to them; as well as which have appeared in federal toasts, and federal newspapers, we should be glad to see Christopher Gore, Timothy Pickering, Rufus King, &c. &c. come out and deny publicly that the question of dividing the union was not seriously discussed at a caucus of which they were members, and which was held at the city of New York, during the last fall. Let them say who, in that caucus advocated and who opposed any measure; whether they “were not all in favor of a division, and differed only as to the boundaries; whether one party did not propose the Potomac, another the Hudson; and whether a third did not contend for three instead of two distinct sovereignties, of which the states south of the Potomac should be one; New York and New England the other; leaving New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Delaware to form a central sovereignty, which it was thought would generally hold the balance of power, and prevent the frequent repetition of wars between the same sovereign confederacies.

To supersede the necessity of writing particularly to every person indebted to the subscriber for this or any other newspaper, he now presents one to every person of the above description (though not in form) requesting them to call at the several places where their newspapers are left, and pay the balance due. Charleston, Aug. 25, On Wednesday the 20th instant, a boat built in this place for the use of the canal between Santee and Cooper rivers, drawing three feet of water, and loaded with 20 tons of country produce, returned to Charleston from Granby. She passed through the canal both in going and returning. From the information of her patron, a similar voyage, both out and home, may be completed in 17 days, while boats using the mouth of the river cannot accomplish the same in less than six weeks, and that with great risk, and only in seasons when there is a high river. The produce of our interior country may now be conveyed to market with more certainty and much less risk, expense, and time than heretofore; and in like manner, our fellow-citizens in the country may be supplied with what they want from Charleston on much better terms than formerly. We cordially congratulate the public that this great and immensely useful work is carried through from river to river, and is so far completed as to be immediately useful, and is found by actual experiment to answer the end proposed. Philip Porter and Moses Largen (brothers-in-law) took their rifles and went in search of deer. They did not travel far together before they agreed to take separate routes. Largen approached a lick and took his stand in a convenient place to watch for game. Not much time had elapsed before he discovered a rustling in a thicket at no great distance, but could not discover the object that occasioned it. Supposing it, however, to be a deer, he fired. The shot took place. He eagerly approached the spot but oh! the shock, the heart-rending pangs which a sight of the unfortunate victim who had fallen occasioned, can more easily be imagined than described—it was Porter! his relative! his friend! his sister’s husband lay weltering in his gore! and the cold hand of death soon placed a seal upon his eyes. To add to the melancholy catastrophe, Mrs. Porter is bereaved of a fond and indulgent husband, and eight children of a tender and affectionate parent. PHILADELPHIA, Sept. 8. At 10 A.M. one league S. of Cape N. Mole, we were captured by a French barge; the mate and two of the seamen taken out, with a great part of the cargo, and a quantity of specie, and a prize master with four men put on board the schr. and ordered for Barracoa. On the 27th, 7 leagues distant from the destination, we with great trouble after having secured part below, and wounded those on deck retook the vessel. "Capt. H. in the scuffle received a wound in the hand. To get rid of a troublesome bargain, we obliged those below to make their departure in the boat under the stern, into which they lowered themselves from the cabin windows. Same day was chased by another barge, but fortunately arrived safe at this port. "American vessels are precluded from taking any produce off the Island, excepting rum and molasses, and several seizures have occurred in consequence of sugar, making a part of their cargo." Health-Office, Philadelphia, September 2. The board of Health, impressed with a sense of Gratitude to the Great Author of all our blessings: thankfully acknowledge his superintending protecting Providence, over this city, in preserving it from the Ravages of sickness of former years. And they can with peculiar satisfaction congratulate their fellow citizens, and their friends in the country, that the city is as perfectly free from sickness, as at any period within their knowledge.

To get rid of a troublesome bargain, we obliged those below to make their departure in the boat under the stern, into which they lowered themselves from the cabin windows. Same day was chased by another barge, but fortunately arrived safe at this port. "American vessels are precluded from taking any produce off the Island, excepting rum and molasses, and several seizures have occurred in consequence of sugar, making a part of their cargo." Health-Office, Philadelphia, September 2. The board of Health, impressed with a sense of Gratitude to the Great Author of all our blessings: thankfully acknowledge his superintending protecting Providence, over this city, in preserving it from the Ravages of sickness of former years. And they can with peculiar satisfaction congratulate their fellow citizens, and their friends in the country, that the city is as perfectly free from sickness, as at any period within their knowledge.

By order of the Board, ‘EDWARD GARRIGUES. BOSTON, Sept. 14. Board of Health, Baltimore, Sept. 4. ‘We have hitherto been able to trace the several cases of the prevailing fever that have occurred on the west side of Jones’s falls to Fell’s Point; but we now think it our duty to inform our fellow citizens, that within a few days past several cases of the said fever have come under the care of physicians on the west side of the falls, that cannot be traced to the Point: We therefore earnestly call upon all the inhabitants in every part of the city, to use their utmost endeavors to remove all filth from their yards and cellars, to keep their gutters constantly clean, and frequently to mix a small quantity of lime with ashes or lye and throw into their necessary; and on all public officers (whose duty it is) to be vigilant in removing all nuisances from the streets, wharves, lanes and alleys of the city, as on these endeavors may greatly depend the possibility of checking the progress of the disease.

The inhabitants are getting over their alarms, and attending to their concerns without fear of living the lower streets and wharves—yet they consider it madness for a stranger to venture himself in this place." A letter from Richmond, dated Sept. 1, 1800, says, "A very important subject now occupies the attention of the Executive. A most alarming plot of the blacks having been discovered which was to have been put in execution last night, had it not been detected—in which an undistinguished massacre of the whites was to have taken place without regard to age or sex. We are happy to add, that the leaders are taken and we have no doubt will be brought to condign punishment." Captain Cox of the brig Two Brothers, from Curacao, arrived at Baltimore, informs that the La Vengeance and General Gonnet, with his squadron of privateers and troops were still at Curacao, and the place in the greatest confusion; most of the inhabitants had left the city; those men capable of bearing arms had repaired to the garrisons; the women and children had retired to the interior parts of the island. It was expected the fate of Gonnet’s mission would be decided in a few hours; he had sent his demands to the governor two or three days previous to the Brothers sailing, some of which were understood to be—A loan of a sum of money, one of the forts to be permitted to hoist the national flag and garrisoned with French troops, to refund the proceeds of the American ship Mary, of Baltimore, condemned there as a prize, which had been lodged in the hands of government, his reasons for cutting down the French flag staff, satisfaction for the banishment of the French general—consequence of which the governor had called a council, the deliberations of which were not publicly known though it was reported that the governor was determined not to comply with their demands, let the consequence be what it would, every preparation was therefore making for resistance. How the affair may terminate, as yet remains doubtful. PORTLAND, September 8.

"SHOP BREAKING. A stranger, of a gigantic and villainous appearance, was noticed in several shops at Succarappa last Friday. His conduct, though difficult, was of that kind as to lead to a suspicion that he had some evil design. He was, in the course of the day, several times into the store of Mr. Hawes, who observing his behavior prudently determined, in company with two others, to sleep in the store. About midnight, the thief broke open the store with an iron bar, came in, and was immediately seized and imprisoned. On examination, he confessed that he had the same night broken open the store of Mr. Merrill, which was but a few rods distant; and the money which he had taken from it was recovered. Two other stores in the neighborhood had, in the course of the week, been broken open, and robbed of money, and not unlikely, by the same experienced villain. His name is not known. He has called it differently at different times. He is now lodged in gaol in this town, and will have his trial at the supreme judicial court to be holden here next week, when justice will undoubtedly be done him. SALEM, September 15. FROM INDIA. When the Bellifarius left Madras, it was expected that war would immediately commence between the English and the Mahrattas."

For this purpose large bodies of troops were marching to the interior, and reinforcements of Europeans were expected from the Cape of Good Hope. The Mahrattas are said to have from 300,000 to 400,000 cavalry—they are all soldiers, and were thought to be more dangerous enemies than Tippo had been. The people at Madras, even Europeans, gave no reasons for the war. The Mahrattas may prove a formidable enemy to the English. In order to conquer Tippo Saib, they had imprudently assisted their natural enemies, and not until it was too late, did they see their error—though the impolicy of their conduct was repeatedly represented to them by Tippo. The English now appear determined to reduce them in their turn—their former friends and allies! Pretences are never wanting, for they can easily be created, and the Governor-General, Lord Morrington, by the last accounts, was determined on hostile measures. The issue, however, may be uncertain—the Mahrattas are not a despicable enemy—they have the best cavalry in all India, and they are a brave and hardy people, not like the Asiatics in general. The English also are watching with a jealous eye the king of Ava and Pegu, and have, it is expected, serious thoughts of waging war in that quarter. The country abounds in Teak Wood, which the English are in want of for Ship Building, and cannot easily procure elsewhere.

In this State, although but few of the votes have been returned, Messrs. Foster, Tenney, Pierce, and Dunham, are undoubtedly elected. Nine towns out of ten, from which we have heard, are nearly unanimous in their favor. Mr. Tenney, it is expected, is chosen to take his seat at the next session. The Kine Pox. By letters from London, dated 18th July, we find that the Cow-Pox is progressing through the kingdom with undiminished credit, and that its being a security against the Small-pox is a matter considered established beyond all controversy. Some have entertained a suspicion that it only secures the constitution from the Small-pox for a time, but Dr. Waterhouse gives us instances of persons who were inoculated and otherwise exposed to the infection of small-pox, one thirty-one years after having the cow-pox; another thirty-six years; and above all, one FIFTY-THREE YEARS after receiving the infection. See the Doctor's treatise just published by Mr. NATUREDE, Boston. Five more of Dr. Waterhouse’s family, being four of his own children and a female domestic, who have passed through the Kine pox are now in Dr. Aspinwall’s hospital to try the experiment of inoculation for the Small-pox.

Congress of the United States. HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES. SATURDAY, Feb. 14. The House proceeded to the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd ballot for President, but the result was invariably 8 for Jefferson, 6 for Burr, two divided. The further balloting was adjourned until Monday, 12 o’clock. A letter from the Secretary of the Treasury was received; but was not read. After the 30th ballot, a motion was made to postpone the next ballot to the 2nd March; which was rejected unanimously by the States. Monday, Feb. 16. The House proceeded to the 34th ballot, The result the same as before. Next ballot postponed until tomorrow, at 12 o’clock, Tuesday, Feb. 17. The House proceeded to the 35th ballot for President. The result the same as before. At one o’clock the 36th ballot was taken, which issued in the election of THOMAS JEFFERSON. After the declaration of the choice, a bill for declaring all letters received by or written to JOHN ADAMS, free of postage, was twice read. European Intelligence, By the British Packet Harlequin, arrived at New-York, from Falmouth, and brought London papers to the 14th of December. The following is a concise abridgment of their contents. ABSTRACT OF NEWS. Accounts from Italy say hostilities were to be recommenced on the 23rd of November. The French Army had made preparatory movements.

European Intelligence, By the British Packet Harlequin, arrived at New-York, from Falmouth, and brought London papers to the 14th of December. The following is a concise abridgment of their contents. ABSTRACT OF NEWS. Accounts from Italy say hostilities were to be recommenced on the 23rd of November. The French Army had made preparatory movements.

The Emperor of Germany has proposed to the French to evacuate Tuscany, but they have declined the measure. Hopes are entertained in Switzerland that that country will be declared neutral by a convention of the belligerent powers. Commotions still exist in that country. The French funds have lately risen. The British funds advanced on the news of Moreau’s victory, as an event leading to peace. The Austrian funds have fallen. It is stated with some confidence that an armed confederacy between Russia, Prussia, Sweden and Denmark, was signed at Petersburg, about the 14th of November. The King of Prussia is to superintend the operations on land, and the other powers those by sea. A Russian fleet is preparing to cruise in the spring. Lord Keith, commander of the English fleet in the Mediterranean, has been ordered to watch the Russians in that sea, and to assist the Turks, if attacked. The Hamburg and Lubeck merchants are afraid their English bills on Russia will be protested. Many failures would be caused thereby. The King of Denmark has presented an elegant sword to the captain of his frigate who opposed the English in attempting to search the vessels under his convoy. The Prussians in the vicinity of Hamburg conduct in an orderly manner, and treat the English with respect. An armistice between the French general in Egypt and the Grand Vizier is reported.

New-London, Feb. 6. The expense incurred in the state of Virginia, in carrying into effect the laws for electing a President and Vice-President of the United States at the two last elections, amounted to—dollars 2427 16. A bill has passed the legislature of New Jersey, authorizing certain persons to build a dam across Great Egg-Harbour River—Yeas 60—Nays 3. By a statement, the value of the real and personal estates within the state of New York, as assessed under a law, for raising a sum of money for the state, amounts to one hundred and six million, 268,295 dollars. Several American vessels within this week past have been carried into St. Martins, but were immediately liberated. Boston, Feb. 25. LATEST FROM FRANCE. By the Governor Strong, from Malaga, we received Paris papers to the 9th December. By them it appears that the re-commencement of hostilities between the French and Austrian main armies took place about the beginning of December, at Hohenlinden, in the circle of Bavaria, in Germany.

The French army was commanded by Moreau; but we do not learn who commanded the Austrians; who were defeated, according to Moreau’s account, with the loss of 80 pieces of artillery, and 10,000 prisoners. Hostilities had also commenced on the Lower Rhine, near Affenhaufen. An article from Milan of the 27th November, mentions, that the armies of Italy were in fight of each other; and great events were momently expected. The Prussian troops have extended the line of demarcation so as to include Cuxhaven or the Elbe, and a part of the mouth of the Weser:—But the King has assured the Senate of Hamburg, that he will not infringe upon their privileges. The French and Dutch governments have taken efficient measures to prevent the exportation of every sort of grain to Great-Britain. And a Paris article of the 7th December, says, the Pacific Congress still continued in session at Luneville; and that the Austrian and French Ministers were continually dispatching messengers to their respective courts. The Archduke Charles is to command the Austrian armies;—with which the Emperor will be present, in person. Feb. 26. CONFIRMATION.

Mr. Burr has written to General S. Smith, and Gen. Dayton, declaring he would not come in President by the influence of the federal party; as it would destroy his purposes.—He has been duped by the democrats.” M’Clay one of the Virginia delegation, tarried the whole of Thursday night at the Capitol, with 12 armed men; to prevent, as he says, a meeting of the federalist there that evening, though such a measure was never, as I have heard, contemplated. So we go. If Jefferson is elected, it may be attributed to these three causes—disgust of some of the federal members; the foes of others; and to the misconduct of Burr.” The democratic paper of the city of Washington says that a memorial to Mr. Thomas to vote for Mr. Jefferson ‘‘was signed by the most respectable federal gentlemen of the city.” It is an important fact, that in all the ballots in Congress, except the first, the individual votes were 53 for Mr. Burr, and 50 for Mr. JEFFERSON. The Hon. Uriah Tracey, has been appointed a Senator of the United States, from the 3rd March next, by the Executive of Connecticut, during the recess of the Legislature thereof. PORTSMOUTH, March 3. Between the hours of three and four last Sunday afternoon, the inhabitants of this town were very much alarmed with the shock of an earthquake, which lasted about two minutes. At the annual meeting held in this town on Monday, the Hon. Woodbury Langdon, Esq. presided as Moderator; the votes were for Governor: His Excellency John T. Gilman, Esq. 101, Hon. Timothy Walker, Esq. 447, Hon. John Langdon, Esq. 2. Councillor: Hon. Joseph Blanchard, Esq. 6, Levi Bartlett, Esq. 446. Senator: Thomas Leavitt, Esq. 94, John Coppard, Esq. 436, Hon. Woodbury Langdon, Esq. 4. County Treasurer: Oliver Peabody, Esq. 100, Josiah Adams, Esq. 443. Recorder of Deeds: Nathaniel Parker, Esq. 102, Josiah Adams, Esq. 445, Samuel Brooks, Esq. Representatives: Hon. John Langdon, Esq., John S. Sherburne, Esq., Col. Clement Storer, and Henry S. Langdon, Esq. COW POX. Extract of a letter from Doctor Lettsom of London to Doctor Barton of Philadelphia. "Vaccine inoculation is becoming more and more general in England and on the European continent. About 16,000 have had the disease, if disease it can be termed, without any case of fatality, and about 3000 have been inoculated again with the common smallpox, without conveying the disease, so that probably soon, no other than the cowpox will be adopted here. I imagine a fatal case will never occur, as there is rarely more than one pustule."

The careless of bad men resemble the fawning of a greyhound, which, while he shows his love, fouls you with his paws. We should never despise people for want of natural parts but for making a wrong use of them; thus, if a man walks lame, he is to be pitied; if he dances lame, he is to be laughed at. A head, like a house, when crammed too full, and no regular order observed in the placing what is in it, is only littered, instead of being furnished. There is a great difference between praying and saying one’s prayers. Obstinate people are never so much so, as when they are in the wrong. Of all brutes, none are so very brutish as human brutes. We sometimes feel what we fear, much more than what we really suffer. Hard to be pleased, and easy to be displeased, is an odious character. The meanest way of praising ourselves is finding fault with others. Marine Intelligence. Sunday arrived sloop Enterprise, capt. Shaw, 21 days from St. Vincents—left there the brig Eagle, capt. Rollins, to sail middle of March—capt. Fernald sailed from there in a schooner for Grenada the 4th February. Yesterday arrived the brig Alligator, capt. Wednesday, January 30, 1810, Although advertising friends occupy so large a portion of our paper, it has not been in our power to gratify our readers with much political matter as they wished—The people look with interest to the speeches of their Representatives in Congress.—on Mr. Giles' resolutions the opposition have been remarkably voluble—The speeches of the AMERICAN party they could not answer— but, in imitation of the men whom they supported, they enveloped themselves in such a wilderness of words, that many who have long consented to walk blindfold in the leading strings of federalism, rather tacitly assented that they were right, than felt convinced that they were so—and could not or would not explore a fertile waste where nothing but deformity met the mental eye. SUPPLEMENT TO THE NEW-HAMPSHIRE GAZETTE. Wednesday, January 30, 1810, Although advertising friends occupy so large a portion of our paper, it has not been in our power to gratify our readers with much political matter as they wished—The people look with interest to the speeches of their Representatives in Congress.—on Mr. Giles' resolutions the opposition have been remarkably voluble—The speeches of the AMERICAN party they could not answer— but, in imitation of the men whom they supported, they enveloped themselves in such a wilderness of words, that many who have long consented to walk blindfold in the leading strings of federalism, rather tacitly assented that they were right, than felt convinced that they were so—and could not or would not explore a fertile waste where nothing but deformity met the mental eye. Mr. Macon, though a decided REPUBLICAN, did not favor the resolutions, and finally voted against them—But he did join the abandoned men who supported Jackson, and condemned their own government—and for no other reason, as can be discerned from their most labored speeches and tirades on the subject, than that it was a collision between an agent of the British, and the American government. The following are extracts from Mr. Macon's speech, in the debate on Mr. Giles' resolutions.

“Mr. Macon said that it appeared to him, the first point for consideration in the resolution ought to be, is it expedient; but it seemed to him that those who had taken part in the debate had looked at everything but the resolution; and he should probably follow the example. The dismissal of a foreign minister is no new case in the country—Genet was dismissed, Yrujo was dismissed, and no bad consequence followed, and why should any be anticipated because Jackson has been dismissed? I will not trouble the committee with reading any part of the documents, they must be tired of hearing parts of them already, and every member has surely read them with attention, beside the nation has them, and will decide on them, without our assistance; to me it appears on a fair examination of his letters, that he was properly dismissed. Permit me, to notice an argument of the gentleman from Connecticut, (Mr. Dana) relative to the disavowal by the British government; if the ground he frames be true, his argument is unanswerable. If I misstate him, I wish he would correct me, because I have no desire to do it; I understood him to say that Mr. Erskine had no full power to do what he did, and that the administration ought or must have known it; I believe, sir, it is as difficult to decide."

In this House, it is well known that I was as much opposed to the motion last spring as I am now to this, and intended to have delivered my sentiments upon it, but was prevented by the House not deciding on it. Why did not the gentleman then come forward and tell us that this boasted arrangement was all nothing? For in the whole correspondence, which was then laid before us, there is not a word about full powers; in fact, the British government in the disavowal has not made this objection; nor has it called the arrangement a treaty; both governments and every man in both countries understood it to be not a treaty, but only an agreement by which the United States engaged to withdraw the operation of a certain law as to Great Britain, provided Great Britain would withdraw her orders in council; both engaged to do certain things, and the United States fairly performed their part. If the President was to blame, the blame does not begin with him; it begins with congress, because congress passed the law, which authorized him to do as he did. He was authorized to suspend the operation of the embargo act, provided France or Great Britain should do certain things.

If the arrangement be a treaty, then Congress passed a law to authorize the President to make a treaty; and if Congress could constitutionally pass a law delegating the power to make treaties. If the President objected, of — "waived" the objections, the nation said to him "well done." If the British government had not disapproved the arrangement and the President and Mr. Jackson differed, we never should in my opinion have heard a word about this want of full power in Erskine, it would not have been thought of. I confess, sir, I have been most egregiously disappointed, since the debate on the resolutions commenced. I did not believe before, that there was a man in the nation who thought the administration hostile to an amicable adjustment of all our disputes with Great Britain, or who could read Mr. Jackson's first letter without feeling the insult offered in that. In that letter he intended either to insult the administration, to laugh at it, or if you please to humbug it.

If the arrangement be a treaty, then Congress passed a law to authorize the President to make a treaty; and if Congress could constitutionally pass a law delegating the power to make treaties. If the President objected, of — "waived" the objections, the nation said to him "well done." If the British government had not disapproved the arrangement and the President and Mr. Jackson differed, we never should in my opinion have heard a word about this want of full power in Erskine, it would not have been thought of. I confess, sir, I have been most egregiously disappointed, since the debate on the resolutions commenced. I did not believe before, that there was a man in the nation who thought the administration hostile to an amicable adjustment of all our disputes with Great Britain, or who could read Mr. Jackson's first letter without feeling the insult offered in that. In that letter he intended either to insult the administration, to laugh at it, or if you please to humbug it.

The embargo, which the gentleman from New York (Mr. Gold) has brought into the debate, produced the arrangement, and the repealing of it the disavowal. At the last session I had notes, with which I thought I could then defend the embargo, and made several attempts to do it, but somehow or other was always prevented. I was then willing to have undertaken it against talents a hundred to one my superior. Gentlemen may laugh, but it is certainly true that by repealing the embargo they gave their party a severe blow, and did the country great injury. The repeal I too was not made until the house had declared that to repeal the embargo and not go to war would be submission; notwithstanding all this, on the question to authorize the President to issue forthwith letters of marque and reprisal, only seventeen voted in the affirmative. The British government sent Mr. Oakley here with instructions, under the firm belief, as I conceive, that the 'embargo' was in force, and had Mr. Erskine, after receiving the instructions, instead of obeying them as he did, informed his government of the great change which had taken place here, he would not believe have been disgraced, but ennobled. The instructions were larger than the change.

The embargo alone, is not worth the hair after being cut—of the head of Sampson. It has had the effect expected—it has operated upon ourselves, and nobody else, and scarcely on ourselves; for no one, I believe, regards it. I have seen letters from England, written as I was told, by respectable men, which stated that the people of England could not have stood the embargo three months longer, and that they were determined to stand it as long as possible; because if they yielded to it, we obtained a victory in a way that would always put them in our power. The nation was prepared to continue the embargo agreeably to the votes of this house. We had made the stand, and ought to have adhered to it. We then solemnly pledged ourselves to the nation, but we did not mind that; we unpledged ourselves with great ease, and I am unwilling to make any pledge to the Executive whatever. It is a little remarkable, that this question about full powers has never been started before either in this country or England.

The Congress, in which he informs us that Jackson had been dismissed and you will not find a single expression in it, that looks as if he was not sincerely desirous to settle our differences with all the world; if there be such an expression I will thank gentlemen to point it out. - After mentioning the disavowal, and the breaking off of the negotiation, does he not plainly tell you, that he is still for another attempt to settle by negotiation! Every part of the message breathes a spirit friendly to the peaceable settlement of all our disputes; according to my understanding it speaks of nothing but peace, not a word to be found in it advising a warlike attitude; no advice to increase the army or navy. It is strange, indeed, that after reading such a message, it should be thought that there was a hostility in the administration to an amicable settlement with Great Britain. - Sir, I have believed (and I hope in God I am mistaken, for no man is more desirous of peace than I am) from the time of the attack on the Chesapeake, that before our differences are settled with England, we should be compelled to go to war with her; for one I would put it off as long as possible.

It will be remembered that the embargo was supported as the only means to keep us out of this war, and as a sure means to bring G. Britain to fair terms; and I believe as much as I do that we shall all die, if it had been continued three months longer, we should have settled every dispute with the English government. The conversations of Mr. Pinkney and Mr. Canning communicated by the President to the house at their request, have been brought into the debate. Unfortunately, from N. York, (Ms. Gold) who mentioned the embargo, he stated a part of them. I am willing to read the policy of that measure on that of the Rights in, the embargo is mentioned. It seems to be the first and the last word with him. If there be a man clear of party feeling, let him read the conversations between Mr. Pinkney & Mr. Canning, and if he does not decide that the embargo was a bitter pill to Mr. Canning, I am greatly mistaken. That we suffered a little under the embargo was never denied; but, adopt what measure you will, that will have half the effect on England that that had, and we shall suffer.

It is the easiest thing in nature to say what you will not do, but it is quite different to say what you will do. Before I sit down, I must ask the gentlemen for the proof, that the Executive is unwilling to settle our disputes with Great Britain by friendly negotiation. The assertion has astonished me. His message of the 29th November, is to my mind complete proof to the contrary; his not treating with Jackson is no proof, because the gentlemen themselves would not have treated with him on the terms proposed; his sending him away is no proof, because he has declared himself ready to treat with any other agent that the British government may appoint. Jackson I believe came, like Rose, to settle no dispute whatever, and if no one would consent to treat with him on the ground proposed by Mr. Canning, what use could there be in his staying here? I cannot conceive any at all. For one I sincerely wish, that no foreign minister were ever to put his foot on our shore, unless sent for some special and particular purpose, and to return immediately after he had completed his business, and so with our ministers. I had rather give one 50,000 dollars for a trip of this kind than 9,000 dollars a year to reside at a foreign court.

If Mr. Jackson was authorized to do anything, it was to reiterate proposals which had been rejected, and which he must have known before he left England, would be again rejected. However, it seems, instead of making proposals to satisfy us for the wrongs and injuries done to us, he politely waited for the administration to make proposals to him. The case of the Executive and Jackson has been compared to common life—an unfortunate comparison. I am sure no case in private life can be found, where the injured party was told—give me your terms, after you have done this, I am willing to talk to you about them. The United States are the injured party, and Great Britain ought in justice to make the propositions for accommodation. However, I would not myself stand on this, so that we could anyhow have our differences fairly settled. Carry this individual comparison to a single case, that one man should without provocation give another a blow in the face—ought the man who received the blow to ask pardon? If he did, every man in the world would think him a very great fool or something worse.

Here then is another obvious advantage in favor of the independence of the judges of the United States; whence is it then, that we hear of the independence of the English judiciary, as being the boast and glory of that country, and with justice too, and at the same time, hear the cry of the immolation of the independence of the judges of the United States; when under the interpretation of the constitution by the favorers of the repeal, the judges here are more independent than the English judges? It can have no other object than to excite a popular clamor, which, if excited at all, can have only a momentary effect, and will be dissipated as soon as the subject shall be thoroughly examined and understood.

The Naturalization bill was read the 3rd time, when the 4th section was recommitted to a committee of the whole. Two engrossed bills, "For the accommodation of persons concerned in certain fisheries therein mentioned;" and, for rebuilding the light houses on Gurnet Point, and at the Eastern end of New-Castle Island; and for erecting a light house on Lynde's Point—were read a third time and passed. "Resolved, That a committee be appointed to inquire into the expediency of providing for the settlement of the claims to the lands held by settlers and traders at Detroit, under the British Treaty. The Senate informed the House they have disagreed to the Act to allow a drawback of duties on goods exported to New-Orleans, etc.—and that they have also postponed to the next session the act for the relief of Philip Sloan. The Senate returned the "Act for fixing the military establishment"—with several amendments, with some of which the House concurred, and with others non-concurrence. TUESDAY, MARCH 9. The Naturalization Bill was read a third time, and passed. WEDNESDAY, MARCH 10. A resolution was offered for adjourning the two Houses on the second Monday in April, when it was moved to postpone the consideration of it until the 4th Monday of March, which, after debate, was carried—Yeas 46—Nays 43.

Mr. Griswold laid the following motion in substance, on the table - P H Resolved, That it is proper to make provision by law towards indemnifying the merchants of the United States for French spoliations, so far as claims for the same have been abandoned by the convention with France. Ordered to lie on the table. FRIDAY, MARCH 12. Mr. Griswold moved that the House go into committee of the whole on the resolution laid by him yesterday on the table for indemnifying for French spoliations. Motion lost without debate—Yeas 35—Nays 60. Dr. Leib reported from a committee appointed to take order in relation to the funeral of Nathworthy Hunter, delegate from the Mississippi Territory, who died last evening, and whose decease had been announced to the House, that it would be proper for the House to attend the funeral tomorrow at twelve o’clock. Agreed to—and information thereof directed to be given to the Senate.

On motion of Mr. Thomas, the House resolved itself into a committee of the whole on the bill for the extinction of state balances—Mr. Varoum in the chair. On the principle of this bill a debate ensued, in which the extinction of the balances was supported by Messrs. Thomas, Randolph, Van Rensselaer, Hill, Van Ness, Gregg, Bayard, Smilie, Macon, S. Smith, Claiborne, and Holland—and opposed by Messrs. Elmer, Bacon, Eustis, Hastings, and Butler. In this debate the usual field of argument, which has been so frequently displayed, was gone into. Our limits do not admit of a detailed notice of the ideas and facts urged. Nor does such a detail appear necessary, as we presume the subject to be familiar to the minds of most of our readers. It may be proper, however, to state the new ground taken by Mr. Thomas, who contended that the rule on which the debts of the several states had been apportioned was an unjust one.

He hated that under the confederation the basis of contribution was land; and that it would have been just that the apportionment of debts incurred during the war should have been in the ratio of the then existing numbers in each state, and not in the ratio of the numbers of the states subsequent thereto. That according to the numbers in the states in the year 1787, or the close of the war, a result very different from that arising from the rule established by the commissioners, viz. — the numbers existing in 1791, would have been formed. Mr. Thomas particularized the varying results derived from the relative numbers in the years 1784, and 1791; and stated that according to the former, New-York instead of being debtor for 2 millions, would be a creditor state for 800,000 dollars. The question was then taken on the committee rising, and reporting the bill without amendment, and carried — Yeas 47 — Nays 33. A motion was then made that the bill be engrossed for a third reading on Tuesday, and carried — Yeas 47 — Nays 35. A motion was then made by Dr. Leib, to recommit the report of the select committee on which the above bill was founded, in order to correct an erroneous statement in relation to Pennsylvania. Carried — Ayes 65 — Noes 67. An end.

The internal taxes, whatever they might be, their wisest, they did not venture until, without the advice of Mr. Jefferson, to make perpetual. Those taxes were temporary; some of them would have ceased to this day, had not the desire of the party to preserve the trappings of monarchy indulged them to pass the law of the 4th of February 1801, by which they were made permanent. To satisfy the public that the design of the opposition in objecting to the repeal of the internal taxes, was solely to embarrass government and not to relieve the poor, who, while they fret it with moderation, are as much comforted by spirits as by tea or sugar; it is proper to examine their conduct while in power, a little more minutely. Instead of lessening the duties on these articles, at the month of February 1797, when they had the benefit of their knowledge of the operation of the duties for more than six years, they increased them. Every member of congress from Connecticut (including Griswold and Dana), every member from New-Hampshire, and every member present from Massachusetts (excepting Wm. Lyman) voted in favor of that measure. At the same session, a law was passed granting relief to distillers, by removing the duty from the amount of spirits and fixing it on the capacity of the still. Every member from the states of New-Hampshire, Massachusetts and Connecticut, voted in favor of this law.

The following appears from the Journals of Congress. Here, people of New England, is a just view of your representatives, who would induce you to believe that the government of the country was sacrificing its interests at the shrine of Virginia’s ambition. It has been said that sound policy required the application of these taxes to the discharge of the national debt. To this it is answered—maintain the economical establishment, the surplus funds arising from the remaining revenues will pay the debt as soon as Congress have by law a right to pay it, and the exorbitant expense of collecting the excise will be avoided. It has been said by opposition that these taxes are repealed and the duties on imported articles continued with a view to destroy commerce. Let the commercial interest reflect. There is not an additional cent imposed on commerce. As the taxes of the nation are lessened, the ability of the people to pay is increased. Let it be reminded with what promptitude the trade of the Mediterranean was protected. The government has completed a treaty with Great Britain, whereby our merchants are enabled to recover their lost property, and continue in the enjoyment of commercial enterprise—above all, that government relying solely on commerce for her revenue stands pledged by interest, the strongest of all ties, to cherish and support it.

Docsa debior forfeit all claims of confidence by uniting rigid economy with a constant attention to business. Congress have repealed the act passed in February 1801, establishing six new circuit courts, and limiting the labors of the judges of the supreme court to the holding of two sessions in a year at the seat of government; and by another act have remedied the evils of the former system, by specifying the districts in which each judge of the supreme court should hold a circuit court, & dispensing with one session of the supreme court; by this they have effected an annual saving of 3,000 dollars, and abolished sixteen useless offices. This measure was objected to, both as unconstitutional and impolitic. As to the constitutionality of the measure, the distinction exists between the supreme and the subordinate courts. The former is created by the constitution, the latter by, & subject to, legislative discretion. One may be abolished; the other cannot. The objection that this doctrine destroys the judicial department, by engulfing it in the vortex of gun'y is unfounded. The judges are not subject to the will of the executive, or even of the legislature. No new system is established, by which a new corps of judges is created. The administration of justice is entrusted, as it has heretofore been, to the judges of the supreme court, whose independence has not been affected, or ever controverted.

The administration of justice is entrusted, as it has heretofore been, to the judges of the supreme court, whose independence has not been affected, or ever controverted.

As to the sufficiency of an annual supreme court, it cannot be doubted, when it is known that for ten years that court decided but forty-three cases, and that at its last session the dockets consisted of eight only, three of which were decided. Assuming the fact that there will be neither a greater or less number of causes before the supreme court for 10 years to come than there was for the first ten years after its establishment, and there appears no reasonable ground on which to calculate for an increase of business; it is easy to see what the comparison was between the services to be rendered and the compensation made according to the provision of the act repealed at the last session of congress. The salaries allowed by law to the judges of that court amount annually to the 11,500 dollars, of course in ten years to 215,000 dollars. The salaries of the clerks for the same time is 2,300 dollars. Total amount of salaries for ten years is 217,300 dollars. In the course of ten years forty-three causes only were decided, as appears by the reports of Dallas.

By this it is manifest that under the last federal judiciary system, which was repealed at the last session of congress, the people of the United States would pay more than five thousand and fifty-three dollars for each decision. Does that man exist who will say the public money should be thus squandered? A revision of the laws relating to naturalization has also taken place. The 2nd of 1798 is repealed, and the former law revised, by which a residence of five years entitles a foreigner of good conduct and reputation to the rights of citizenship. The justice due to a large number of people who emigrated under the faith of existing laws, and the policy of opening the wilderness and acquiring the arts and manufactures of Europe required this revision. It is only a revival of the Washington system. Congress have continued to the officers residing at the seat of government the compensation they enjoyed under the act of 1799. This has been the subject of much newspaper abuse; it has been falsely represented as an augmentation of salaries. The government has been charged with a departure from economical principles, and those gentlemen who supported the measure but opposed the grant in 1799, have been charged with inconsistency.

The charges will not be accredited, when it is known the expense of living is considerably higher at the seat of government than at Philadelphia, To prove this fact it is only necessary to resort to the acts of the late federal, and of the last session of congress. The act of 1799 ascertained as well the compensation of the clerks of the officers. When the offices were removed to Washington the increased expense of living rendered it necessary to augment the compensation of the clerks, They were accordingly increased fifteen per cent. The act allowing them fifteen per cent. expired last winter—it was revived—here is the concurrent testimony of both parties uniting in this proposition, there is a difference of fifteen per cent in the price of living. To cover this difference of expenditure the salaries of 1799 were established for two years, In fact there was not a member of the opposition who contended the salaries were too high. To facilitate the progress of information, and private intercourse an increased expenditure of the revenue of the general post office has been authorized, both to ensure the more safe and expeditious transportation of the mails and to extend the benefits of the establishment to the inhabitants residing upon or near almost sixty new established post roads. It was proposed to remove the postage from newspapers.

The danger of retarding the progress of the mails, and destroying country presses, prevented the adoption of this measure. This postage is not a tax. It does not amount to one-fourth part of the monies expended in their conveyance by government. In addition to these measures, the compensations of the collectors of the revenue have been reduced. This has effected an annual saving of about 17,000 dollars. The prompt and ready payment of the public monies, and the eventual responsibility of the officers of government, have been secured by annex declaring, that each bond shall be a lien on the real estates of both principal and surety, and shall be renewed once in four years. The object of every grant of money has been specified with accuracy and precision to ensure its just application, and to limit the powers of executive officers as far as possible. The danger of war with the savages has been removed by providing for a general establishment of our boundary lines, and for a due regulation of the intercourse between this nation and their tribes. And lastly—The people of the territory northwest of the river have been elevated to the rank of freemen and the consequent blessings of self-government, by an act authorizing them to call a convention, form a constitution, organize a government, and become a member of the union.

A view to pay only those who are actively employed, has been produced a further saving of $89,000 by Congress—by reducing a part of the army $582,000—by reducing a part of the navy $200,000—by repealing the whole system of internal taxation, there has been saved to the people out of the fees of the excise officers $135,000 dols. over and above the sum necessary to defray the collections of imposts to an amount equal to the whole revenue derived from internal taxation; it being the difference between the expenses of the two systems $135,000. By abolishing the late judicial system and establishing the former system $3,000—by reducing the commission of the collectors of customs, say $17,000—Total amount of Dols. 1,107,695 91" Annual savings one million one hundred and seven thousand six hundred and ninety-five dollars and ninety-one cents. The benefit of the reduction of expenditure will be more felt and appreciated by all classes when they know that these annual savings exceed the whole expense of all the state governments in the union, so that in a pecuniary point of view, they are more than equal to bestowing upon the people free from expense the whole benefits of state government.
