The following is a statement of the annual expenditures of the several states: New-Hampshire expends yearly $38,000 Massachusetts $60,000 Connecticut $45,000 Vermont $25,000 Rhode-Island $6,000 New-York $130,000 New-Jersey $35,000 Pennsylvania $150,000 Delaware $11,000 Maryland $289,000 Virginia $2,156,000 North Carolina $85,000 South Carolina $150,000 Kentucky $50,000 Tennessee $10,000 Georgia $42,000 Total, one million and six thousand dollars, $1,006,000 Which deducted from the aforesaid reductions leaves the sum of 47,695 dollars and 91 cents. The excess of the reductions beyond the whole expense of the state governments. The statement of state expenditures is not accurate, it is substantially true, and it is believed that the gross amount is equal to the expenditure of the whole states: The reader will reflect that in those states where the expenditures are small, the relief to the people is annually much greater than the expenses of their state government. Pursuing the same system of policy for twelve years, the period of time between the commencement of the present government and the close of Adams' administration, would, upon the principle that money is worth an annual interest of six per cent, exceed the amount of monies drawn from the people by taxation, the sum of eighteen million six hundred and eighty-six thousand seven hundred and.

Supported by the contents of Foreign journals, it appears the French Minister at Constantinople had dispatches of great importance; that the English Minister at Vienna received a messenger from Constantinople with dispatches of great importance also; the Grand Seignior and the Divan, expected the ultimatum of England with impatience, as it was reported Austria and Russia had agreed to seize upon her Western Provinces, which are in a state of anarchy; that the Archduke Charles had called from his hermitage, Field Marshal Cobourg, and is busily engaged with him in organizing the army; that the Austrian troops in Hungary are in motion; and their designs of seizing upon several Turkish Provinces is no longer doubtful; that 24,000 men in Transylvania alone; that numerous Austrian armies are assembling in Eastern Galicia to seize Moldavia; and that corps of troops are on the frontiers of Bosnia and Servia, which are to co-operate with Russian troops destined to take possession of the Turkish towns of Bender and Aikaman, While these formidable measures are pursuing against the Turks, they are embroiled with the English on account of the massacre of the Beys. The Turkish empire left alone, and attacked as it will be by all the great military powers of Europe, must fall; Bonaparte will then obtain his objects, Egypt and Greece, in defiance of the British Marine!

Marquis Cornwallis and suite arrived at London from Amiens on the 9th March. The dissolution of the British Parliament is again talked of. A PROCLAMATION: By his Excellency Thomas Picton, Esq. Brigadier General of his Majesty's Forces, Governor and Commander in Chief of the island of Trinidad, and its Dependencies, etc. IT. being made clearly to appear, by the representation of the Planters, Inhabitants, etc., that there still exists a scarcity of all articles of PROVISION absolutely necessary for the support of the slaves employed in carrying on the cultivation of the Island; and that the arrival of new settlers, and the daily importation of slaves from the other islands, operate to increase an evil, which already gives cause to serious alarm: And, it appearing, on strict investigation, that the quantity of Rum and Molasses manufactured in the Island, is far insufficient for the payment of the necessary supplies of these essential articles: I have thought fit to issue this my Proclamation, To publish and declare, that it shall be lawful for vessels, the property of the subjects of the United States of America, coming directly from the said States, with Provisions and Lumber of all kinds, the growth and produce of that country, to take and receive in exchange to the exact value of their respective cargoes, and no more, the following articles, viz. Sugar, Rum and Molasses.

Isaac Tuoms, Esq., Barza Haywarp, Daniel Snowaudhenezr WarRen, Esquires. Counties of Lincoln, Hancock, Washington and Kennebeck, Hon. Nathaniel Dummer & John Chandler, Esqrs. The Hon. Messrs. Frye, Thomson, Haywarp & Dunmer were chosen. A report was received from the committee appointed to examine the returns of votes for Governor and Lieutenant Governor. It stated, that the whole number of votes for Governor was 49583, of which His Excellency CALEB STRONG had 2998, and is chosen; That the whole number of votes for Lieutenant Governor was 46386, of which His Honor EDWARD H. ROBBINS had 8317, and is chosen. By an arrival at New York, from Cape Francois, intelligence has been received, that some days after the negotiation between Leclerc and Christophe, a decisive engagement took place between the French and Toussaint's troops; in which the former were victorious:—Toussaint then proposed to capitulate on honorable terms; but Leclerc demanded an unconditional submission;—to which the black General, and Dessalines, were at last obliged to submit. Toussaint is to remain on his own plantation, until orders respecting him are received from Bonaparte; and his troops were proceeding to the plantations, to labor as cultivators—Gen. Boudet, on invitation of Pelage, had sailed from St. Domingo, with some troops, to take possession of Guadaloupe. Bill of Mortality. DIED— At Mount-Vernon, on the 22nd ult., Mrs.

Then rose up Cerinthus and said unto them, though it is true that Paul teaches that Christ is God, yet I will pledge my honor that I can bring more arguments against the doctrine than he can for it. 11. Now when he had thus spoken, they all took new courage, hoping that their united exertions would not be in vain. 12. And they cast him out notwithstanding all his pretended zeal for the honor of Christ. 17. Now when Cerenthius saw that he was cast out, and that his doctrine was cast out with him, he was filled with wrath, and said unto them, 18. I am determined to be revenged on thee for thy cruel treatment, and that my doctrine shall be spread in the world. 19. And he went unto Anti-Christ, and said unto him, these men are endeavoring to overthrow the government, for I have heard them say that CHRIST is not only a God, but that he is a King, and a great high Priest. 20. And they have also said, that as a King, he has all power in heaven and in earth. 21. They likewise say that Christ will reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet, and if this is true, we must submit among the rest. 22. Now when Anti-Christ heard this, he was filled with astonishment, and said unto them that stood by him, 23. The doctrine of CHRIST has spread much faster since we began to oppose it, than it did when we killed his followers. 24.

"RLI R T VSRR 1 T B R R JUST PUBLISHED, ARTICLES of Faith & Church Building, Written by Elder E. SMITH, and adopted by a number of Elders and Brethren, who compose the Christian Conference. This little book is earnestly recommended to the perusal of all who are desirous of knowing the Primitive Apostolic Order of Church Building, order and discipline. — And may be purchased at the respective Book-stores of C. PEIRCE, and of N. S. & W. PEIRCE, in Buck-street. Price 7d. ALSO— just received from London, and now re-published, and for sale as above, Dr. Jenkins’ masterly reply to Mr. Peter Edwards. Entitled, A Defence of the Baptists, against the aspersions and misrepresentations of Mr. Peter Edwards, late Pastor at Portsea, Hants, in his book, entitled Candid Reasons, &c. &c. Dr. Jenkins says, "I have deliberately perused Mr. Edwards’ book, but as to the word Candid, I found no traces of it, or pretensions to it, except in the title page. But candor ought to be the vehicle in which truth is brought to light; and I think Mr. Edwards would have better recommended this work, if, while he studied Paedobaptism, he had studied also that charity which suff ereth long, and is kind, vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up, not easily provoked, &c, &c." It is hoped every person who has read Dr. O. alias Peter Edwards’ book, will also read this. Portsmouth, Jan. 18.

Boards and Joists. Portsmouth, Jan. 11, 1803. A SPECULATION. To be sold, for fifteen hundred dollars, a valuable lot of LAND, on which there were two buildings before the late fire, that would rent for 300 dollars a year, situated on the north side of Daniel-street, only 6 rods east of the corners of Market and Court-streets; containing an excellent well of water, which was never known to fail; a branch of the Aqueduct, cellar walls, Pavements, Bricks, &c. &c. The lot being nearly 120 feet deep, cannot be injured by widening the street. But, it is conceived, its value will be enhanced, if the plan of the Selectmen is carried into effect.—Inquire of the Printers. Jan. 18. A SCHOOL. Mr. George Grey Osborne, proposes opening a School, at the dwelling-house of Mrs. Elizabeth Brown, in Washington-street, for teaching Arithmetic, & Navigation only; where punctual attendance will be given, and favors gratefully acknowledged.

To be sold, for fifteen hundred dollars, a valuable lot of LAND, on which there were two buildings before the late fire, that would rent for 300 dollars a year, situated on the north side of Daniel-street, only 6 rods east of the corners of Market and Court-streets; containing an excellent well of water, which was never known to fail; a branch of the Aqueduct, cellar walls, Pavements, Bricks, &c. &c. The lot being nearly 120 feet deep, cannot be injured by widening the street. But, it is conceived, its value will be enhanced, if the plan of the Selectmen is carried into effect.—Inquire of the Printers. Jan. 18. A SCHOOL. Mr. George Grey Osborne, proposes opening a School, at the dwelling-house of Mrs. Elizabeth Brown, in Washington-street, for teaching Arithmetic, & Navigation only; where punctual attendance will be given, and favors gratefully acknowledged.

THE subscriber having determined to go to Paris, as soon as possible, in order to obtain payment of a large demand against the Republic, laid in before the proper Board some years ago; informs all Merchants and others, who have demands against the French Government, that he would gladly assist in their recovery, uniting his endeavors with those of the American Consul, or any Agent already appointed— By being on the spot, he is persuaded, that he can do more toward expediting a settlement, than can be done, merely by writing and employing a person residing there. For works thus approv’d, thus highly regarded, Well may all things be courted but loss! Man’s sentence reversed, and Jesus rewarded, Speak peace to the vile from the cross. Here then let us boast; here’s hope, a sure balm. For Him who's alive evermore. For hope built on self, no longer let’s canker; But trusting on God, and adore. No wisdom turns from His work all divine, On the billows of error to toss. Redeem'd by Him, all His people will join For balance, and gain is by loss. PUBLIC NOTICE is hereby given that the Legislature of the State of New-Hampshire at their last session granted a tax of two cents on each acre of land in the town of CON CORD county of Grafton, (Public lands excepted) for the purpose of making & repairing Highways in said Town of Concord; and appointed the subscribers a committee to assess, collect, and appropriate the same, and in said grant, granted liberty to the resident & non-resident landowners in said Concord, to work out their taxes on said highways as said committee.

Shall direct, any time between the first day of June, and the fifteenth day of September in the year when said tax is assessed at the rate of six cents the hour for every able bodied man, finding his own tools and diet, and the same price per yoke for good oxen; and we the subscribers have assessed said tax, and will be prepared and ready to receive the work agreeable to the true intent and meaning of said grant. Weymouth. Tuesday, April 24, 1804. NEWS EXPECTED. Accounts from France to the 20th, and from England to the 24th March, may be expected in the course of a few days; vessels sailing from those places, at the period mentioned, having been spoken with by some of the late arrivals at this port. One of the vessels spoken is the Mars bound from Liverpool to New-York; the other the Eagle, from Bordeaux for Baltimore. They have probably both arrived. From the EAST-INDIES. Capt. Myrick, from Batavia, in the ship Indus, informs, that a French squadron of one 74, two frigates, and the corvette Berceau, [probably, that commanded by admiral Linois] sailed from Batavia the 8th December—which, previous to the arrival of the Indus, had destroyed the English pepper magazines at Bencoolen, (on the island of Sumatra,) to the amount, it was said, of from 18 to 20,000 piculs. And that the same squadron had captured an English ship at Bencoolen, with a valuable cargo of Calcutta and Madras goods, and sent her to the Isle of France. Accounts from the coast of Africa state, that the Isle of Goree had been assaulted and captured by a French national vessel, and privateers from Cayenne.

One of the vessels spoken is the Mars bound from Liverpool to New-York; the other the Eagle, from Bordeaux for Baltimore. They have probably both arrived. From the EAST-INDIES. Capt. Myrick, from Batavia, in the ship Indus, informs, that a French squadron of one 74, two frigates, and the corvette Berceau, [probably, that commanded by admiral Linois] sailed from Batavia the 8th December—which, previous to the arrival of the Indus, had destroyed the English pepper magazines at Bencoolen, (on the island of Sumatra,) to the amount, it was said, of from 18 to 20,000 piculs. And that the same squadron had captured an English ship at Bencoolen, with a valuable cargo of Calcutta and Madras goods, and sent her to the Isle of France. Accounts from the coast of Africa state, that the Isle of Goree had been assaulted and captured by a French national vessel, and privateers from Cayenne.

‘Captain’ Center, of the ship Thomas Gordon, who arrived at New-York, from Madeira, informed that a severe shock of an earthquake was felt there at 6 o’clock in the morning of the 5th of March, which lasted about fifteen seconds, and shook the tiles off the houses; it was very sensibly felt on board the shipping in the harbour. As Captain Center sailed the same day, he had no opportunity to hear what damage was done by it. The general opinion was, “Had it lasted fifty seconds longer, it would have shook down the houses.” This shock added to the late calamity at Madeira, had very much alarmed the inhabitants who began to think themselves very precariously situated. DOMESTIC. THE reinforcement preparing at Washington, for our squadron in the Mediterranean is to consist of the United States, of 44 guns, President, of 44, Congress, of 36, and Constellation, of 36; to be commanded by captains L. Barron, Rodgers, J. Barron, and Campbell. The John Adams, armed en flute, goes out as a store ship, to be commanded by Lt. Chauncy. When this reinforcement arrives, Commodore Preble’s squadron will consist of the Constitution, President, and United States of 44 guns; Congress and Constellation, of 36; John Adams, 32; Syren, Capt. Stuart, of 16; Argus, Capt. Hull, 16; Nautilus, Capt. Summers, of 16; Enterprise, Capt. Decatur, of 14; and Vixen, Capt. Smith, of 14 guns; in all 11 vessels.

Although I was not of suitable age to participate (in any great degree) in our glorious Struggle for independence, yet I ever do feel, and trust while I retain my understanding, I ever shall, cherish its sacred and incontrovertible principles; I have to add, that, I am a warm admirer of the Jeffersonian administration, believing this to be the true and faithful deposit of that glorious principle." Marine Memoranda. Portsmouth, April 24, 1804. Thursday arrived here brig Lazzie, Capt. Hopkins, 60 days from Nantz. Spoke, lat. 47, 30, long. 90, brig Concord, Mason, of Kennebunk, from London for Baltimore, out 7 days, all well. Lat. 44, 40, long. 14, brig Lucretia, Ramsden, from New York, bound to Nantz, 58 days out, leaking very bad. Lat. 45, 19, long. 55, spoke brig Massachusetts, Stanwood, from Georgetown, bound to Europe, 89 days out. Sunday, arrived here, Schr's Dove, Capt. Samuel Rice, in 61 days from Guadeloupe. Natural birth.—That the people of the kingdom are all of them the subjects of the washing of regeneration. The Apostle says, "not by works of righteousness which we have done, but of his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration," &c. Here we have a second washing for the church, added to the first cleansing by blood. And by the second, men begin to know and partake of the first, and of the joy it gives. But there is a third washing belonging to this church, and which belongs to none but visible members of it—This washing relates to the appearance of the church in this world, and while it is for the comfort of believers, it is to distinguish the visible members of Christ’s Church, from the world. This washing with water, or baptism, is an outward appointed sign representing the true cleansing before spoken of—And the Apostle connects them together, saying, Christ loved the church and gave himself for it, that he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word—Denoting either that the baptism for the church is by or according to his word; or that true cleansing is by the word, and the visible figurative cleansing is by baptism signifying the other, and connected with his love and gift.

This cleansing by washing in baptism, is not as the others are, necessary to salvation, for some of the members of the true church, never have the opportunity for it, but where there is access to the or dinance, the visible members of the true church, are to be thus washed and distin guished, according to Christ’s mind here ex pressed—And if he has constituted the in fants of believers members of his church, (as may appear in the sequel,) they are so be thus washed, and marked as his. If the Baptists saw the glory of the kingdom, which cannot be separated from the grace of it, they would not deny this distinguishing washing to infants made objects of it by grace. But if they see not the one body, how can they rightly take up the one baptism belonging to it? If they saw the spiritual glory of the kingdom, they would not join their opponents in admitting a worldly church as connected in any wise with Christ. Nor would they express cha rity for such. They would see that the one baptism is precious and peculiar, and is incompatible with a worldly self-righteous church or people, and with all pretended baptism of old or young there; They would deny all worldly baptism in any mode, on broader ground; namely, that the anti christian church cannot have the Christian baptism.

Public notice is hereby given that the inhabitants of Stratford, in the county of Grafton, have petitioned the General Court, representing that they have two roads about eleven miles in length, through said Stratford, to keep in repair (that being the main country river road, and the road leading to Shelburne). That there is now wanted a back road, north and south, through said Stratford, in order to meet a back road from Stewartstown, through Colebrook, Cockburn, and Wales' location, which will shorten the distance from Stewartstown to Northumberland and Shelburne road, a number of miles. And praying that a tax of three cents per acre on all the land in said town (public rights excepted) may be granted them, to be expended in cutting, clearing, and bridging said north and south road, and repairing the aforementioned roads. Ordered, That the petitioners be heard before the General Court on the Tuesday of their next Session, and that the petitioners cause that the substance of said petition and order of Court thereon be published in the New-Hampshire Gazette, three weeks successively, and the last publication to be at least six weeks prior to said day of hearing, that any person or persons may then appear and show cause (if any they have) why the prayer thereof may not be granted. ATTEST. NATH'L. PARKER, Dep'y Sec'y. Concord, June 9, 1803.

Public notice is hereby given that the inhabitants of Stratford, in the county of Grafton, have petitioned the General Court, representing that they have two roads about eleven miles in length, through said Stratford, to keep in repair (that being the main country river road, and the road leading to Shelburne). That there is now wanted a back road, north and south, through said Stratford, in order to meet a back road from Stewartstown, through Colebrook, Cockburn, and Wales' location, which will shorten the distance from Stewartstown to Northumberland and Shelburne road, a number of miles. And praying that a tax of three cents per acre on all the land in said town (public rights excepted) may be granted them, to be expended in cutting, clearing, and bridging said north and south road, and repairing the aforementioned roads. Ordered, That the petitioners be heard before the General Court on the Tuesday of their next Session, and that the petitioners cause that the substance of said petition and order of Court thereon be published in the New-Hampshire Gazette, three weeks successively, and the last publication to be at least six weeks prior to said day of hearing, that any person or persons may then appear and show cause (if any they have) why the prayer thereof may not be granted. ATTEST. NATH'L. PARKER, Dep'y Sec'y. Concord, June 9, 1803.

PUBLIC NOTICE is hereby giv- en, that the Selectmen and oth ers, inhabitants of WOLFEBOROUGH, have petitioned the General Court, representing, that said town was originally granted to a very few persons; That they have so managed the settlement that there is no land granted for the benefit of schools, or any other public uses for the benefit of the first settlers in said town—That said petitioners are many of them poor, and others in but moderate circumstances—They therefore pray that they may have liberty to tax all

The lands in said town, 2½ cents on one hundred dollars on the estimated value of said land, for one year, viz. the year 1804, to enable them to build the necessary school-houses in said town—that they may be enabled to give their children decent educations—And further stating, that they are of opinion the proprietors will not be injured by the granting the prayer of said petition, as it will increase the value of their property, and promote a laudable and good purpose; and gain them the esteem of the inhabitants. ORDERED, that the petitioners be heard before the General Court on the second Wednesday of their next session, and that they cause the substance of said petition and order of court thereon, to be published three weeks successively in the New-Hampshire Gazette, the last publication of which to be at least six weeks prior to said day of hearing, that any person or persons may then appear and show cause, (if any they have,) why the prayer thereof may not be granted. On Thursday, July 4th, the Students of the University joined to celebrate the day. A procession was formed at the College and moved thence to the Chapel, where the throne of Grace being addressed by the President, an oration was pronounced by James Brackett, at once eloquent and impressive. The procession then moved to the Booth where the following toasts were drank under the discharge of cannon. 1. The day we celebrate—the birthday of Liberty and Independence; May we testify our readiness to defend its rights, by our enjoyment of its blessings. 2. The United States of America; May party animosities and political contentions soon be floating on that sea, whose waters wash the shores of other worlds. 3. Thomas Jefferson, President of the United States; May his measures be such, as shall advance the honor and happiness of the nation. 4. The State of New-Hampshire; So long as her hills are crowned with verdure so long may her children continue to preserve their political integrity. 5. John Langdon; By measures the most salutary, may he convince his constituents, that wisdom and virtue are the basis of good government. 6. The firm patriots of '76; Ever zealous to defend the rights of their country, and more ready to die freemen, than to live slaves. 7. The political constitution of the United States—firm and unshaken as its founders.

John Tavior Gilman; May he reap satisfaction from the consideration, of having faithfully discharged the duties of his office. A thunderbolt of vengeance, and an eternal remorse of conscience to the destroyers of good government. 10. The American Navy; May we never have occasion to chain our fleet on the ocean, as did Xerxes, in order to oppose a foreign enemy. 11. The memory of WASHINGTON—peace to his ashes. 12. The sovereignty of the people—by which our glory, our happiness and independence have been achieved. 13. The Territory of Louisiana; May it prove an additional advantage to the nation. 14. Liberty and Independence; May they, like the morning stars, unite in harmony; and all the sons of Columbia shout for joy. 18. "We are all Republicans—We are all Federalists." State of New Hampshire, Rockingham, ss. To James Drake, Justice of the Peace, The subscriber being a proprietor, owner of more than one sixteenth part of the land in Wales' Location, which has been of late annexed to the town of Cockburn, county of Coos, in said state, requests you to warn the proprietors of said Wales' Location, now annexed to Cockburn, to meet at the dwelling house of Samuel Bishop in said Cockburn, on the second Tuesday of August next, at ten o’clock forenoon, to act on the following business. 1st. To choose a Moderator and a Clerk. 2nd. To see if the proprietors will accept of the last survey of said Location and all the proceedings of the former proprietary meetings. 3rd. To see how they will settle with those who are living on said Location and whether they will appoint an agent so that purpose or not. 4th. To see how much they will allow Samuel G. Bishop, for surveying said Location, and for tending proprietary meetings, and transacting their business. 5th. To act on all other business which they may think expedient relative to said proprietors. Samuel G. Bishop. In pursuance of the foregoing request, I hereby notify and warn all the proprietors of the above mentioned Wales' Location, now annexed to Cockburn, to meet at the time, place, and for the purpose specified above. James Drake, Justice of the Peace. Pittsfield, June 26, 1805.

The Anglo-Federal editors have recently changed their ground of abuse, and now inveigh with fitly malignity against Mr. Jefferson, because a few French privateers have infested the coasts of the Carolinas, and exercised a spirit of marauding that has been uniformly common to the pursuits of privateers of all nations: but in this spirit of naval peculation, the several governments to which such privateers belong have never been considered as responsible, in any other way, than as private actions (or individual malefaction could be enforced by evidence, and the perpetrators mulcted or punished by fine or imprisonment, or both. Then wherefore is this hue and cry raised against the wisdom of the Executive authority, for suffering this diminutive evil, and laboring to attach the despoilment to the government of France?

The answer will be brief and clearly it arises from a tremulous hope in this monarchical junto, to make the people unmindful, or forgetful, of the numerous insults & injuries that have been committed against their dignity and prosperity, by the frigates of his Britannic majesty, whose depredations and insolence have not merely been "winked" at, or countenanced by the British administration, but the very in sulters have been raised to higher credit and advantages in their fatal navy, against whom most heavy complaints were made by the American government, at the common desire of the aggrieved citizens of America. The Centinel, in speaking of such depredations and offenses, expresses a dismay with regret; that we have not a naval establishment, equal to the re sistance of these enormities; and would infer, from its non-existence, that Mr. Jefferson was regardless of the public good: yet this loud yell among the royalists, for the formation of a navy, never occurred when the Cambrian frigate of England, and other British ships of war, of the same country, were anchored within our harbor at New York, to menace our constituted authorities, and carry our seamen into an infernal captivity. On these trying occasions the federal lambs were either silently enjoying these degrading offenses, on the part of their beloved friends and allies, the British, or extenuating or apologizing for.

Many politicians have adopted a proverb, that the want of news is an indication of the prosperous state of the world; what then must we think of the prosperity of our political affairs, when there is not even a single measure of our general government, which can excite disquiet and discussion, though there is a party in this country, who with all the anxious avidity of the hawk, are continually watching for their prey? No wars, no armies to disgust us by their presence and cast a gloom over our future prospects; no excise gatherers to gauge our stills, to measure our windows, and to excite our indignation; no sedition law to muzzle the press and introduce suspicions into the convivial circle; no proscription. Our government seems to have realized that admirable theory, which the most-enlightened politicians have delighted to contemplate; where the administration is scarcely seen on the theatre of action, and man is left to the undisturbed exercise of his individual energies. Not a solitary basis can be found for even federal cavil or federal denunciation.... Richmond Eng. By a circular letter from the Secretary of State dated on the 12th July, 1805, the Consuls and Commercial Agents of the U. States are instructed to forbear to issue any certificate whatever relative to purchases of foreign vessels by citizens of the U. States, except to such persons as may satisfy the Consuls and Commercial Agents, that the purchase was made without knowing this alteration in their instructions; and they are also restrained from allowing the exception itself after the expiration of two months from the date of the advertisement they are directed to publish of this instruction. JULY 19. Among the new arrangements of the General Post Office lately adopted, it is with great pleasure we state that a contract has been entered into for a line of stages, to convey the mail weekly, to Frankfort, in Kentucky, to commence on the first day of October next. When this arrangement shall have been carried into effect, the whole seventeen states will be united by a connected line of stages. It is unnecessary to say a word of the vast advantages that will be derived from this measure. It is, however, a merited tribute to the services of the Postmaster General, to remark that his spirited and successful arrangements to extend and accelerate the progress of the mail, are the best and most conclusive replies which can be made to the calumnies with.

which party and innocently assails his conduct—N. Int. ‘New-York, July 8. A gentleman who came passenger in the brig New-York, informs us that the British Guineaman which had an engagement with 2 French privateers off Savannah, had arrived at Tybee, after beating them both off. She shattered one of them nearly to pieces, and would have taken her had she had a sufficient number of men. The Guineamen lost two men, and her carpenter had both his legs shot off. By the ship Rose in Bloom, we have received Charleston papers to the 13th inst. Capt. Burdick informs us that previous to his sailing a report prevailed there that the British frigate Leander had a few days before sent her boats up the River St. Mary’s and retook a ship and a brig which had been captured a short time before by a privateer fitted out from St. Augustine; and had also taken a French or Spanish privateer, supposed to be that which had made the above captures. By Charleston papers to the 9th inst., we observe, that the ship Two Friends, captured off that harbor by a French privateer, has been retaken and carried into one of the Bahamas. FISHERMEN IMPRESSED With great satisfaction, we notice the impressment of our fishermen by the British. Several fishing vessels from Marblehead, fallen in with English ships cruising.

Surely it is enough in all conscience to see TWO THOUSAND SEAMEN taken from the merchant ships of the United States, ing less than two years 3 and now, being borne with that outrage, we offer to witness still further injury, and the fishermen are to be torn from their families and country; to fight in the wars of George the Third! Will our coasting vessels be safe in future? Perhaps not—and it may be found that we shall be visited in our very harbors by British cruisers, hunting after their prey! The Ville de Milan was lately captured from the French, and as the Capt. declared, "wanted hands." Good God! "wanted hands," and what was that to us? Are we to find them? It seems we are—but if so, better stop all intercourse with Great Britain immediately, and let the "green mountain boys" march to Canada, than to sleep much longer in inglorious ease. FROM PLYMOUTH, JULY 20. Sch. Miles Standish, Capt. Davie, arrived this day from Lisbon—48 days passage. - Capt. Dutton came passenger, and is the bearer of important dispatches for government from M., Munroe, respecting the negotiations between Spain and the United States... Mr. M., had left Madrid, the negotiations having been broken off. - Capt. D. proceeds on to Washington immediately; via Boston. - -

To the Printers of the N. H. Gazette, In your Gazette of the 25th inst. I have seen a piece signed by Jacob Peasley, sworn to before Thomas Page, Justice of the Peace, and directed to the printers of the Oracle Post, stating that having observed in their paper of the 9th of September last a publication over the signature of "Veritas" wherein it is wickedly attempted to bring the state Legislature into disgrace in the eyes of the people,—He thinks it a duty he owes to the public and to truth to disprove the assertion therein made, "that he on the said trial at the last session of the General Court, voted for Mr. Peabody as State Treasurer, and does therefore certify and declare that he did not vote for Mr. Peabody in June last." I should not have thought it necessary to notice this extraordinary publication, had I not repeatedly asserted that Mr. Peasley told me he did vote for me. I did not suppose it to be the intention of the writer to call my veracity in question,—Under this impression silence would be criminal, and I feel it to be a duty I owe to myself, as well as to the public and to truth to state facts, that my fellow-citizens may form a correct opinion how far I was justified in making the assertion;—On the week following the choice of Treasurer in June last, James Wilson, Esq.

The member from Peterborough, called on me and explained that it was the intention of the friends of Mr. Chamberlain to procure the signatures of those members of the Legislature who voted for me on the last trial, to a writing, declaring the fact, in order to show that the charge made against him by Mr. Morrill was without foundation. He stated also that Mr. Pearce, the member from Kingston had said he would neither sign such writing, nor give information to any person but me; for whom he did vote, Mr. Wilson said that it was his wish, and the wish of Mr. Chamberlain's friends, that I should apply to Mr. Pearce for the information. It cannot be supposed the task was so agreeable one, but under existing circumstances I thought it my duty to undertake it, I introduced the subject to Mr. Pearce by observing that my only motive in the application was to free Mr. Chamberlain from, what I conceived, an unjust aspersion. That he might declare without hesitation for whom he did vote, and that I should never think hard of him if he had voted against me. He asked me who told me that he did not vote for me, I told him no one, and that it was wholly immaterial, as it respected myself, for whom he did vote.

The papers, Luderdland, that I told My, Peabody did vote for him the Rest ballot ing—But I did not tell him so. I know what I said to him. He asked me if I was willing to tell him who I voted for as Treasurer. I answered that I was, and told him I voted for him twice, and immediately went over to tell him how he came to lose the office. But he, (Peabody) added that he did not say when he voted for him, whether this year, or at some other time or times— Upon which I asked him if he did not mean by what he said to Mr. Peabody to have him understand that he voted for him as State Treasurer at last June election, the time when Mr. Peabody spoke to him on the subject ? To which he answered yes. I did mean to have him understand me so, but I did not vote for him as Treasurer last year, and can make oath to it. "Signed, Daniel Blasdell." I shall now leave it to my fellow citizens to compare the oath of Mr. Peabody with the above statement, and the certificate of - the Hon. Mr. Blaisdell, and to make their own comments. S. OLIVER PEABODY, Exeter, Oct. 2, 1854.

and to the happiness of United America---The great question of Electors for President & Vice President, will then be decided; it must on that day be determined, whether THOMAS JEFFERSON, or CHARLES C. PINCKNEY, shall preside for the next four years, over the Union; It will then be concluded whether the State of Massachusetts will hold that distinguished place in the Union, to which she is so pre-eminently entitled; or whether she will belong to that minority which are opposed to the present Administration of our National Government. Our beloved PRESIDENT, has not merely abstained from doing evil, but he has been conspicuously active in doing good; he has been assailed on all sides, by showers of envenomed arrows, from his opponents, and he has remained uninjured amidst the storm; his robe of office, like Caesar’s mantle, has been pierced by the daggers of unprincipled assassins; they have endeavored to plant daggers in his pillow by night, and serpents in his path by day; The daggers have become blunted, and the serpents harmless, when opposed to his shield of virtue,—The general Electoral Ticket was adopted by the majority of the Legislature of Massachusetts, to prevent Mr. JEFFERSON having one vote from this State.

Consider before you answer, and once resolved, be strong; two nominations have taken place—DANIEL CLEAVES, of Biddeford, and RICHARD CUTTS, of Pepperellboro’—Newspaper panegyric seldom has much effect, as it is frequently written by a too partial friend. Newspaper slander usually falls harmless to the ground, being usually inserted by a secret enemy; yet to examine public men and public measures free from personal invective is ever justifiable and praiseworthy. Unfortunate must be the situation of that man who is to be exalted by abusing his rival opponent. The advocates for Daniel Cleaves will not have resort to the same measures which have been presented by the writer of the two pieces in favor of Richard Cutts in the New-Hampshire Gazette, under the signatures of “Wells” and “Vox Disiri.” Mr. Cleaves is too well known and estimated in York District, to require the aid of fulsome eulogium; his character is too firmly established to be shaken or injured by personal abuse.

The advocates for Daniel Cleaves will not have resort to the same measures which have been presented by the writer of the two pieces in favor of Richard Cutts in the New-Hampshire Gazette, under the signatures of “Wells” and “Vox Disiri.” Mr. Cleaves is too well known and estimated in York District, to require the aid of fulsome eulogium; his character is too firmly established to be shaken or injured by personal abuse.

Amendment to the Constitution.

The following Letter from the Secretary of State of the United States, officially notifying the Ratification of the Amendment to the Federal Constitution, has been received by the Executive of this State: — Department of State, Sept. 24th, 1804. (CIRCULAR) Sir, I have the honor to notify to you, in pursuance of the act of Congress, passed on the 26th of March last, entitled “An act supplementary to the act entitled “An act relative to the election of a President and Vice-President of the United States, and fixing the officer who shall act as President, in case of vacancies in the offices both of President and Vice President,” — That the amendments proposed during the last session of Congress to the constitution of the United States, respecting the manner of voting for President and Vice-President of the United States, has been ratified by the legislatures of three fourths of the several states, to wit, by those of Vermont, Rhode Island, New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Maryland, Virginia, Ohio, Kentucky, Tennessee, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Georgia. I request you to be pleased to acknowledge the receipt hereof. I have the honor to be, With very great respect, Sir, Your most obed’t serv’t, James Madison. His Excellency The Governor of the State of New Jersey.

Boston, OCT. 6. West-India and Southern Storms. Since our last, we have received the following particulars: In the gale at St. Thomas, from 4th to 5th Sept., a fleet of vessels, principally Americans, destroyed; and in some places, lay three deep! An eastern schooner laden with lumber, upset, one man killed, number wounded. Schr Hiram, Bacon, of Barnstable, for Boston, was safe, and no damage; the Fair Trader, Crawford, of Boston, had been ashore, but got off. In Martinique, out of 12 sail at that place, all but 5 had been lost. A heavy gale has been experienced at New Providence; but no material damage is said to have been done. The gale was felt at Jacmel; but no very great damage done. At St. Croix, no material damage was done. At St. Pierres, Martinique, it is said all the vessels in the road, except 5, were totally lost. At St. Kitts, St. Barts, St. Eustatia and Nevis, most of the vessels are reported to have been lost. From Curacao and St. Vincents, we have no accounts of damage, although there have been arrivals at New-York, which left those places September 5-6. At Guadaloupe, it is stated that the shipping suffered very much, as well as at Tortola, where it is mentioned that only 4 escaped out of 40.

At Turks Island, fix American vessels were driven on shore; three of them entirely lost. Accounts from Turks-Island inform that Colonel Murray, of that place, had issued a Proclamation, declaring his intention of taking possession of all vessels and cargoes that should be stranded or cast away on that Island. In pursuance of which he had taken possession of the American schooners Martin and Catherine, which had run aground on the beach, and was using his endeavors to get them off, for the benefit (as he avowed) of the owners and underwriters. However strange this line of conduct may appear, he was countenanced in it by the Governor of that place. The American Captains who have had the misfortune to lose their vessels, etc. at Turks Island by the gale, have also experienced much plunder by the negroes;—one of them, after cautioning in vain the negroes not to board his vessel, fired upon them, but without hurting anyone; one of the king's agents, on hearing of this, immediately forbade them, and all others, from doing the like, under pain of imprisonment. The brig —; Riley, of Portsmouth, sailed from St. Thomas 1st Sept. and was parted with by Capt. Starr at New York the day before the gale came on.

The day after the | the gale saw a wreck and a number of broken pieces, among them a table, which Capt. Starr was positive he had seen in Capt. Riley’s cabin—Capt. S. also saw two 74’ from Kingston, Jam. one of them with all her masts gone; the other had half houses standing, (one the Agamemnon, the other the admiral ship;) and an English ship, bound to Jam. with her foremast and bowsprit gone. From Savannah.--Fort Green, at Cockspur Island, is completely destroyed, and all the buildings destroyed.—Of the soldiers, 7 of those who were there escaped by getting upon the roof of the last house which fell, with 14 others, men and women; soon after floating, the roof parted; and they severally escaped to land on Wilmington Island—— A letter from Savannah, of 10th Sept. says it is impossible to describe to you, the losses and appearances of things here, goods, buildings, dead bodies, animals, &c. among the ruins, shock the eye, and the distress of merchants, &c. is indescribable.

A Synopsis of all the votes given by the People for Representatives to Congress, in August.—Viz. For the federalists, duly given, "returned and counted, : 10,978 By Dunstable, not returned, : 45 By Bartlett, not returned, : 0 By Landaff, returned too late, : 17 By Atkinson, not certified, : 8 By Eaton, not certified, : 0 By Derryfield, not counted, : 91 By Sutton, not counted, : 0 Total: 11,076. For the republicans, duly returned and counted, : 4,278 By Bartlett, not returned, : 75 By Dunstable, not returned, : 63 By Landaff, returned too late, : 38 By Atkinson, not certified, : 57 By Eaton, not certified, : 71 By Derryfield, not counted, : 30 By Sutton, not counted, : 90 Total: 4,306. Amount of federal & republican votes: 16,384 Scattering: 8 Whole number of votes given for Representatives throughout the State: 16,392 10,886 being a majority, Whereof the feds. had 11,076. Leaving a federal majority of one hundred and ninety votes. Lisa, duty which every citizen owes to him self, his country, and posterity, to enquire into the merits of the respective candidates; to weigh their public conduct with the professions of those friends and advocates who recommend them; and decide independently. The Republican candidates have never been honored with a seat in the councils of the nation; we are, therefore, unable to determine their comparative claims to a station of such high importance; but from the talents, industry, and application to business, which they have discovered, in the legislature of this State, (of which it is believed they have all at different times been members) we have a right to augur, that they will not disgrace their constituents, by supineness or inaction; and from their known patriotism, and civic virtues, we are sure, they will not misrepresent the feelings and wishes of New Hampshire, by opposing the government, in every measure, wherein the honor and independence of the United States, comes in contact with the capricious tyranny of Britain. Three of the federal candidates are now members of Congress, and the other two, are recommended, as men of the same kind. We can, therefore, easily form an opinion of their merits. We can all recollect the election of 1808, and the promises and hopes, that were then held out. The feder.

The electoral ticket, at that time, was composed of men, selected with great care, from the party that lays claim to "the talents" of the State; it was the panacea with which all the evils of the body politic were to be cured. To obtain their election no effort was left untried; every nerve of the party was called into action; detachments of runners from Massachusetts pervaded the State; the roads groaned under the weight of iniquitous pamphlets and handbills; the most scandalous falsehoods were circulated; and those bank-directors whose nefarious, swindling practices, have since come to light, to the ruin of thousands of innocent individuals, were, by their overbearing and "oppressive conduct towards those who had transactions with them, mainly instrumental in securing that success, which, to our eternal disgrace, has authorized the British faction in Boston, to boast that they governed "the politics of New-Hampshire, if not of more so. If the electors will take these circumstances into consideration, and examine the conduct of the sitting members, they will not hesitate on whom to bestow their suffrages. A little more than half their time of service has elapsed, during which, two sessions of Congress have been held. At no period of our political existence has the situation of public affairs been more critical.

And who are they that thus arrogate the right of being your dictators! Are they renowned for wisdom? Have they trod the mazy paths of political science? Are they better informed in the foreign relations of our country than yourselves? Or have they a more valuable stake in society? I boldly answer—No. The mechanics, more than any other set of men, are deeply interested in having the commerce of the country fixed on a permanent and honorable basis. The merchant may enrich himself by the national degradation: and at the expiration of the two or three years (which will probably be consumed in perfecting anew the colonial system of England, and cutting off our trade with all parts of the world) may retire with an ample fortune, and no longer need those sources of wealth, which, by opposing the government, and advocating the enemies of his country, he has assisted in destroying. But the mechanic, who earns his bread with the sweat of his brow, and is contented and happy, if he can bring the year about decently.

In this case; on the other hand, we are warranted in depriving him, weakening him, and reducing him to accept of equal conditions. His men may also be attacked and seized wherever there is a act of exercising hostility. Thus a passage may not only be refused to the ministers of an enemy sent to other sovereigns, but if they undertake to pass privately, and without permission, into places belonging to their master's enemy, they are liable to be arrested; and of this the last war furnishes a signal instance. An ambassador of France going to Berlin, through the imprudence of his guides, took his way through a village within the electorate of Hanover, of which the sovereign, the king of England, was at war with France; he was arrested and sent over to England. As his Britannic majesty had herein made use of the rights of war, neither the courts of France nor that of Prussia complained about it. The reasons which render embassies necessary, and envoys sacred and inviolable, are of no less force in times of war than in times of profound peace; the necessity is the same.

Upon the receipt of this information, that Chieftain assembled together such troops of the victorious army as he had in readiness, and proceeded, by rapid marches, to meet the Russians. As soon as the two armies came within sight of each other, the enemy opened a heavy fire from their artillery, which destroyed a portion of the Persian troops. Upon this, Mahomed Houssain Khan, renowned for bravery, calling to mind certain of the proverb (which may be translated—" The better part of valour is discretion") —had recourse to the warfare of flight. He thus inveigled the Russians to follow him and directed his way towards the fortress of Abomce, where the tents of his soldiers were intermixed with the dwellings of the inhabitants. The pursuit was kept up by the enemy with much ardor and precipitation, until they were in the range of the fort, when the Persian artillery opened, and at the first discharge, a vast number of the Russian soldiers were consumed in lessening of mortality. At the same moment, the victorious troops of Mahomed Houssain Khan put to flight the ranks of the discomfited, and withdrew.

Stalls fell a prey to the sword, many guns were made prisoners, the greater part of their gun - attrements fell into the hands of the Persians. The Commander in Chief fled towards Teheran. As soon as Mahomed Houssain Khan was completed of the defeat and flight of the enemy, he transmitted an account of his victory to the Prince of the World, Abbas Mirza, who ascended the Throne of Royalty at Teheran. At the same time Mahomed Houssain Khan himself proceeded towards Teheran in pursuit of the Russians. When the intelligence reached the Prince Abbas Mirza, he immediately forwarded a detail of the circumstances of the victory to the King and taking the field in person, with a powerful army, also set out in the direction of Teheran, with a fixed determination in his valiant mind, to extirpate the Russian nation! Mahomed Kurrcem Khan Afshaar (a relation to the Prime Minister, Mirza Mahomed Shussee) received instructions from the King to spread abroad the tidings of this joyful event. Three dispatches upon the subject were accordingly sent from Tehran, one to the Prince of the World, Ruler of Persia and Khokhalpoys, of all the Havens and Shores, and of the Land of Char, another to Mahomed Nizam Khan, Lord of the Sea—and a third to the British Envoy.

Agreeably to our promise we this day submit to our readers extracts from Vattel of considerable length, which merit a dispassionate attention, not merely because they vindicate the course pursued by our government, and indeed manifest its mildness, but because they define the existing character of Mr. Jackson, notwithstanding the necessary step taken by the President, and show especially that he still preserves all the inviolability attached by the law of nations to a public minister. Had the President even gone further than he has, and ordered him to leave the country, while he remained in it he would continue to enjoy all the immunities attached to his appointment.

The inviolability of his person and the respect due to his office would be in no wise impaired. It requires no argument to show that, in a case where the government has gone a much lesser length, the same inviolability and respect attach to him. Although the President has refused to receive any further communications from him, he is still a public minister and the representative of the British government in many important respects. Our comparative unacquaintance with the law of nations, arising from the infancy of our national existence and our fortunate freedom from foreign connections or collisions, render the diffusion of these truths at this time more important, lest the indignation likely to be excited by Mr. Jackson's conduct should prompt any of our citizens in the warmth of their feelings to offer an insult to him, or be wanting in those offices which his station entitles him to claim. The people of America have ordained and established that the powers of government shall be vested in three great departments—the Legislative, the Executive, and the Judicial. They have laid that there shall be a house of representatives, the members of which shall be chosen by the people of the several states, every second year.

Though this house is composed of members chosen by the people immediately; though they can have no other interest than the great community from which they were sent; though they must return to the common mass in the short period of two years, yet enlightened America did not see proper to entrust the power of making laws to this body alone; they knew that the history of man and the experience of ages bore testimony against the safety of committing this high power to any one assembly not checked by some other body. They have therefore erected another branch of the legislature, called the senate, the members of which are not to be elected by the people immediately, but by the sovereignties of the several States: they are to be chosen for six years and not for two, and the qualification requisite to entitle those to a seat is different from that of a member of this House. To these bodies are given the power of initiating all laws, but after a bill has passed both of these Houses, before it becomes of binding obligation on the nation, it must be approved of by the President; it is a dead letter until life is given by the executive. The President is elected not by the people, not by the legislatures of the several States, not by either House of Congress, but by electors chosen by the people.

Vol. V WASHINGTON, THURSDAY, JANUARY 30, 1801. The election of the President of the United States may be constitutionally made either by electors, specially appointed for that purpose, or by the House of Representatives, on failure of a majority of electoral votes in favor of one candidate. The former mode of election has a decided tendency to produce intrigue, faction, and abuse of power; the first accords precisely with our political habits and may, in effect, be the most popular election in the union; for as the extent of the power of the electors and the sole object of it are always foreknown, each individual voter may confer his suffrage on the electoral candidates and have the privilege to vote according to his own wishes. Our security for the uniform and salutary adoption of the desirable, rather than the mischievous mode of election, is very intimately to depend on the first steps which are taken to select and to nominate persons qualified to sustain the high duties of the first magistrate. It is not easy to conceive more than three ways of commencing the first movements towards a Presidential election. First, it may be left to the uncontrived movements of the people at large in each state.

But, on the other side, it is true also, that goods taken to America, bona fide, for American consumption, might afterwards be conveyed to the mother country, in consequence of the state of the markets, without the clog of a duty: so if, in the first case, what was lawful prize by our general law might escape; in the second case, what was lawful trade in favor of our enemies, was by the treaty prohibited, and rendered liable to capture. But the most material consideration as to the article in question is that it only attempts to do what Lord Hawkesbury had before attempted to do: viz. to settle what should be evidence of an interrupted voyage. It insists on a criterion of such interruption being given by the Americans, much more satisfactory than that which Lord Hawkesbury, in a memorable letter to Rufus King, (officially communicated to him at the commencement of the war) promises should be received as evidence of the continuity being broken. That letter cannot be lost sight of in this dispute—for what is the fact?

These ministers make a hasty and gratuitous promise to America; they then break it in a flagrant and vexatious manner; the Americans take fire, and remonstrate; and when the whole intercourse between the two countries is brought back to the state in which it originally stood before the expiration of the treaty in 1794, (a treaty always held to be very favorable to Great Britain by those who now govern America), these very persons cry out concession and submission, because their predecessors grant in return for a treaty of commerce, less than they gratuitously, and without being even asked, actually promised. They say, nothing is given to our commerce by the treaty. To answer this, it is only necessary to say—Look to our exports; and to recollect that unless such treaty was in existence, they would be at liberty to give any preference to foreigners over us, and even to pass prohibitory laws, which, though very hurtful to themselves, would be much more so to us; and yet they might be such as we could not in justice make a ground of quarrel, and such as many governments have (in spite of their own interests).

Either at the suggestion of the other, from false notions of the principles of commerce, or from political animosity, frequently adopted. To argue against the possibility of such a policy being acted on by any commercial nation is peculiarly ill-timed, and absurd in the mouths of men who are recommending us, at the risk of a breach with the country who takes near a fifth of our exports, to harass a trade with our enemies which can afford them neither ships nor men. LONDON, Nov. 17. At length the mou of retaliation is promulgated, and by the orders of the King in Council, which we this day insert, the law established among civilized nations, by which the horrors of war were to be limited to the powers actually engaged, are all totally abolished, and its hardships are to be extended to peaceable nations. This most lamentable condition of humanity is said to be rendered necessary— I. Because the Emperor of the French began the desolation; and 2. Because neutral nations (meaning, we suppose America) did not oppose it. The measure stands upon these foundations.

Whether they are sufficient to atone for the horrors which our enemy attempted in vain to inflict, but which we, to a certain degree, may execute, it will be for politicians and moralists to determine. There is a singular coincidence in this measure, which gives rise to an interesting problem in political science. Two great powers, Britain and France, concur in one and the same measure, having in view opposite results. France means to affect, and, if possible, destroy our commerce—we mean to protect, and, if possible, extend it; and we both look for this, and by the same means. Time alone can tell which of us is in the right. In the meantime, in viewing the probable operation of this measure, it is in vain to shut our eyes to the broad and clear fact that America only is the neutral power to be affected by the measure; for we unfortunately have no longer any other neutral flag, except indeed such as those of Papenburg and Kniphausen. It is not to be inquired so particularly what right the Americans, who tamely acquiesced.

Mr. Rose at length reached Washington; his first requisition was that the affair of the Chesapeake should be separated from all other subjects. The reader is desired to mark this. His first demand was, not that the pro- tection should be revoked before the negotiation ran upon; but that the subjects should be treated separately. Why was this made the first step, when it was intended also, if this were denied, to take the other? Consis- tency would have dictated a different arrangement; the question, whether the affair of the Chesapeake should be distinctly considered, was its own subject of discussion appurtenant to, and forming a part of the negotiation, and ought, therefore, to have followed, in- stead of preceding, the demand for the revocation of the Proclamation; for if the President had refused to revoke his proclamation, according to Mr. Rose's instructions there was an end to the business.

Out of their own interest, we should have afforded to the British Europe the spectacle of a bully, full of words, but ready, at the least appearance of danger, to shrink from the most moderate course to. Such, as we have already shown, was the universal opinion of the proclamation when issued, even by the systematic opponents of the administration; and that proclamation, we repeat it, made the continuance of its restrictions coeval with the refusal to grant reparation and to control excesses. Such would have been the effect of this concession on us. What would have been the effect on the British government, had it acceded to the proposition made by our government? The outrage committed on the Chesapeake had been acknowledged by her to be unauthorized, and to require reparation. She had, consequently, declared herself under a moral obligation to make reparation. In this point, the two governments are agreed. In granting this reparation, then, the British government could only perform a solemn, undisputed duty. She could not disgrace herself; in her own eyes, she could not sully her honor in the eyes of the world.

The last argument has been already sufficiently noticed, and it has been made manifestly to appear, that, taking the whole conduct of the British government into consideration, considering the enormity of the original outrage, the persistence of those who committed it, even after the disavowal, to infringe the proclamation, the nakedness of the disavowal itself, the entire omission so far to make reparation as it is in the power of Britain herself to make it without consulting us by punishing her officers and giving up the men taken from the Chesapeake, the total silence as to the nature of the reparation meant to be offered, and the contemporaneous issue of orders every feature of which is marked with hostility, there exists not a shadow of right on her part to require from us an act not of justice, but of weakness, so far as it related to ourselves, and of generosity, perhaps credulity, so far as it related to her.

It is not a declaration of independence—but a decision is implied in the proposition, that is to say, the rights, honor and independence of the United States are violated by the late edicts of Great Britain and France, and they cannot submit to the said edicts, to secure the United States of America as free, sovereign and independent. On the fourth day of the year one thousand seven hundred and eighty-six, the United States of America were declared free, sovereign and independent states—amid the roar of cannon, the shouts of thousands, and the clangor of arms. It was a day of gladness and joy, of gratitude and strong hopes—it passed over, and yet the sun set not on their fears; but all, in the aid of Heaven and the justice of their cause, in the end it be hoped, will terminate in peace and happiness. Great Britain itself, after a bloody seven years war, was compelled to acknowledge, in due form and by solemn treaty, that the United States of America were free, sovereign and independent as they had declared themselves to be, and that declaration is engraved on the tablet of eternity, and will never be erased.

Philadelphia, June 29. Captain Ellis, of the brig Eliza, from Malaga and Gibraltar, arrived at the Lazaretto, informs, that it was reported at Gibraltar, previously to his sailing, that the Prince of Peace was displaced, and the count de Florida Blanca re-established at the court of Madrid.—The politicians at Gibraltar were anxiously awaiting the confirmation of that important intelligence. NEW YORK, June 29. FROM SURINAM. A respectable commercial friend has favored the office of the Morning Chronicle, with the following important official paper, relative to the Midc of the United States with the colony of Surinam. PROCLAMATION. By his Excellency Major General Sir Charles Green, commanding His Majesty's land forces, and Governor of the colony of Surinam, &c. &c. WHEREAS it is expedient that regulations should be established respecting the trade to and from this colony in neutral vessels until his majesty's pleasure should be known, I have thought fit by virtue of the power and authority in me vested, to publish this my proclamation hereby declaring.

I have now thought proper to direct that all the persons included in the above description are to appear at the government house tomorrow morning at nine o'clock, to take oath of allegiance to his Britannic majesty; and in order that these presents may come to the knowledge of those concerned, we do direct the same to be published and affixed, as is customary. Given at Paramaribo the 8th June, and the 44th year of his majesty's reign. CHARLES GREEN, Major General. By his command, R. ROSS, Secretary. God save the king. George Creager, Sheriff, Frederick County. June 25— A. Negro was committed as a runaway to the jail of Frederick county, who calls himself GEORGE LANGSTON, and he belongs to Mr. Isaac Langston of Hertford county, North Carolina; he is about 37 years of age, five feet 7 inches high, a well-made fellow—his clothing are a woollen coat with a blue cape, cotton trimmed waistcoat and trousers and a tow linen shirt, he also has four scars on the back of his neck. If his master does not release him, he will be sold for the jail fees agreeably to law. George Creager, Sheriff, of Frederick county. June 25— Was committed to the jail of Baltimore county as a Runaway on the 14th February last, a Negro woman who calls herself MILLY THOMAS— she is about 35 or 40 years of age, 5 feet 4 inches high, and of a brown complexion. She says she does belong to Mr. William Briscoe of Charles county in the state of Maryland. If her owner does not release her, she will be sold for her jail fees, according to law. Thomas Bailey, Sheriff of Balt. County. Baltimore

May 20, 1810 Valuable Land for Sale The executors of the last will and testament of Anthony Holme, deceased, will sell at private sale about forty acres of land adjoining the city of Washington at the northern extremity of 20th street west. This land is generally allowed to be one of the handsomest situations near the city, having a beautiful prospect of nearly the whole of the city of Washington, Alexandria, and George Town, and any person inclinable to purchase this valuable property, will be shown the same, and know the terms, by application to the subscriber near the premises. JOHN HOLME&D. Public Sale By virtue of a decree of the circuit court of the district of Columbia for the county of Washington sitting as a court of chancery, at the suit of William H. Dorsey, Nicholas Hedges, George Craig, and Adam Whann, against Agnes Jackson, executrix; William Jackson, executor; Jonathan Jackson, Matthew Jackson, Elizabeth Jackson, and Susanna Jackson, infant heirs of Jonathan Jackson, deceased, defendants. Will public auction on the 10th of July to the highest bidder on the premises all the right, title, and interest of Jonathan Jackson, deceased, to the following lots of ground in the city of Washington: lots numbered 67 and 68 in square numbered 75, and the lot numbered 164. June 27—4w Here was committed to the jail of Frederick county, a runaway, a negro man who calls himself Jim, and a mulatto woman who calls herself Milly, and says they belong to Mr. Peter Lurklus of Fauquier county, Virginia; said Jim is thirty-four or five years of age, five feet ten or eleven high, a stout well-made fellow, his rig are a blue coat and waistcoat, tow -linen shirt and trowsers, he has also a scar on his breast. Milly is also twenty-five years of age, six feet one or two inches high, slim and well made, her clothing are a homespun short gown, white linsey petticoat and a brown linen shift. If their owner does not release them from jail they will be sold for their fees agreeably to law. GEORGE CREAGER, Sheriff, Frederick County. June 9— By virtue of an order of the honorable judge Clauch, made in the case of a Barclay an insolvent debtor, the subscriber, trustee of said insolvent, will sell at auction to the highest bidder on Saturday the fifteenth day of June next, at Mr. Morn's.

That such was the mildness, moderation, and wisdom of Lord Hardwick's administration, that he was obliged to push on the catastrophe, and bring out his associates under discipline, lest his extended and deep-laid rebellion should cease, from the causes that urged it being daily removed, and gradually dissolving away. Mr. Ekins further complimented Lord Hardwick's government, who, he said, appeared to be perfectly convinced of the necessity of governing that brave people with a light and delicate hand, and seemed to have adopted the principle of the great Earl of Chatham, who, speaking of America, said: "Be to her virtues ever kind; Be to her faults a little blind; Let all her ways be unconfin'd; Clap not a padlock on her mind." The learned counsel returned to the subject of Mr. Emmett's trial, and observed that so far from Mr. Plunkett having libelled the unfortunate man in his speech to the evidence, that he had wholly employed his address in reading a useful lesson to the misguided part of His Majesty's subjects: — assuring those who expected happiness from French assistance and French principles, that they would be miserably abused; that the leading feature of the French government was ambition, and everything that was the reverse of Washington, and contrary to all they anticipated.

At that moment, said Mr. Erskine, the applying the axe to the neck of Mr. Emmett was nothing; the public example everything. The defendant, he said, had not merely thrown out the ambiguous voces; but day after day had been writing and sending forth his libels among the community. It was no defence to say, that Mr. Cobbett was an admirer of his king and constitution, if he was constantly libelling the ministers of that king, and transgressing the laws of that constitution. It was nothing for him to say, "I respect my religion and my God," if he broke the ten commandments daily. The Saviour of man said, "by their fruits shall ye know them," and the court would judge of Mr. Cobbett by his works. He next entered upon an explanation of the libels, and urged that it was impossible their allusion could be misrepresented, or their libellous intention mistaken; concluding this branch of his argument by saying that the defendant might be a man with a strong and vigorous mind, and that the talents of such a man could not be controlled; yet he should take care, in the exercise of that mind and talent, not to slander another's reputation by the wicked efforts of his superior genius. The more esteemed the man for learning, the more his productions were admired. The.

Among the most agreeable legacies of this nature left by eminent literary characters, our readers will recollect the interesting narratives of Franklin, Hume, and Gibbon. The plain and unadorned statements they have made have given us a more correct insight into their characters and have more successfully contributed to shield their fame from unjust assertion than all the eulogiums pronounced by their admirers. We may be permitted to indulge the hope that the artless narrative of Priestley, who united to the consciousness of talent felt by a great mind the simplicity inspired by true genius, will form the best monument to the purity of his motives and to the beneficence of a spirit actively occupied through a long life in the service of his fellow men. The same papers state the re-election of Mr. Ashton as beyond doubt from the votes already ascertained, and that Thomas Blount will likewise be elected. The executive of Virginia (in the recess of the Legislature) have appointed William B. Giles and Andrew Moore, Senators in the Congress of the United States, the former to supply the vacancy occasioned by the resignation of Abraham Venable, and the latter to supply the vacancy occasioned by Wilson C. Nicholas.

Mr. Crowshield, from the Committee of Commerce and Manufactures, to whom was yesterday referred the petition relative to a vessel at Norfolk, stated a bill for the relief of Theodorick Armstead, which was referred to a committee of the whole today. The bill authorizes the collector at Norfolk to admit to entry 1200 demijohns of brandy imported by T. Armstead in the brig George from the Island of Tenerife. The House went immediately into committee of the whole—Mr. Varnum in the Chair—Mr. Newton fully explained the peculiar circumstances of this case, and called for the reading of the documents relative to it; from which it appeared that sometime since the owner of the brig George hired her to go to Tenerife, where he took a cargo for the Havana; hearing subsequently of the late British orders, he thought it prudent to return to Norfolk, where he now lies; but owing to the revenue laws of the U.S. he is prohibited from entering brandy in quantities as small as those contained in the demijohns. He, therefore, asks permission to land these articles on paying the usual duties.

Smith, Boyle and Earle. IN SENATE OF THE UNITED STATES, December 8th, 1805. The President communicated the following letter and report. Navy Department, 5th Dec. 1805. Sir, In obedience to the resolution of the Senate of this day, requiring the secretary of the navy to lay before the Senate, the reasons why an additional appropriation is required for the naval service for the current year," I have the honor to state, That out of the sum appropriated for the support of the navy, for the year 1804, the sum of 312,370 dollars has been paid for extra expenses, not contemplated in my estimate for that year. Statement A gives a view of these expenses. The sum of 87,630 dollars has moreover, been paid out of the money appropriated for the support of the navy, for the year 1805, for expenses incurred during the year 1804, by the squadron fitted out under the act, entitled "An act further to protect the commerce and seamen of the United States against the Barbary powers," and by commodore Preble in his preparatory arrangements for attacking Tripoli.

Sir, In obedience to the resolution of the Senate of this day, requiring the secretary of the navy to lay before the Senate, the reasons why an additional appropriation is required for the naval service for the current year," I have the honor to state, That out of the sum appropriated for the support of the navy, for the year 1804, the sum of 312,370 dollars has been paid for extra expenses, not contemplated in my estimate for that year. Statement A gives a view of these expenses. The sum of 87,630 dollars has moreover, been paid out of the money appropriated for the support of the navy, for the year 1805, for expenses incurred during the year 1804, by the squadron fitted out under the act, entitled "An act further to protect the commerce and seamen of the United States against the Barbary powers," and by commodore Preble in his preparatory arrangements for attacking Tripoli.

We shall endeavor to procure a copy of it for our next. From the Norfolk Public Ledger of Dec. 9. A letter received by a gentleman in this place from his correspondent in Lisbon, dated the 1st of September, states, that advices had been that day received from Madrid, of much importance, the particulars of which had not transpired. It is however affirmed that the enemies of the Queen and Prince of Peace, had proceeded to oppose them by violence. That the Spanish troops in the interest of, and favoring the party of the Prince of Anurias, had fallen upon the Swiss Guards of the Prince of Peace, and had killed the greater part of them. The letter states further, that in the best informed circles, it is confidently believed that a complete revolution in the politics of Spain was effected. The respectable source from whence we derive this information, leaves little doubt with us, of its veracity in substance. It is not improbable when we come to learn further particulars, that we shall find this event, connected with matters of the highest importance. The Queen or rather the Prince of Peace, it is well.

The French minister there, on the subject of the seizure by the French, in the Elbe, of the American ship Nienstaden, which, without any legal condemnation, had been brought to Hamburg and offered for sale. Mr. Forbes had publicly cautioned all persons against purchasing the ship, and had caused legal and quiet possession to be taken by the owner, (a Mr. Keith, of Alexandria, Va.) after which a party of French had forcibly dispossessed the rightful owner in the Harbor of Hamburg. The affair was thus situated when Capt. C. left Hamburg, and the Consul had demanded indemnity, or a restoration of the property, of the Senate of that city. Salem Cat. THEATRE.
