At the distance of six feet from the surface, a grave was discovered, in which was found a coffin of hard pitch pine, commonly called the Norway pine, very little decayed, which, on being opened, contained another of the same wood, very handsomely made, and not at all injured; the lid of this being lifted showed a body wrapped in a tarred sheet, that, on being removed from the fate, presented the countenance of a man that appeared quite recently to have died; his flesh was fresh and florid, as though just shaved; -the flesh hard to the touch, and every appearance of a new corpse, from a short and not painful illness; two or three sprigs of myrtle or box, were just cut from the stock, were also lying on the outside of the tarred sheets. Both coffins had on their lids, in brass nails, the letters J. T. and a gravestone, at the head of the grave, declared the person interred there to be Mr. John Thomas, of the Island of Barbados, aged 45 years, who died 25th June, A. D. 1726, more than eighty-two years ago. A number of persons who came to see this curious fact, from the fineness of the preservation, and the manner of it, induced the wardens to direct the coffin to be closed again and buried, which it is, at the N. E. corner of the church, in a yellow clay, mixed with small stones and gravel.

The Sixth anniversary of the Arlington Sheep Shearing was celebrated on Thursday last the 30th ult. The badness of the prevented so large a company from attending, as had been expected. Apparently, about 150 persons were present. The show commenced at half past twelve, and the cups were adjudged to Daniel M. Chichester, and John C. Scott, Esqs. for the best Tup and best pair of Ewe Lambs of one year old. During the show a Fair was held, for the sale of Domestic Fabrics, and many were sold, at good prices. A bill of Woolen Yarn exclusively spun, and weigh- ing a pound, was sold for the enormous price of Four dollars. At five o'clock the company adjourned to dine under the Tent of Washington.

The subscriber, having declined his interest in the undertaking, has assigned his interest to Mr. Cole, and the establishment is now under his management. I trust it will be conducted with ability and impartiality, and the patronage which it will receive from a generous public. JAMES WHALEY. The Editor will endeavor to render it an ornament to the Wheeling Repository. An elegant and commodious printing office, and a numerous and well assorted collection of types will ensure neatness and accuracy in the execution of work. The establishment is now in complete operation; and we flatter ourselves, that it will be found equal, in every respect, to any in this part of the country. Subscriptions will be thankfully received, and the paper punctually forwarded to any place.

So the account given of our clergy, will no doubt be relished by every sectarian as a compliment to his own pastor: but the man who has been acquainted with the country more at large, and who has seen clergymen labouring only to make proselytes, and damning all who differ from them in opinion, will smile at the irony contained in the statement, that their chief concern is, to teach the living how to live and the dying how to die.’ The Rev. Thomas L. Birch, a countryman of Mr. Sampson’s, and a fellow-sufferer for the same principles, will consider Mr. Sampson’s opinion of the clergy, as a bitter sarcasm upon those among whom it has been his misfortune to be thrown. Politicians may be divided also, respecting Mr. Sampson’s opinions of the Philosopher who is at the head of our affairs. Those who have heard and believed the stories of Mrs. Walker and Cambridge Jones, and those who consider Hamilton as the father of our system of finance, will laugh out, to hear that this Philosopher “keeps his own conscience, and his own accounts; pays his own debts and the nation's debts, and has hoarded up eight millions and an half in the treasury” while those who do not believe these things, will perceive in this sentence a delicate compliment to the Philosopher, and a good-humoured rebuke upon his enemies.

Those good people among us who are governed altogether by appearances, who will not degrade themselves by going to market, and who are ashamed to be seen in a suit of clothes of their own manufacture, will treat the idea of "an engraving to show him hitching his bridle to a peg," as a quiz; while others will view it as truly characteristical of a Philosopher. But however we may differ about the application of Mr. Sampson's satire to our own affairs, all will agree that the whole letter is a sprightly, pleasant, and spirited satire upon Englishmen, and upon their notions and opinions of this country. His witty and satirical attacks upon Parkinson and Anacreon Moore, must be peculiarly grateful to the American reader. These two men, after traveling through the United States, and partaking of the attention and hospitality of all our most distinguished citizens, returned to England and published their journals, in which they have indulged themselves in the most shameful misrepresentations of the American people, their character and manners. Though Mr. Sampson's ridicule of these journals cannot be fully understood, except by those who have read them, yet it will be in some degree intelligible to all, and his manner must excite risibility, even where the matter is somewhat obscure. Those good people among us who are governed altogether by appearances, who will not degrade themselves by going to market, and who are ashamed to be seen in a suit of clothes of their own manufacture, will treat the idea of "an engraving to show him hitching his bridle to a peg," as a quiz; while others will view it as truly characteristical of a Philosopher. But however we may differ about the application of Mr. Sampson's satire to our own affairs, all will agree that the whole letter is a sprightly, pleasant, and spirited satire upon Englishmen, and upon their notions and opinions of this country. My Lord—According to your orders, I was landed in this city on the 4th of July, 1806, by Capt. Sutton, of the Windsor Castle. I was sorry His Majesty’s ministers had judged it unsafe that I should be seen at Halifax, as I needed to recruit my health, and to reinforce my principles. I feared to distress your Lordship’s humanity with the account of my sufferings, or I should have written sooner. My first sickness was the yellow jaundice, of which I nearly died. I was afterwards seized with the rheumatism, and nearly lost my limbs. I am now, thank God, in good health and spirits, and shall take every means of showing myself grateful for past favors. The day I arrived, they were commemorating their independence—carousing, singing republican songs, drinking revolutionary toasts, bonfires blazing, cannons firing, and huzzaing for liberty! I was in expectation that the Lord Mayor would have brought the military, and fired on them; but the Mayor is not a lord; and I was informed he was seen drinking with the soldiers. They were also making an outcry about a Yankee sailor, called Pearce, that was killed off by Capt. Whitby. It is a pity we hadn’t them in Ireland—we might have ten thousand of them shot in a day—and not a word about them.

Tim tract contains 257 acres, a considerable part of which is cleared, and is in good order for cultivation. The soil is upon the whole very convenient for a farmer; the land, from its situation between the two rivers, and in a great measure surrounded by the hills, is of a most excellent quality. As it is remote from any other land belonging to the subscriber, he would prefer selling it; and his price is sixty pounds per acre. But if he cannot sell, he will rent it at the rate of 75 pounds per annum, payable ten years, and in either case, possession will be given the first day of December next, with the liberty of sowing a crop. If any person, having viewed the premises, should wish to purchase or to lease upon these terms, he will please to apply to the subscriber who resides in Shenandoah County. THOMAS ALLEN, sen. 1806. WILL be sold, on the third Saturday in October next, on the premises, to the highest bidder, for cash, a house and LOT, containing one-fourth of an acre, situate on the west side of the road and convenient to water; the said House and Lot being conveyed to the subscriber to secure a debt. THOMAS GRIGGS. 15, 1808. FOR SALE, a new set of HOBSON'S EDITION OF THE ENCYCLOPEDIA.

Public Sale. WILL be sold, on Tuesday next, at Thomas W. Middle Creek, all the property of the late John County, consisting of the following articles: One strong Road Wagon, three good Horses and Gears, all in complete order for immediate use, two stout Horses, a quantity of Wheat and Corn, and sundry articles too numerous for insertion. The sale will commence at ten o’clock. A reasonable credit will be given, the purchaser giving bond and approved security. All those indebted to the said estate, in any manner, are requested to make immediate payment; and those having claims, are desired to bring them on or before the first day of April next, properly attested, for settlement. All those who neglect this notice, will please to recollect, that their accounts will not be received after that time. ANTHONY LEE, Acting Adm'r. Berkeley, February 27, 1820. Public Sale. WILL be sold to the highest bidder, for ready money, on Monday the 3rd instant, at a farm called Hill and Dale, near Battle Town, in the County of Frederick, three Young Negro Men, from 18 to 30 years of age, also, all the crop of Corn, Rye, and Grain of every description, and all the Horses, Cattle and Farming Utensils, now on the said farm, which can be shown at any previous time to the sale, on application to Mr. Shively, the Overseer.

Just received an extensive assortment of best warranted BOLTING CLOTHS, of every description, which will be sold unusually low, by KENNEDYS & RAGAN. Hagers-town, June 5, 1806. [ly] FOR SALE, A TRACT of LAND, containing about 900 acres, one half of which is cleared, the balance well timbered and a considerable quantity of well watered meadow. On the premises is a good Merchant Mill and Distillery, on a never-failing stream of water, and in sight of the Potomac River. This tract can be divided into several different tenements, with a Dwelling House and Barn to each; it is of the first-rate limestone quality, and is situated in Berkeley County, Virginia, on Potomac River, 11 miles from Martinsburg, 4 from Williamsport, and 9 from Mercersburg. This land will be sold together, or divided into two tracts, as may best suit the purchaser. A good bargain will be given to a purchaser, in the Mill and one half the land, on paying about two-thirds of the purchase money in hand. For terms, apply to the subscriber on the premises. GEORGE NEWKIRK. The defendants, Benjamin Couchman, Frederick Couchman, Michael Couchman, and Malachi Couchman, not having entered their appearance agreeable to an act of Assembly and the rules of this Court, and it appearing to the satisfaction of the Court, that they are not inhabitants of this Commonwealth, on the motion of the Complainant with his Counsel, it is ordered, that the said Benjamin Couchman, Frederick Couchman, Michael Couchman, and Malachi Couchman do appear here on the Monday after the third Tuesday in April next, to answer the bill of the Complainant, and that a copy of this order be forthwith inserted in the Berkeley and Jefferson Intelligencer for two months successively, and published at the door of the Court-House of the said County. A Copy. Teste, DAVID HUNTER c.b.c. ONE CENT REWARD. Ran away from the subscriber on Thursday the 9th instant, a bound girl named ELIZABETH HUNT, about seventeen years of age. [No. 19 of Volume VI.] FRIDAY, August 4, 1804. From the New-York Evening-Post, of July 16. TO THE AMERICAN PUBLIC. The shocking catastrophe which has recently occurred, terminating the life of Alexander Hamilton, and which has spread a gloom over our city that will not be speedily dissipated, demands that the circumstances which led to it or were intimately connected with it, should not be concealed from the world. When they shall be truly and fairly disclosed, however some may question the soundness of his judgment on this occa- sion, all must be ready to do justice to the purity of his motives, and the nobleness of his nature. It will only here be added, that the authenticity of the do- cuments and the accuracy of the infor- mation which we have at last obtained, are beyond any question; and must put an end to all mistake or misrepresentation. The following is the correspondence that passed between Gen. Hamilton and Col. Burr, together with an explanation of the conduct, motives and views of Gen. H. written with his own hand the even- ing before the meeting took place and only to have been seen in the deplorable event that followed. No. 1.—New-York, June 18, 1804. SIR— I send for your perusal a letter signed Charles D. Cooper, which though apparently published some time ago, has but very recently come to my knowledge.

Mr. Van Ness, who does me the favor to deliver this, will point out to you that clause of the letter to which I particularly request your attention. You must perceive, sir, the necessity of a prompt and unqualified acknowledgment or denial of the use of any expression which would warrant the assertions of Dr. Cooper. I have the honor to be, your ob't serv't A. BURR. Gen. Hamilton. No. 2—New-York, June 20, 1804. Sir—I have merely reflected on the subject of your letter of the 18th instant, and the more I have reflected, the more I have become convinced that I could not, without manifest impropriety, make the avowal or disavowal which you think necessary. The clause pointed out by Mr. Van Ness is in these terms, 'I could detail to you a still more despicable opinion which Hamilton has expressed of Mr. Burr.' To endeavor to discover the meaning of this declaration, I was obliged to seek in the antecedent part of this letter for the opinion to which it referred as having been already disclosed; I found it in these words, 'Gen. Hamilton and Judge Kent have declared in substance that they looked upon Mr. Burr to be a dangerous man, and one who ought not to be trusted with the reins of government.'

Hamilton, a declaration whether he has charged Colonel Burr with any particular instance of dishonorable conduct, or had impeached his private character; either in the conversation alluded to by Dr. Cooper, or in any other particular instance to be specified. He would be able to answer consistently with his honor, and in truth, in substance, that the conversation to which Dr. Cooper alluded, turned wholly on political topics, and did not attribute to Colonel Burr any instance of dishonorable conduct, nor relate to his private character; and in relation to any other conversation of General Hamilton that Colonel Burr will animadvert, a prompt and frank avowal or denial will do. On the 6th June Mr. P. received the following answer: "No. 6- Sir, The letter which you yesterday delivered me, and your subsequent communication in Colonel Burr's factory accommodation. The injury complained of and the reparation expected, are so definitely expressed in Col. Burr's letter of the 21st instant, that there is not perceived a necessity for further explanation on his part. The difficulty that would result from confining the inquiry to any particular times and occasions must be manifest. The denial of a specified conversation only, would leave strong implications that on other occasions improper language had been used—When and where injurious opinions and expressions have been uttered by General Hamilton must be best known to him, and of him only will Colonel Burr enquire."

No denial or declaration will be satisfactory, unless it be general, so as wholly to exclude the idea that rumors derogatory to Colonel Burr’s honor have originated with General Hamilton or have been wrongly inferred from anything he has said. A definite reply to a re- quisition of this nature was demanded by Colonel Burr’s letter of the 21st inst. This being refused invites the alterna- tive alluded to in Gen. H*a. letter of the 30th. It was required by the position in which the controversy was placed by General Hamilton on Friday last, and I was immediately furnished with a com- munication demanding a personal inter- view. The necessity of this measure has not in the opinion of Colonel Burr, been diminished by the General’s last letter, or any communication which has since been received. I am consequently again instructed to deliver you a message, as soon as it may be convenient for you to receive it. I beg therefore you will be so good as to inform me at what hour I can have the pleasure of seeing you. Your most obedt, and very humble servt, W. P. VAN NESS. Nathaniel Pendleton, Esq. No. 9—26th June, 1804 Sir, I have communicated the letter which you did me the honor to write to me of this date, to General Hamilton.

The act of Congress of February 3rd, 1805, for building and employing a number of gun-boats, is now in a course of execution to the extent there provided for. The obstacle to naval enterprise which vessels of this construction offer for our sea-port towns, their utility towards supporting within our waters the authority of the laws, the promptness with which they are manned by the seamen and militia of the place in the moment they are wanting, the facility of their assembling from different parts of the coast to any point where they are required in greater force than ordinary, the economy of their maintenance and preservation from decay when not in actual service, and the competence of our finances to this defensive provision without any new burden, are considerations which will have due weight with Congress in deciding on the expediency of adding to their number from year to year, as experience shall test their utility, until all our important harbours, by these and auxiliary means, shall be secured against insult and opposition to the laws. No circumstance has arisen since your last session which calls for any augmentation of our regular military force. Should any improvement occur in the militia system, that will always be seasonable. Accounts of the receipts and expenditures of the last year, with estimates for the ensuing one, will, as usual, be laid before you.

But in the discharge of the great duties confided to you by our country, you will take a broader view of the field of legislation. Whether the great interests of agriculture, manufactures, commerce or navigation, can, within the pale of your constitutional powers, be aided in any of their relations? Whether laws are provided in all cases where they are wanting? Whether those provided are exactly what they should be? Whether any abuses take place in their administration or in that of the public revenues? Whether the organization of the public agencies, or of the public force is perfect in all its parts? In fine, whether anything can be done to advance the general good? —are questions within the limits of your functions, which will necessarily occupy your attention. In these and all other matters, which you in your wisdom may propose for the good of our country, you may count with assurances on my hearty co-operation and faithful execution. Th: JEFFERSON. Samuel Hiker, of the state of New York, in the room of John Smith appointed a senator of the United States, and Simon Lamed of the state of Massachusetts, in the room of Thompson J. Skinner, resigned. These were severally sworn to support the constitution of the United States, and thereupon took their seats. On motion of Mr. J. Randolph, it was ordered that the clerk (Mr. John Beckley) notify the Senate that a quorum of the House was formed and ready to proceed to business. Mr. Beckley mentioned to the Speaker that the members of the Senate had adjourned half an hour ago, but had not formed a quorum. Letters from the Governors of Virginia and Massachusetts were received by the Speaker and laid on the table without being read, as well as another in the German language. Pursuant to the standing rules and orders of the House, the following committees were appointed, viz. A committee of Elections, consisting of Messrs. Findley, Varnum, Livingston, Kennedy, Eppes, Clagett and Elmer. A committee of Ways and Means consisting of Messrs. J. Randolph, Joseph Clay, G. Griswold, Boyle, Davenport, N. R. Moore and Meriwether. One of Commerce and Manufactures, consisting of Messrs. S. L. Mitchell, Crowninshield, M'Creery, Leib, Newton, Earn and Chittenden. Another of Claims, consisting of Messrs. J. C. Smith, Holmes, Chamberlain, Stanford, Plater and Bedinger.

Adjourned. November 6. Mr. J. Randolph requested information from the Chair as to the situation in which the articles of impeachment against Samuel Chase, one of the associate justices of the supreme court of the United States, were left at the last session. The house would recollect that they were then merely reported and ordered to be printed. If that business was to be prosecuted, he conceived it of importance that the party should have all the time to prepare for his defence that their political existence would allow him. Was it the opinion of the speaker that this subject was before the committee of revision and unfinished business, or should it be referred to a special committee to prepare articles of law. The Speaker judged that it was before the committee of revision.

Resolved, That the President of the United States be requested to present in the name of Congress to Captain Stephen Decatur, a sword of the value of dollars, and to each of the officers and crew of the U. States' Ketch Intrepid, months pay, as a testimony of the high sense entertained by Congress of the gallantry, good conduct and services of Capt. Decatur, the officers and crew of the said Ketch, in attacking and destroying a Tripolitan frigate of 44 guns, late the United States' frigate Philadelphia. The resolution was referred to a committee of the whole on the State of the Union, and ordered to be printed. November 9. The petition of John Steele, presented last session, and the petition of George Little, late of the Boston frigate, now first presented for indemnity against a judgment in the Supreme Court for 10,183 dollars 89 cents damages, for the illegal detention of a foreign vessel taken in the West-Indies, in the year 1799, were referred to the committee of claims. Dr. Mitchell moved the order of the day on the President's message, but on Mr. J. Randolph's request for a little more time for members to digest and arrange the various important points contained in that communication, Dr. Mitchell withdrew his motion.

PHILADELPHIA, Nov. 13. By Capt. Gilder from Cape Francois, we have the following melancholy account:—The humanity of Captain Gibson, of the Pilgrim, having induced him to take on board some French whites, who wished to escape the dreadful cruelty of the Blacks, they were missed, and a general search took place. When the Blacks discovered the above passengers on board the Pilgrim, on which they took the captain.

The Legislature of Delaware, on Monday last, made choice of the following gentlemen for electors of President and Vice-President, Maxwell Bines, of New Castle, George Kennard, of Kent, and Thomas Fisher, of Sussex county—All Federal Republicans. The following day, the Hon. James A. Bayard, was elected a senator of the United States for the state of Delaware, to serve until the 4th of March next; in the room of the Hon. William M. Wells, resigned. In January next, the Legislature will have to elect a Senator of the United States for the term of six years from the 4th of March next, when we hope Mr. Bayard will be chosen—At the present juncture, when the small states are almost swallowed up by the large ones, and an overpowering majority transact business by a species of dumb legislation, the influence of Mr. Bayard in the House of Representatives cannot be as great as in the Senate; there, the large and small states are upon an equality; there, some respect is paid to reason and eloquence, and there, he will be more immediately in the cabinet of the Executive.

A wide field was held by complete titles; a considerable part in a written commission of sale. Not a small proportion is held by occupancy, while a simple verbal practice has always been countenanced, that proof men, when they found themselves at ease, might at their own convenience apply for and obtain complete titles. In the meantime, such imperfect rights were suffered by the government to descend by inheritance and even to be transferred by private contract. When requisite, they have been marked by judicial authority and sold for the payment of debts. Until within a few years, the governor of Upper Louisiana was authorized to make a survey of any extent. In the exercise of this discretionary power, errors were committed; a few enormous grants were created. About three years ago, he was restricted in this branch of his duty; since which he has been authorized to make surveys in the following manner: Two hundred acres for each man and wife, fifty acres for each child, and twenty for each slave. Hence the quantity of land allowed to settlers depended on the size of each family; and for this quantity of land, they paid no more than the expense of survey. These surveys served to entitle the settlers to the governor, and after him, the intendant at New-Orleans was alone authorized to exercise grants on the receipt of the surveys from the settlers. The administration of the land office is at present under the care of the public.

Below the efry, however, the lands decline so rapidly that beyond fifteen miles the soil is not well adapted to it. Above the Iberville the cape would be affected by the cold, and its produce therefore be uncertain. Within these limits, the best planters admit that one quarter of the cultivated lands of any considerable plantation may be planted in cane, one quarter left in pasture, and the remaining half employed for provisions, etc., and some reserve for change of crops. One Parisian Arpent of one hundred and eighty feet square may be expected to produce on an average twelve hundred weight of sugar, and fifty gallons of rum. From the above data, admitting that both tiers of the ire planted lot ninety arches in extent, and about three fourths of a mile in depth, it signifies that the annual product might amount to round numbers to twenty-five thousand, with more. Young planters say that one-third, or even one-half of arable land might be cultivated with ease.

When the auditor considers the case as mature, he issues his decree, which receives its binding force from the governor’s signature, where the case depends before. Therein an appeal to Havana, if applied for within four days after the date of the decree, in causes above a certain value. An ulterior appeal lies to the audiencia which formerly sat at St. Domingo, but which is now removed to some part of Cuba, and from thence to the council of the Indies in Seville. Suits are of various dimensions. In pecuniary matters, the laws encourage summary proceedings. All executions must be had on bond in four days, and space on a note of hand after the party acknowledges it, or after his signature is proved. Moveable property is sold after giving nine days' warning, provided it be three times publicly cried in that interval. Landed property must be likewise cried three times, with an interval of nine days between each, and it may then be sold. All property taken in execution must be appraised and sold for at least half of the appraisement. In pecuniary matters, the governor decides verbally without appeal when the sum does not exceed one hundred dollars. The Alcaldes have the same privilege when the amount is not above twenty dollars.

Every half signature, or flourish (which is usually affixed on common occasions), fifty cents for every whole signature, and two dollars and three fourths for every attendance—as at a sale, or the taking of evidence. The fees of the Abogado, or person consulted by the judges on law points, are twelve and a half cents for every leaf of which the process consists, and four dollars for every point of law cited. Those of the attorney, when employed, are sixty-two and a half cents for a simple petition, or escrito; but if it should be necessary to read a process in order to form his petition, and it should require much time and labour, he is compensated in proportion, besides twelve and a half cents per leaf for perusing the papers. For attendance on any business he is allowed one dollar and fifty cents for the assistance of two and a half hours. The notary has fifty cents for each decree or order of the judge, twenty-five cents for a notification in his office, and fifty cents for one out of it, but within the city he gets one dollar and seven-eighths for every attendance of two and a half hours on business, and twenty-five cents additional for every leaf of paper written by him.

A message was received from the Senate, stating that they had passed the act for the creation of a stock, as prescribed by the Louisiana treaty, with an amendment. Referred to the committee of ways and means. A message was received from the President as follows: To the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States. By the copy now communicated, of a letter from Captain Bainbridge of the Philadelphia frigate to our consul at Gibraltar, you will learn that an act of hostility has been committed on a merchant vessel of the United States, by an armed ship of the Emperor of Morocco. This conduct, on the part of that power, is without cause and without explanation. It is fortunate that Captain Bainbridge fell in with, and took the capturing vessel and her prize; and I have the satisfaction to inform you that, about the date of this transaction, such a force would be arriving in the neighborhood of Gibraltar, both from the East and the West, as leaves less to be feared for our commerce from the suddenness of the aggression.

*• On the fourth of September, the Constitution frigate, Captain Preble, with Mr. Lear on board, was within two days' sail of Gibraltar, where the Philadelphia would then be arrived with her prize; and such explanations would probably be instituted as the state of things required, and as might perhaps arrest the progress of hostilities. “ In the meantime, it is for Congress to consider the provisional authorities which may be necessary to restrain the depredations of this power, should they be continued.” - TH: JEFFERSON Referred to Messrs Kustis, J. Clay, Sands, M’Creery, and Dana. DOMESTIC INTELLIGENCE. NEW-YORK, November 5. Capt. Gibbs, of the Washington, 53 days from Rotterdam, informs, that he passed Calais the 30th of September, at which time he discovered 9 sail of frigates and gun boats, keeping up a constant fire on that place. He shortly after spoke a Duagenesa pilot boat, who informed him, that they were under the command of Sir S. Smith, and Gen. Moore. They had commenced the morning before at sunrise, and when out of sight he heard the continual reports of their guns. Capt.

Brown arrived yesterday from Lisbon, informs that a report was prevalent there about three days before he sailed, that Admiral Cornwallis had fallen in with off Brest, 15 sail of the line and five French frigates, he captured one of the line of battle ships & the 5 frigates, the latter having 1000 troops each supposed for Ireland; also that a skirmish had taken place between some French and Spanish troops on the frontiers, the issue was that the French were repulsed. It was firmly believed at Lisbon that Bonaparte would, at all hazards attempt the invasion of England. There had been two Moorish frigates and two galleys that against the Americans, one of the frigates arrived at Lisbon a few days before captain B. sailed, the other was taken some time since by one of our frigates. They had captured a Boston brig, which has since been retaken by Captain Bainbridge. CHARLESTON, October 31. A small French schooner arrived in this port on Saturday last from Barracoa, in the island of Cuba, having on board 37 inhabitants of Port-au-Prince, which place was evacuated about four weeks ago by the French troops; as many of the inhabitants as could find passages fled to Cuba in the most distressed condition; the remainder have submitted to the brigands, who it is said have treated them with humanity.

PARODY. FROM SHAKESPEARE’S HAMLET. BONAPARTE SOLUS. To invade, or not to invade, that is the question. Whether 'tis better for the mind to suffer The stings of envy, and of foiled ambition, Or to take arms against a host of Britons, And by opposing, end them? To invade— To fight? No more; and by a fight, to say, we end Our warfare, and the thousand British triumphs That France submits to. 'Tis a consummation Devoutly to be wished. To invade—To To fight? Perchance to fall: aye, there's the rub— For in that fight what hearts of oak may strike, When we have shuffled off our ships from port, Must give us pause. There's the respect That makes our armaments of so short life. For who would bear the jests and laugh of this isle, The People's scorn, the Press's con tumely, The pangs of prolonged war, the cannon's roar, The insolence of conquerors, and the spurn, That vanquished France, so often to England takes, When we ourselves might our quietus By an invasion?

HENRY BIRD, AUCTIONEER, RETURNS his respectful thanks to those who have employed him in that line, particularly the Executors of the late Gen. George Washington. The approbation of a number of characters of such respectability, is to him highly flat tering. He trusts that from his knowledge in that business, his readiness to attend at any distance, and his moderate charges, will entitle him to a share of public patronage. He continues his STARCH and HAIR POWDER manufactory, and has on hand at present, a quantity of both, of the first quality. Orders left with Mr. John Albertis will be attended to. July 8, 1803. James S. Lane & Co. Shepherdstown, July 1, 1803. CHEAP SPRING and SUMMER GOODS. The subscriber has just received, and is now opening at his Store in Martinsburg, a Large and General Assortment of Fresh Goods, bought in the City of Philadelphia, which have been selected from the latest importations from Europe and the East Indies. Also, a complete Assortment of Stationery, Consisting of Histories, Travels, Novels, School-Books, &c. A general Assortment of Groceries, Hardware and Cutlery, Weaver's Reeds, Corn-crackers and Dutch Scythes. Stones, Bair Iron, both from Hughes' and Speers' Iron-Works. As the greater part of these Goods have been purchased with Cash, he flatters himself he will be able to sell them on very reasonable terms for Cash or Country Produce. He returns sincere thanks to his friends for the encouragement he has received in his line of business for ten years past, and hopes to merit a continuation. William Riddle. June 3, 1803. NEW STORE. Elder & Cooper have opened adjoining the Globe a large and general assortment of Dry Goods, groceries. Also, a number of articles in the Paint, Dye-stuff & Drug line, which they offer for sale at moderate profits for Cash or Country Produce, and beg leave to solicit a share in the custom of the place and neighborhood. Martinsburg, June 3, 1803.

WANTED IMMEDIATELY An Apprentice to the HAT TING BUSINESS, an active well-disposed Boy, between 14 and 16 years of AGE. CHARLES D. STEWART. Martinsburg, July 1, 1803. BLANK DEEDS For sale at this Office. NEW STORE. The subscribers take leave to inform their friends, and the public generally, that they have removed their Store across the Street, into the corner Brick House, near the Market, wherein addition to their former stock, they have opened a Large and General Assortment of SPRING GOODS The same being purchased for Cash, from the latest arrivals in Philadelphia, Baltimore and Alexandria, by one of the firm, they are confident that they will now be able to sell Goods cheaper by 13 1-3 per cent, than any sold in this place before; and to convince our friends and the public, we only solicit them to give us a call, for GREAT Bargains can be had of us, for CASH or COUNTRY PRODUCE. N. B. Cash will be given for Merchantable wheat, delivered at our Mill. P. Henbousch, Martinsburg, May 13, 1803. FIFTY DOLLARS REWARD.

The government of the Navy of the United States, adopted by an act of the Congress of the United States, passed on the 23rd day of April, 1800, entitled, "An act for the better government of the navy of the United States." It appears to the court that after the British officer left the Chesapeake, bearing a positive refusal from Commodore Barron to the demand which had been made by Capt. Humphries, and after Commodore Barron was himself satisfied that an attack upon his ship would be made, he did not take prompt, necessary, and efficient means to prepare his ship for battle. That his first order was merely to clear his gun deck, and the second given after the lapse of some time, was to get his men to quarters secretly, without beat of drum; although with such a crew as he had on board, and in such a situation as the ship then was. It was not to be expected that such orders could be effectually accomplished. It appears to the court that the conduct of Commodore Barron during the attack of the Leopard manifested great indecision, and a disposition to negotiate, rather than a determination bravely to defend his ship.

Sailed from CrotMiadt, on the 15th of June, with a complete change of Miuistry, the former Minis- ters, and only immediate aftern had resigned, was done, in consequence the conditions of the treaty with France, which was unpopular. The new admi- nistration, are of course rather in favour of France. Apprehensions were enter- tained of a hostile visit from the British, and defensive preparations were making. From HAMBURG. We have been favoured with papers to the 5th of October, and have made a few translations from them. New mea- sures are adopted for the purpose of re- stricting British Commerce, which will seriously affect the United States, the only neutral nation. The war is to con- tinue between Denmark and Great Bri- tain—and the former, it appears, are to receive French aid as soon as Hind ope. HAMBURG, Septic. It is confirmed, that the king of Swe- den speaks in strong terms against the English expedition, and is very much affected by the reduction of Copenhagen. AUGSBURG, Sept, 18. An embargo has been laid at Leghorn, in order that all English property there may be seized. Similar measures of seizure are to be pursued in all other parts of the independent kingdom of Etruria. PARIS, Sept, 12. The French have been put in possession of the Seven Isles by the Russians.

The Treaty of Tofte was signed on the 18th of May 1807 between Lieutenant General Cathcart, commander in chief of his Britannic Majesty's forces in Zealand, and General Peymann, knight of the order of Dannebrog, and commander in chief of his Danish Majesty's forces in Zealand. Art. 1. When the ratifications have been signed and ratified, the troops of his Britannic Majesty are to be put in possession of the citadel. A guard of his Britannic Majesty's troops shall likewise be placed in the dockyards. 3. The ships and vessels of whatever description, with all the naval stores belonging to his Danish Majesty, shall be delivered into the charge of such persons as may be appointed by the commanders in chief of his Britannic Majesty's forces; and they are to be put in immediate possession of the dockyards, and all the buildings and storehouses. 4. The store ships and transports in the service of his Britannic Majesty are to be allowed to come into the harbor for the purpose of embarking such stores and troops as they have brought into this island.

Accounts had been received at Bordeaux, from Mr. Armstrong, at Paris, stating that a number of American seamen, taken on board of English vessels, during the war had been liberated. A letter had been received at Bordeaux, from a very respectable source in London, dated Sept. 20, stating, "that nothing definitive had taken place between the American and English governments." An article under Genoa dated Sept. 17, states, "That the American consul has been arrested, and seals put upon his papers." No reasons were assigned for the arrest nor is it probable any will be given. Neither by compulsion—nor voluntary consent, are the French disposed to give reasons for their conduct at any time. The Swedish Island of Rhgen has been surrendered to the French. Letters from Paris state that the boundaries of Louisiana have been settled by the French emperor to the satisfaction of our Minister at Paris. NORFOLK, November 20. Yesterday Capt. Tomlin, of the fast-sailing ship Pocahontas, of this port, came up to town, having left his ship in the bay bound up to Baltimore, from Liverpool. Capt. T, left Liverpool on the 4th of October, brought London papers to the 1st of that month, and has favored us with a complete file from the 10th September upwards. We have endeavored to present as much of the contents of these papers, no time and our limits would permit.

With respect to American affairs, we regret to say, that they are by no means in that state for immediate adjustment, that accounts by way of Boston have induced us to imagine. We have given in one view all the most prominent articles upon American affairs, which appeared in the London papers from the 1st to the 29th of September. They are contradictory and of course very unsatisfactory. The false rumor of Mr. Monroe's decease excited much speculation with some agitation. Upon comparing the papers with letters by this ship and with private information, we think there is no reason to apprehend an unfavorable issue to the negotiation; of which the detention of the Revenge, and Mr. Monroe’s stay, are evidences, because if a negotiation was not depending, and which did not promise a favorable result, our ministers would have desisted from all further attempt. Mr. Monroe at one time fully expected to return in the Pocahontas, but was delayed on public affairs. We have the most satisfactory information, that nothing is less desirable in England than a war with the United States. We understand from good authority, that on the 14th of September, Mr. Monroe delivered a memorial to the British government, demanding a final answer previous to his departure for the United States, for which he was already prepared, and did expect to depart immediately.

At this juncture the intelligence of the surrender of Copenhagen, the disasters in South America, and the measures of France against Portugal, with other important affairs on the continent of Europe, particularly with Russia, so pressed upon the British ministers, as to induce them to solicit Mr. Monroe's indulgence. Mr. Monroe's accordingly agreed to remain, and we have good reason to believe that the ultimatum of the British government was delivered on the 5th of October, and moreover we understand, "That no act of hostility will be committed by Great Britain, until this ultimatum has been submitted to, and acted upon by this government." Of the contents of this ultimatum it would be ridiculous in us to attempt a conjecture, but it is easy to infer that all the demands of our government have not been acceded to, but we venture to assert that the British government have not unequivocally denied any pretensions on its part to search a national ship of the United States. The disastrous result in South America has produced much discontent and a great loss. Nothing, it appears, could have been less expected. Accounts to the 15th September had been received from Lisbon, the demands by Buonaparte for money were so great as to determine, it is said, a refusal, and it is added that the court, and many of the principal persons in that country were preparing to embark for the Brazil.

Mr. Monroe's accordingly agreed to remain, and we have good reason to believe that the ultimatum of the British government was delivered on the 5th of October, and moreover we understand, "That no act of hostility will be committed by Great Britain, until this ultimatum has been submitted to, and acted upon by this government." Of the contents of this ultimatum it would be ridiculous in us to attempt a conjecture, but it is easy to infer that all the demands of our government have not been acceded to, but we venture to assert that the British government have not unequivocally denied any pretensions on its part to search a national ship of the United States. The disastrous result in South America has produced much discontent and a great loss. Nothing, it appears, could have been less expected. The children up to waste and pillage, I wish the press-gang, or the drum With its Tantara sound would come, And sweep him from the village! I said not this because he loves Through the long day to swear and tipple; But for the poor dear sake of one, To whom a foul deed he had done, A friendless Man, a travelling Cripple. For this poor crawling helpless Wretch Some horseman who was passing by, A penny on the ground had thrown; But the poor Cripple was alone And could not stoop—no help was nigh. Inch-thick the dust lay on the ground For it had long been droughty weather; So with his staff the Cripple wrought Among the dust, till he had brought The halfpennies together. It chanced that Andrew passed that way Just at the time; and there he found The Cripple in the midday heat Standing alone, and at his feet He saw the penny on the ground. He stopped and took the penny up: And when the Cripple nearer drew, Quoth Andrew, "A under half-crown, What a man finds is all his own, And to my friend good day to you."

Escaped out of the jail of Berkeley County, on the evening of the 28th December, a man by the name of Folding Lewis, about five feet six or eight inches high, stout made, of a very dark complexion, black eyes, a down look, and a scar on his left temple; had on when he went away, a blue roundabout and linen trousers, but it is probable he has changed his clothes, and it is supposed he will make towards the southward as he has relations in South Carolina; he was committed for having stabbed a man so that his bowels were let out, and otherwise scarifying him about the throat and face with a knife. Also, another man by the name of Levi Austin, about five feet five or seven inches high, slender made, one eye either blue or gray, and the other blind, with a green patch over it, tied hair, had on when he went away, a dark green cloth coat, and corded pantaloons, he was committed for felony. Whosoever takes up the said Folding Lewis and returns him to the said jail, shall receive thirty dollars, and for the said Levi Austin, fifteen dollars reward, paid by me - Moses Collins, Jailor. January 1, 1808. The following BLANKS, printed with **W and ELTC A ST TIT E.

Nearly two years have elapsed since the dissolution of the partnership of Morrow, Ferrier, Brown, during which time I have anxiously been waiting for those persons indebted to said concern to come forward and discharge their respective accounts, in which I have been disappointed. I now request all those indebted to said concern, or to myself in any manner whatever, to make immediate payment to Mr. Robert Worthington, whom I have authorized to receive the same. Those who neglect attending to this notice within a short time must calculate upon suits being commenced, as it's impossible to give any longer indulgence. John Morrow. Shepherd's Town, Nov. 27, 1807. Virginia Lands for Sale. The subscriber offers for sale several tracts of Limestone Land, of the first-rate quality, containing from 150 to 500 acres, well watered and timbered, lying within half a mile of the Potomac River, in Berkeley County, about seven miles above Williamsport and ten from Martinsburg. For terms apply to the subscriber on the premises, George Newkirk. September 18, 1807. Notice. A bargain may be had for the purchase of the place where John Files and Basil Cross now reside, containing five hundred acres of good limestone land, binding on Opequon Creek, distant about five miles from this place and six from Shepherd's Town.

Martinsburg, November 6, 1807. Notice is hereby given to all persons in Berkeley County, Virginia, that are or were indebted to me, which I have assigned to Walter Turner, not to pay him or his agents any money as aforesaid, that they have not paid, for they in justice are not his property, as I have lately found a discharge from him and his wife for the consideration for which the bonds were assigned on Maj. John Robinson and Mr. Robert Christy, and the other assignments were made for him to collect the money for me; I had lost the receipts as aforesaid, and was not able to prove the contents, and he came from Chillicothe and tormented me when I was in confusion, so that I consented to assign them to him; but since I have found it I have applied to him to release the claim and to amend our answers before the trial of the suit in Berkeley, in which said debts are contested, but he still refuses. Robert Wilcox. November 13, 1807.

Martinsburg, Virginia; Printer No. 32 of Vol. X. FRIDAY, December 30, 1848. Whole No. 500. The Spirit of the Age. Terms of subscribing and advertising—Distant must in variably pay in advance. Sub scribers, two dollars per an num, if paid within three months, and two dollars and fifty cents if delayed until the end of the year. No subscrip tion will be discontinued until arrearages are paid; and a fail ure to notify a discontinuance of the paper, at the end of the time subscribed for, will be considered a new engagement. The price of Advertisements, to transient subscribers, is one dollar per square for three weeks' insertion, and for a longer time ?1 50 cents per square. To yearly ad vertisers there will continue to be a reduction of one-fourth on the above charges. A settlement of all accounts with us, will range from two to six years, and some as long as eight years. It is not our wish to oppress at any time, much less at a period when the industrious mechanic and laborer finds it difficult to obtain the means of support. We are disposed to make every reasonable effort in our power, and therefore will give liberal indulgence to those who are unable to discharge their accounts promptly.

Being almost out of print and with the hope that its circulation will be of great public good, and have a tendency to point out to searchers after righteousness the true path which it may be found. He trusts that it will richly repay those for its perusal who are in search of Divine truths; all who wish to see the glorious Gospel promoted and diffused in our land, he doubts not, will feel a disposition to encourage this scarce and valuable work. The publisher is not actuated by interested views in offering this work to the public; his sole object is the dissemination of truths necessary for every human being, that he may be acquainted with. He only wishes to obtain as many subscribers as will pay for the printing, his own situation being such as to put it out of his power to have it republished without the aid of others. The work will probably make from 313 to 300 duodecimo pages; it shall be well printed on good paper, and the price, half-bound, shall not exceed one dollar; those who wish them bound in leather can have them at the additional expense of binding; if the number of subscribers should fall equal to his expectation, the price in all probability will be put to press for printing. Subscriptions received at the store of the publisher. John Huntington. Junius, 1811.

JAMES CLARKE. December 16, 1806. DOCUMENTS ACCOMPANYING THE MESSAGE OF THE PRESIDENT. (CONTINUED.) Extracts of a letter from Mr. Madison, secretary of state, to Mr. Pinkney, minister of the United States at London, dated Department of State, December 23, 1807. Mr. Erskine having been so good as to let me know that the mail of this evening will carry his dispatches for a British packet, which will sail from New-York immediately on their arrival there, and other conveyances now failing, I avail myself of the opportunity to enclose you a copy of a message from the president to congress, and their act in pursuance of it, laying an immediate embargo on our vessels and exports. The policy and the causes of the measure are explained in the message itself.

But it may be proper to authorize you to assure the British government, as has been just expressed to its minister here, that the act is a measure of precaution only, called for by the occasion; that it is to be considered as neither hostile in its character, nor as justifying, or inviting to hostility with any nation whatever, and particularly as opposing no obstacle whatever to amicable negotiations and satisfactory adjustments with Great Britain, on the subjects of difference between the two countries. The suddenness of the present opportunity does not allow me time to add more than a newspaper, containing a part of the proceedings of congress in relation to the embargo. P. S. As you may be able to find conveyances to Paris, whither none will for some time offer hence, I request the favor of you to communicate to General Armstrong the contents of this letter, and through him, or otherwise, to Mr. Brent at Madrid." Extract from the same to the same, dated Department of State, February 19, 1808. "A vessel having been engaged to carry from the port of New York public dispatches and mercantile letters to Europe.

Mr. Ermine was asked whether his government distinguished between the operation of the French decree, municipally on land, and its operation on the high seas. On this point he was unable to answer. He also was to an enquiry whether the late British decrees had reference to the late extension of the French decree with respect to the United States. He seemed also, as is perhaps the case with his government, to have taken very little into consideration the violation of neutral commerce, and through them the vast injury to France antecedent to the Berlin decree. It is probable that something final is to pass between us on this fact." Extract of a letter from the same. In regard to ourselves it might, for a long time to come supercede the use of the word. Spain had Mexico and a great part of South America, still left which might as occasion should offer, be bought and that, in the event of ill treatment from France or Britain, purchase could be resorted to, as both nations had colonies, about which they did not much care, and waste lands, which he made no doubt they would sell cheap to put an end to disputes. Other members aught talk of national honour but for his part, he did not choose that it should mar a good bargain. He quoted Adam Smith to show the great increase in the value of lands in some countries of Europe on which he grounded an estimate of the value of the Floridas a century hence, and in conclusion, said the report should have his decided sentence. A member from New Jersey next rose. I admit, sir, said he, all the statements of the honorable gentleman who first addressed you today, but I am nevertheless against the report, and hope it will not be adopted. The important question before us has not yet, as it strikes me, been viewed in its true light. The real party to this dispute with us is France. I hope this is seen. Adopt the report on your table and war with France, not Spain, is the consequence.

Spain had Mexico and a great part of South America, still left which might as occasion should offer, be bought and that, in the event of ill treatment from France or Britain, purchase could be resorted to, as both nations had colonies, about which they did not much care, and waste lands, which he made no doubt they would sell cheap to put an end to disputes. Other members aught talk of national honour but for his part, he did not choose that it should mar a good bargain. He quoted Adam Smith to show the great increase in the value of lands in some countries of Europe on which he grounded an estimate of the value of the Floridas a century hence, and in conclusion, said the report should have his decided sentence. A member from New Jersey next rose. I admit, sir, said he, all the statements of the honorable gentleman who first addressed you today, but I am nevertheless against the report, and hope it will not be adopted. The important question before us has not yet, as it strikes me, been viewed in its true light. The real party to this dispute with us is France. I hope this is seen. Adopt the report on your table and war with France, not Spain, is the consequence.

Mercy! Mr. Chairman, when the long sword of the minister now in your metropolis is seen shining in the drawing rooms, or trailing through yonder avenue, who does not shudder at the anticipated vengeance of the Emperor? Who does not think of Lindi? Who does not think of Marengo, where he said it was his custom to "sleep upon the field of battle"? Is it not madness to talk of fighting such a man? I, for one, renounce all the honor that would flow from a conflict with him. At the present critical juncture, Sir John Falstaff's notions beat and the American people, "the better part of valor is discretion." Hordes of Gallic regiments stand with their swords half unsheathed ready to strike us. The caution of the legislature would be trusted, return them safely to their scabbards. The arm lifted up to strike, a reflecting man would stay by a soothing douceur. The Floridas, he said, formed a fertile and valuable country, but with humility, he preferred taking peaceable possession of them for a few millions of dollars to fighting battles there. Here the usual hour of adjournment having passed, the committee rose, reported progress, and obtained leave to sit again. MARTINSBURG, April 25. On Monday last an election was held In this town, for the purpose of choosing two representatives for the County of Berkeley in the State Legislature.

He meant to try Mr. Jef ferson by the same scale which had been adopted in the trial of John Adams, and the same measure should be meted out to him that had been meted out to another. He attacked Burr, Rppssand Jackson in language personal had pointed beyond example. They each made an attempt at a defence; but it was barely an attempt. [New-York Herald] A young government like it, yet con- stitutional, has already taken a root that will never be eradicated. The pure de mocrats, who hate the leaves and the shoots but love the tree, are already fear rolling among them to see and corruptly intriguing for office through the instrumentality of the next presidential election. The factions are the New-York faction (or Clin ton faction); the Madison faction, and the Monroe faction. All the baiting portions of the different factions expect in turn, Secretaryships, Am bassadorships, Contractorships, Collect orships, and all the glittering objects of sotic worship. Mr. Bidwell pares menace___r. is to be secretary of state, or of the treas ury, should Madison succeed; Mr. Ran dolph is to be what he pleases, should Monroe succeed; should De Witt Clinton succeed, the devil and all will be promot ed. Monroe is expected home shortly to make his bids.

The following melancholy article is copied from the Pennsylvania Correspondent, printed at Doylestown, in Bucks County, Pennsylvania. "News of murders and robberies generally excites a greater degree of interest than information of any other kind. Intelligence is circulating in this neighborhood, of which the following is the substance. Its authenticity is not sworn to, but should it prove to have been a melancholy reality, the public shall hear more about it. A man living on or near the Dry Lands, who had to pay the sum of 800l. about the first of April, called on his neighbor who kept a public house, informed him of the payment he had to make, and observed, he had the whole amount at his own house, except 15l. which he wished to borrow for a few weeks. The landlord very cheerfully agreed to lend the sum required, stating that he had it not in possession, but expected to go abroad the next day to collect the money, and would return in the evening when his neighbor might call and receive the sum wanted.

Each taking a pistol they cautiously approached the lighted window, where with astonishment they beheld three men with blackened faces, counting money at a table. Each of the spectators singled out his man, and two of the midnight plunderers fell lifeless on the floor; the third was met at the door, but conscious guilt had unnerved his arm, he was soon dispatched. Reader, if you have tears, prepare to shed them now. The agitated husband went into his bedchamber, where the wife of his bosom and three young children were weltering in blood, and closing their eyes in death, having been inhumanely butchered in the unsuspecting moments of sleep by the three persons before mentioned. My informant could not give the names of the parties, but states that on washing the blackened faces of the robbers, they proved to be the brothers of the owner of the neighboring, and EPIGRAM. Said a Reverend Divine, "Here's a trick, my lad, Under guidance of worldly dominion. I much fear your conduct has been very bad, Let me know your religious opinion." Quoth Pat, "My opinion's the same to a hair As Murphy’s who keeps at the sign of the Bear." "How now," cried the Parson, "You rascal, so sly! Why am I thus insulted by your reverence, must know, 'Tis thinks I shan’t pay him the score that I owe— By my soul, and I think for myself."

J. J. LANCASTER THEODORE MENENGER is authorized to settle the accounts of Doctor Edward Coorad, late of this place—Those indebted will oblige by paying the amount of their accounts— Suits will be instituted against such as do not show a disposition to settle. Martinsburg, September 25, 1807. NOTICE. I had flattered myself that long before this, it would be in my power to collect many but there is yet very con- siderable debts due to me; I now for the last time remind those indebted to me, to settle before the first day of No vember next, as suits will positively be taken against those who fail to make payment on, or before that time. JAMES CAMPBELL. Sept. 25, 1807. I REQUEST those indebted to the estate of Robert Lyle, deceased, to make immediate payment and final settlement of that estate, as a public sale of the personal property will take place in the month of October next, when no further indulgence can be given. JAMES CAMPBELL, Guardian. Sept. 25, 1807. CHARLES-TOWN RACES. THE Charles-Town Jockey Club Purse will be run for as usual, on the third Wednesday in October next. It is expected that the racing will continue only two days, which will make each day's stake better than it has been heretofore. GEORGE HITE, Secretary. Charles-Town, September 11, 1807. CAME to the plantation of James Strode, dec’d, on the 15th of July last, a red sorrel horse colt, with a small star, supposed to be one year old last spring, appraised to sixteen dollars.

WILL be offered at public vendue, on Wednesday the 21st instant, at the place where the subscriber now lives, about two miles from Martinsburg, Young Horses, Milch Cows, Young Cattle, Household and Kitchen Furniture, Farming Implements, and a quantity of Corn. Nine months credit will be given on bond with approved security. ELIZABETH VANCE. October 9, 1807. BY virtue of a deed of trust, executed by James Morrow to the subscriber, to secure a sum of money thereto mentioned, due from the said Morrow to William Sommerville, will be sold, on the premises, to the highest bidder for ready money, on Saturday the 14th inst., a House and half Lot of Ground, the property of the said Morrow, situate on Water street in the town of Martinsburg. WILLIAM BELL, Trustee. October 9, 1807. Public Sale. WILL be sold at public sale, on Monday the 19th instant, at the house of the subscriber in Martinsburg, a variety of Household Furniture, consisting in part of a number of Feather Beds, Bedding and Bedsteads, Tables, etc. A credit will be given, on bond with approved security. The subscriber wishes to rent the house he now lives in, lately occupied as a tavern by Mr. Brady, the property of Ignatius O’Ferrall, and so well known as a public house, as to render a description of it unnecessary. Possession may be had on the 1st day of January next, which will be the 30th instant. ROBERT GREGORY. October 5, 1807.

WILL be offered at public vendue, on Wednesday the 21st instant, at the place where the subscriber now lives, about two miles from Martinsburg, Young Horses, Milch Cows, Young Cattle, Household and Kitchen Furniture, Farming Implements, and a quantity of Corn. Nine months credit will be given on bond with approved security. ELIZABETH VANCE. October 9, 1807. BY virtue of a deed of trust, executed by James Morrow to the subscriber, to secure a sum of money thereto mentioned, due from the said Morrow to William Sommerville, will be sold, on the premises, to the highest bidder for ready money, on Saturday the 14th inst., a House and half Lot of Ground, the property of the said Morrow, situate on Water street in the town of Martinsburg. WILLIAM BELL, Trustee. October 9, 1807. Public Sale. WILL be sold at public sale, on Monday the 19th instant, at the house of the subscriber in Martinsburg, a variety of Household Furniture, consisting in part of a number of Feather Beds, Bedding and Bedsteads, Tables, etc. A credit will be given, on bond with approved security. The subscriber wishes to rent the house he now lives in, lately occupied as a tavern by Mr. Brady, the property of Ignatius O’Ferrall, and so well known as a public house, as to render a description of it unnecessary. Possession may be had on the 1st day of January next, which will be the 30th instant. ROBERT GREGORY. October 5, 1807.

Dry Goods and Groceries, which will be sold on the very lowest terms, for Cash or Country Produce, or for short credit to punctual customers. JAMES FAULKNER. Martinsburg, September 21, 1807. PURSUANT to the last will and testament of Edward Watkins, deceased, will be sold at public auction, at Culpeper Court-House, on the first day of January next, about forty-five choice healthy Virginia born slaves, Men and Women, Boys and Girls, mostly young and very likely; sundry articles of household furniture, twelve months' credit will be allowed to the purchaser, who must execute bonds with approved security for the purchase money, before any property will be delivered. WILLIAM PENDLETON, Ex'or. Meklenburg County, Virginia, 1807. Fifty Dollars Reward. ESCAPED by breaking through the wall of the jail of Berkeley county, a certain George Hebler aka* Joseph Keskr, who was found guilty by an examining Court of Horse stealing, he is a German, in appearance soft or silly, but a great villain, about thirty-five years of age, five feet nine or ten inches high, dark hair and of a pale countenance, he has been sick in prison, had on and took with him a crossbarred coat and striped pantaloons of home made cotton, and cloth clothes of a lead color. Also, certain Isaac Compton, who was found guilty of burglary, he is about thirty!

On Saturday last, a negro man riding a dark iron grey mare, about six or seven years old, about fourteen hands and a half high, with two white spots near the root of her tail, with a taffeta bridle having a plated bit, and a leather collar with a piece of rope attached to it on her, in attempting to cross the Potomac river at Burns’s ford below Shepherd’s-Town, where the subscriber resides, in consequence of the river being too high to ford, fell off in the river and was afterwards seen swimming or floating down the river; upon being disengaged from her rider the mare returned to the Virginia shore, and was taken up by the subscriber, any person owning the mare, bridle, etc. may have them again by applying to the subscriber and paying him for his expense and trouble with her. CHRISTOPHER HIAT. Sept. 11, 1801. Strayed or stolen from the subscriber’s plantation, near Martinsburg, on Sunday night the 14th instant, a bright bay horse with a dark mane and tail, one of his hind feet supposed to be white, and has a blaze in his face, is about fifteen hands high, and was eight years old last spring, has been drove to a wagon, and his shoulders are hurt with the collar, trots naturally and was shod all around.

Five dollars will be given for returning said horse, if strayed or if stolen, and the thief convicted, fifteen dollars. HUGH V. PATTERSON. Sept. 18, 1807. PARIS, Inside; >4; . Under the present form of our government and considering the genius which directs everything, it is no wonder that much profound secrecy has been hitherto preserved respecting the destination of the Toulon fleet. Four different plans had been laid before the Emperor, relative to the destination of that fleet, which was victualled at all events for a long period. He cancelled and burned some of those plans, and sent himself the plan he had adopted to Toulon to be followed—so that those in his confidence did not know which plan his Majesty had chosen. The Emperor has provided the Minister of the Interior Company, with the necessary powers to organize the three Chinese departments. From the 9th of June, all the acts of that Minister must be obeyed as forms in the whole compass of these force departments. BELFAST, July 5. We are not able to satisfy the public not falling mis to intercept the they are on their return, as reported by the Curieex. Admiral Sir Robert Calder, foe wind, has been reinforced off Ferrol, by the Windsor Castle and Barfleur, of 64 guns, and the Triumph Princess Royal, and Warrior, of 74 guns each. And considerable additions have been made to the Roche. I and Charlton Stockading syndrom. -f CHARLESTON, August 23.

The brig Eliza, captain Taylor, arrived yesterday in 38 days from Malaga, furnishes the following intelligence. All classes of people leap with joy at the deliverance without the terror or the coil-* sympathy does honour to the national character, and we ought to do nothing to damp it. But what is the sober account of the news from Tripoli? Well, it is clear that the first account that Tripoli was taken by the forces under the ex-Bashaw is not correct. If it was, the Usurper would have been the real reigning sovereign, and with him must the peace have been concluded. The contrary would seem to be the truth. — The article from the Salem Register, which is the last, informs us that there had indeed been a battle at Derna, but concerning it is uncertain on which side of victory was declared. The effect, however, of the battle, was a negotiation for peace. Of course the negotiation must have been with the reigning Bashaw. What the terms of peace are we know not, it is said they are honorable to the United States. Two questions will arise. One whether a peace feagdt indeed is and at what price! Pen. in administration may have so far changed their opinion on this and other subjects, as to hold it compatible with national honor to ship a peace now, though they formerly set up the most lamentable howls about national degradation, because President Washington bought a peace of the same power.

When we take the terms, if our cabinet and so forth remember another of so far forget the whole course of their conduct, as to act for once with a little consistency, then, law, and see the terms we shall be able to form an opinion about their goodness. In the mean time we have to remark and we shall soon dismiss the subject, that after the squadron, (because) gambols we are indebted for the liberties of our unfortunate fellow-citizens to the intrepidity and boldness of an individual, by leading an army of rebellious subjects, in the place of a pretender to his brother's throne. And we confess our curiosity is broad awake to know what provisions have been made in the treaty in behalf of the pretender himself, Sidi Hamet Caramanli. Because we happen to remember that Mr. Secretary Madison once wrote a letter on this subject which contained about important, though it must be acknowledged vague promises in behalf of Sidi.

In a letter to Mr. Eaton dated August 1803, our good Secretary thus expressed himself, Although it does not accord with the general sentiments or views of the United States to interfere in the domestic controversies of other countries, it cannot be unfair, in the prosecution of a just war, or the accomplishment of a just peace, to take advantage of the hostile cooperation of others, for therefore as the views of the may contribute to our success, them may be used for the purpose. Should this aid be found inapplicable, or the object unattainable, it will be due to the honor of the United States, and to the expectations he will naturally have formed, to treat his disappointment with tenderness, and to restore him (as near as may be) to the situation from which he was drawn, or to some other convenient arrangement that may be more eligible to him—In case of a treaty of peace with the ruling Bashaw of Tripoli, perhaps it may be possible to make some stipulations formal or informal in favor of the Brother, which may be a desirable alleviation of his misfortune for Mr. Madison’s letter.

Accounts are received at New-York from Marseilles. All reports of the current month concur in the authenticity of the information respecting the French having ceded one half of the Island of Cuba to the French. It is reported in this city, that the British minister, the Marquis of Trujo having determined to leave the U.S. has demanded his passports from our government. The report adds, that the President observed in reply, that we had no such etiquette in this country, and that it was in the power of a foreign minister to quit the United States when and how he pleased. A file of New-Orleans papers, which winch, by yesterday's western mail, contain a spirit of defiance and paaiarde. They contain but few facts of any great moment; and these appear rather in the form of floating rumours, than in the firm and authenticated language of truth. The papers of September state from sources that may be relied on, that an army of 6000 men is on its march to strengthen the Spanish.

If the study of human nature be of any importance to mankind—if the splendid achievements of antiquity be worthy of remembrance in later times—the utility of the en terprising work, for which these proposals are issued, must be generally acknowledged. The publishers of this proposed edition promise to have it accurately printed on good paper; and as most of the engravings in the original editions are so badly executed as to be a blemish instead of an ornament to the work, they intend to publish only the maps, and such of the other plates as are absolutely necessary to elucidate the subjects, and aid the readers in their researches; which will of course render it costlier, but not inferior, to foreign editions. Mr. Rollin was a writer who improved and adorned every subject of his pen. His graceful and captivating style seems to impart beauty to nature, and majesty to truth; and his history has stood the test of years, without the marks of time or neglect, that it begets itself, to gain respect for its antiquity, and excellence by preference. For the extent of his knowledge, the grandeur and variety of his topics, and the happy talent of conveying pleasure with his instruction, Mr. Rollin has rarely been surpassed. He sometimes carries you to the field of Mars, and terrifies you with sounds of battle, cries of desolation, and trophies of conquest. At other times he shows you the infant beginnings of art and science, the small circles on which they moved, and gradually widens your view of their expanded improvements. Again.

For the present we shall confine our remarks to the mob, who, from the indifference of the authorities, take place on the levee every Sunday. By perusing a few of these lines, we may conclude that we were in a state of anarchy. Not less than twenty persons were, with clubs, sticks of wood, etc., laid prostrate on the ground at one time on Sunday last, many of whom were accidentally passing the street. If there were no lives lost, it is not the police of the city we are to thank; should these disorders continue unchecked, we may expect to see the streets flow with the blood of the citizens. A patrol of half a dozen men would be sufficient to prevent these evils. If these measures are not speedily taken, we must arm for our own defense, and owe our safety to our courage. No particulars were received, but the fleet was expected down to Gibraltar every day, in case the report proved to be true. Capt. Brown left Gibraltar on the 6th June. Extract of a letter from Gibraltar, dated June 6, 1804, to a gentleman in this town. “By an American vessel, arrived yesterday, the captain has made a deposition that on passing Toulon, he saw the English and French fleets engaging. The American consul has since had a letter, and it is reported that the British have totally defeated the French, and taken eight sail of the line.—Though the intelligence is not completely satisfactory, it is generally believed that there has been an action." We think it proper to observe that in another letter, received by the same conveyance and dated at the same place and moment, no mention is made of this event. What degree of truth is therefore to be attached to this news, we know not. Time must determine.

From the Wed Indict.—Captain Johnson arrived at New York, from Guadaloupe, informs, that two or three days before he left that place, which was on the 16th July, he learnt from three gentlemen who had escaped and arrived there the night previous, that the inhabitants of Martinique hourly expected that place would surrender to the British squadron then before the town. Provisions at Martinique were very scarce, owing to the vigilance of the blockading squadron, suffering none to enter. Several privateers had been fitted out at Guadaloupe for St. Domingo, with express orders, to take, sink and destroy all American vessels, bound to or from there. Six of these privateers, mounting from ten to fourteen guns and full of men, had already sailed from Point Petre to attack American vessels. A person was detected on Friday last by Gilbert and Dean in attempting to obtain the prize of one hundred dollars in the last drawn class of South Carolina Lottery, by a ticket, the number of which had been altered from 44 to 41. After an examination before judge Bourne, he was committed to prison for further trial. The man is from New Salem, and has been working on the State Prison at Charlestown, where it is probable he will soon become a tenant.
