Other candidates may be named; but it is hoped a spirit of union will govern in the choice. For Lincoln, we understand that the Hon. David Cobb, Mark L. Hill and William King, Esq’rs. are in nomination. Kennebec is considered as given up for the present, as a sporting ground for the Jacobins. Gen. Chandler, will probably succeed in that county. JMR. JENKS, THE most respectable talents, the most unimpeachable integrity, and the most ardent patriotism, however valuable to the possessor in private life, may by age and infirmity, be rendered useless to the public. Few men, perhaps, have been more respectable for talents, integrity, and patriotism than the Hon. John Cushing, Esq. who was chosen to represent this county in the Senate of this Commonwealth; but who, from advanced age, and bodily infirmities, has been absent from the General Court the whole of the present session: — And never, perhaps, was there a session when the presence of men of consistent principles was more necessary. Viewing the subject as here represented, and believing most sincerely that the interest of the country requires it, I ask leave to nominate AMMI RUHAMAH MITCHELL, Esq. of North Yarmouth, as a gentleman whose talents, integrity and patriotism, seem to point him out in a peculiar manner as a suitable successor to Mr. Cushing, in the Senate of this Commonwealth.

The people of the county are requested to take the subject seriously into consideration, and at the ensuing election, to vote as they may think the public good shall require. A FREEHOLDER. M*. JIN K31 YOU are requested to mention to the electors of York county, that the Hon, SIMON FRYE, and JOHN LORD Esq. will be liberally supported as Senators at the ensuing election. Other candidates are undoubtedly respectable; But certainly none can be named who will serve us with greater ability and effect, and none who from their local situation, as well as every other circumstance, will, arise so great a number of votes. A VOTER. County Register of Deeds. MR. JENKS, AS a County Register, give one leave to offer a candidate from the country.—ANDREW R. GIDDINGS, Esq. of Pejepscot, has every requisite ability to execute the office with honor to himself and justice to the country, in the opinion of very many YEOMEN. Freeport, February 29th. N. E. He will remove to Portland if he should be chosen. MS. JENKS. AS a report has prevailed in town that the office of register of deeds would not be acceptable to Mr. STEPHEN WAITE, I feel authorized, and think it my duty to declare that it is without foundation. The modesty of this gen.

Sobriety, fidelity, neat and elegant penmanship, are any recommendations in a candidate, he will most certainly receive liberal support on the day of election — and the county may be persuaded that from his services they will receive all that satisfaction which they have a right to expect. A. B, Mr. Pink, PERMIT me through the medium of your paper, and among the numerous and respectable candidates for the office of Register of Deeds, to apprize the voters of this county that Capt. LEVI CUTTER, of North Yarmouth, will receive a handsome support in that town and its vicinity. His respectability of character, regular habits, agreeable manners, and his qualifications to discharge the duties of that office with correctness and dispatch, all recommend him to the notice of his fellow citizens, and entitle him to their confidence and support. I am also authorized to state from good authority, that the suggestions which have been circulated that Capt. Cutter declines being considered as a candidate, are totally incorrect, and without the least foundation. A CITIZEN. CCJ* Several other electioneering favors, are unavoidably omitted. Fire. —On Tuesday evening last, a fire broke out at Freeport Landing, in the store of Mr. Samuel Porter, which consumed the store and all the goods. Nothing but the books were saved. Store and goods, estimated at 4500 dollars.

The improvement of your mind has not kept pace with the increase of your wealth. Fortune has made you a rich man, but Nature never designed you for a great one. Content yourself then, with your riches, hug them to your bosom, exert every nerve, call into action every faculty of your mind, to add to your enormous mass of treasure, but do not aspire to a situation for which Nature never designed you. Have you not of late greatly improved your fortune? Has not the restrictive policy of the Administration added thousands to your wealth, while it has reduced to poverty the middling, industrious and enterprising Merchant? Did you not approve of the Embargo, because it conduced to your interest, while it preyed like a Vulture on the vitals of the nation? Did you not make immense sums by that measure? Have you not then thrived on the misfortunes, banqueted on the woes, and fattened on the miseries of the people? Is not the Emperor of France thousands of your property in his grasp? On that account, do you not wish to conciliate the favor of his Despotic Majesty? Would you not kiss the toe of the insolent Corsican for one approving smile? Would you not rather sacrifice national interest, honor and dignity, than lose your cash in the French funds?

I put the question to your conscience, have you the requisite qualifications for the office of Lt. Governor? Are your pretensions superior to those of Gen. Cobb? Do you not aspire to honor to promote your own private interest, rather than the public good? Is not avarice your ruling passion? While you were filling your coffers, Gen. Cobb grew grey in the service of his country. He was the friend and companion of Washington. Ought the veteran to go unrewarded? Shall ingratitude "sharper than a serpent's tooth" embitter the last moments of a life spent in the service of his country? Shall he descend to the grave with his country's curses on his head? You, Sir, may rob him of office, but you can never rob him of his well-earned fame. The name of Cobb will shed a luster on the page of American History for ages after that of Gray shall have been forgotten. WAYNE Plain Common Sense. 1. Bonaparte is aiming at universal dominion—No man will deny this—His government is a military despotism. 2. He knows he cannot maintain this government, unless the people are kept ignorant and poor. 3. He keeps them ignorant by completely destroying the liberty of the Press. No printer dare publish one word on politics without his express permission. 4. He keeps them poor, by destroying all Commerce, and the means of supporting it.

This he has done wholly in France, and is doing it as much in every part of Europe. He knows that a commercial people will become informed and in love with liberty. Hence Commerce in all its branches is despised by him. 5. For the same reason he is anxious for destroying the commerce of America, because it aids Britain—and because he believes he can never conquer Britain unless he can prevent our trading with her. 6. Hence he approved of our Embargo as a wise measure because it essentially advanced his plans. 7. He approved of it also, because it gradually tends to lessen the power of this country; and in fact, has already drained our treasury, and infused among the people a spirit of idleness and immorality. 8. From the above we plainly see, how strong the influence of Bonaparte must be in this country: when we behold such mighty effects resulting from it. We see that our rulers are led on to adopt the measures he wishes, and which are absolutely necessary to the continuance of his iron despotism. 9. The above facts also show the hatred to commerce which exists in the southern States, and their anxiety to make us weak as they are. 10.

The influence of France appears also, in this, that while she is at this moment seizing all American property in France— burning and sinking our ships—and confining our seamen in dungeons our government is as silent as the grave on the subject. 11. It appeals in this, that the Baltimore Whig, a paper warm on the democratic side, has published to the world that 'tis time to destroy our present federal Constitution, and have a President and Senate for life. Exactly in the same manner as Napoleon trampled on the necks of the French people and mounted the throne. 12. It appears also in this, that our future King is already in Baltimore.—A Prince of Napoleon's family is in the heart of this country educated under a French Master. Why is he educated here, unless by degrees to prepare us for the name of a King and for a Monarchy. 13. It appears also in this, that there are among us thousands who are continually preaching French politics, and attempting more and more to divide us and inflame our passions—exactly as has been done by France in all the countries they have subdued. The people are desired to read the above remarks and say if they are not true.

I am not disposed to find fault with any man for worshipping God in the manner most agreeable to him: but when the Bible and the Pulpit are used for such mean and party purposes, 'tis certainly an abuse which calls aloud for the check of public opinion and censure. AN OLD MAN. Ahoi! Shipmates—heave to a bit. Throw your top-sails to the masts, and let us come alongside. Now d’ye see on the first Monday of April, which mind ye is close aboard of us, there’s to be a new choice of officers on board the good ship Massachusetts—and hark'e, some of the crew are determined the present worthy Commanders shan’t navigate her the next cruise—Now every man of ye well knows there’s always some lubberly fellows, mere cabin-window gentry, that think they know all a seaman’s duty, when, splinter my standards if they can splice, reef, steer, or box the compass; who can’t tell the larboard from the starboard bow—aye, nor a clue line from a top-mast back-stay. And these milk sops, d’ye see, are trying to pick a quarrel amongst the officers & crew, because what, why by the powers, because d’ye see, every sail isn’t handed when they think it’s best, and by the bye, I suppose their being turned out last voyage, didn’t sit very well in their crops.

This day you are notified to elect your Town Officers—and it is the duty of every Federalist, for every voter that is not willing to have a set of Jacobin rulers, to be present at the opening of the meeting. The democrats have been plotting in private to trick you in the elections of this day. Suffer not this reproach to come upon you through supineness or forgetfulness. At the ringing of the bell, duty calls to you to repair to the Court-House. London dates to Jan. 20th, are received. The British cabinet had not, at the above date, come to any decision respecting the rupture with Mr. Jackson, but were still deliberating on the course they would pursue. Parliament was to convene in a few days, when the question would be decided. It was reported in England, that some kind of an arrangement was entered into about the 6th of January, between the French and our government, but of the nature and extent of the arrangement, no intimation is given. The circumstance had given rise to an idea that it was the determination of the United States to go to war with England. The United States’ frigate John Adams, sailed from the Downs, Jan. 17, for Amsterdam. Her arrival in the United States is daily expected. Letters have been received at Washington, from Morlaix, Fr.

So late as January, which make no mention of a settlement with France. Bonaparte has had another attack of the epilepsy, but recovered in a few days. We again say, that the story in circulation about several gentlemen in this town having turned democrats, is a base slander. They are as true as ever in the good cause; and on this very day, those same gentlemen will be rechosen, by the suffrages of their fellow citizens, to the offices they now fill. Poor souls the democrats are! To support their cause, they are endeavoring to get the weight of some federal worth into their scale. Hence the above lie was made and propagated. Parson Merrill's story in the Argus, about General Cobb, is just equal to democratic reason and candor. The conversation he speaks of, was in May, 1808—almost two years ago and never was thought of till now! Did he wait it as a good story, to tell when other lies were worn out; or did he consider the whole as mere chit-chat, and not worth mentioning, till some demo pumped it out of him? They publish the names of three gentlemen from this town, who do not own so much navigation as Win.

That in case it shall appear to Congress that all fair attempts to remove said Orders and Decrees by negotiation, shall have been exhausted, and they shall find it necessary to assume any other attitude of resistance, it will be the duty of the whole people of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts, to rally round the standard of their own nation and its government, and to afford them their utmost support by all Constitutional means in their power. The above Resolves were committed to Messrs. Con Cresswell, Hough, of J. Adrain and Ivei, with instructions to report at the next session. REPORT. The Committee to whom was referred the two Resolutions, that accompany this Report, and which were proposed for the consideration of this House, have duly attended to their commission, and ask leave to report, that, in their opinion, it is inexpedient to pass the same for the following reasons: By the Constitution of the United States, the foreign relations thereof are, exclusively, vested in the national government. With that government rests the obligation to consider of, and act upon the doings of other nations—with it rests, also, a knowledge of the conduct of other nations—their motives and pretensions, and how far the same may have been influenced, or encouraged by the government of the United States.

The communications, which have passed between the United States, and the nations referred to, in the proposed Resolutions, are in a great degree unknown to the Legislature of Massachusetts; any opinion, therefore, of the House of Representatives, on this subject, would be founded on an imperfect knowledge of what relates thereto, and might, from the same cause be erroneous. The House could not rely on the partial information, which is allowed to escape from the Executive Cabinet, much less, on obscure, fecret feflions of Congress, for the correctness of any opinion, they might form on so important a matter.

A nation, previously committed by her, through the commerce of neutral nations, could never be admitted as true in tact, or if true, as just in principle, in regard to the United States. The principle said to have been assumed by Great Britain, in 1756, which has been pressed into the service of those who are delirious to find an apology, if not a justification of every outrage, committed by France, although adopted in the early part of the last war, was so modified, as to afford no cause of complaint to the United States during the latter years of that contest, and it is believed, that a similar temper of accommodation has been maintained by the same power towards the United States, in the present war. The Utrecht Gazette, July, 1756, declares, if any Dutchman carry any goods or merchandise of the growth or manufacture of the enemies of France, they shall be deemed good prize, but the ships shall be discharged. On the 1st July they again decreed as on the 23rd May. Twenty-seven days afterwards, this Decree was repealed, and that of the 9th May remained in force until 4th January, 1795.

The Decree of Berlin thereby violating the rights of the United States, infringing the law of nations, and prostrating the commercial rights of all neutral States. This decree is substantially and almost literally the same as that passed by the French Directory in 1798, and which President Adams in his speech to Congress, in December following, pronounced to be "an unequivocal act of war, which interest as well as honor called upon the nation firmly to resist." Congress accordingly proceeded to pass laws, annulling the treaties with France, prohibiting all commercial intercourse with the French dominions, and providing for the equipment of a naval force for the defense of our just rights. The country cannot have forgotten the protection afforded to trade by these measures so honorable to the nation—measures by which our flag was respected in every sea, and the skill and courage of our officers and seamen displayed in battle with the ships of France. It was in consequence of these decisive acts that an early communication was made to our government of the desire of France to return to the relations of peace and to the authority of public law. The convention which was soon after concluded by our government with the person who now sways the scepter of France, accomplished those important objects. Had our rulers, after the promulgation of the decree of Berlin, followed the example of their predecessors, the English orders would not have been issued.

Nor should we now have to deplore the distress that afflicts the country. If, then, these evils might have been avoided, by imitating the example of 1798, may they not yet be remedied, by retracing the erroneous steps which have been taken, and by adopting anew those measures which have proved efficacious? To this end, let Congress repeal the Embargo, annul the Convention with France, forbid all commercial intercourse with the French dominion, arm our public and private ships, and UNFURL THE REPUBLICAN BANNER AGAINST THE IMPERIALS AND RD. This done, the English Orders would cease to operate, we would hear no more of the unparalleled folly of contending, at the same time, with all the great powers of Europe—our trade to every region of the globe, except France and her dependencies, would again recover and flourish—our agriculture would feel the influence of the emancipation of trade, and hand in hand, with general prosperity, the revenue of the nation would once more exceed its expenditure. Therefore, Resolved, That it is inexpedient for this House to adopt and pass the Resolutions proposed under the Committee of J. C. GORE. House of Reps, January 26, 1809. FRIDAY, FEB. 3. This day the above Report was taken into consideration, and opposed by Messrs. Crowell, Winthrop, Morton, and Hinckley; and advocated by Messrs. Channing, Holbrook, Jackson, and Loring. The debate continued until part 7.

Another important event is to be added to the many that have occurred of late years; a Revolution has broken out in Sweden, and the gallant Monarch has been deposed. His uncle has seized the reins of government, and in a proclamation addressed to the people, declares his nephew incapable of conducting the affairs of the nation. The details of the Revolution we have not yet received. It was probably concerted by the Duke of Sudermania and some of the Nobles at Stockholm, with the Commanders of the troops on the frontiers of Norway. The revolutionary symptoms developed themselves first among the troops. The want of clothing and provisions had created great discontent which was fomented by the Commander in Chief, who broke up from his position, and began his march to Stockholm to demand a Diet of the States. On their march they published a Proclamation in which they stated that their views were merely these; that the States of the Realm and the Legislators shall be at liberty to assemble and deliberate without control.

The proclamation draws a picture of the wretched state of Sweden; and in speaking of Great Britain and France it says, that the former, the ally of Sweden, shall learn to appreciate and value a nation which knows how to break its fetters, and that the latter shall be taught to respect a people anxious to rival her military prowess. The Proclamation contains a solemn declaration, that not a single inch more of Swedish territory shall be given up to the enemy. The Duke of Sudermania, not waiting for the meeting of the States, deposed the King by his own authority, and assumed the Government. His Majesty was put under arrest as he was about to set out for his country residence. When the guard surrounded him, he drew his sword, but he was soon overpowered, and when the last advice left Stockholm, he was a close prisoner. That this revolution has been of French contrivance we are not able to pronounce, though many will be inclined to suspect that it is.

March 18. The Marshal Duke of Auerstadt has arrived here. It is reported that this place is to be the headquarters of the Rhine army. From the Tyrol, we learn that a considerable French army is entering the Venetian territory. LONDON, MARCH 27. Dutch papers have been received to the 22nd instant, and though they do not announce the commencement of hostilities, they afford us additional proofs that war is inevitable. The first column of Oudinot’s army, 30,000 strong, is now at Augsburg. The second column filed off through Ulm, on the 1st, and proceeded in the same direction. The number of French in Germany, including the Rhenish contingents, is estimated at 180,000 men. The Austrian troops are encamped at Egra, in Bohemia, Linz, in Upper Austria, and on the side of Italy.

Considerable apprehensions are entertained in Saxony, on account of the contiguity of the Austrian army, and the treasure and archives have been sent off in great haste from Dresden. From Russia, we have not yet sufficient information to assert that she will take part with Austria, but we have a strong belief that she will. Count Wurmbrand, an Austrian officer, is reported to be gone to Turkey, to arrange with the Russian General the march of the Russian army from Turkey into Galicia. Our latest intelligence from Austria announces that in imitation of the Spaniards, the students of the universities and high schools had offered to serve their country in separate regiments, which offer the government had accepted. A number of officers in the Austrian army, born subjects of the Princes of the Rhenish League, had on the other hand, demanded their dismission, being unwilling to fight against their countrymen. In Austria, the military preparations still continue. Besides the camps forming at Egra, in Bohemia, at Lintz, Upper Austria, and on the side of Italy, it is also said that a fourth army is to be formed in the territory of Salzburg.

MARCH 28 A flag of truce arrived yesterday afternoon at Dover, with a Russian Messenger on board. He came from Boulogne in a French schooner, and his name is DeSass. He left Russia the latter end of February. At seven o’clock last night he set off for London, in a post chaise and four, and arrived in town this morning. The flag of truce returned to Boulogne as soon as she had landed him. It is supposed by some, that he is bearer of another joint Overture from France and Russia, but had that been the case, he would have been dispatched from Paris, & not from Petersburg. Others assert that he is come with dispatches for the Russian Admiral. Portugal. Gen. Sherbrook’s division, as we have before stated, had arrived at Lisbon, making the British force in that quarter amount to from 18 to 20,000 men. We have before stated that the Marquis de Romana had retreated upon Chaves in good order.

The accounts now received are rather confused, but so far as we can understand them, he has since retreated from that quarter, which seems now to be occupied by a French force of about 7000 men. It appears, by some letters, that Romana has proceeded towards Lisbon, proposing to unite with the British and Portuguese in that quarter, and to act in conjunction with them against the common enemy. Spain.—Important and interesting intelligence was received this morning by government. The precise particulars we have not been able to learn, but the news is from the eastern provinces of Spain, where the Spaniards have gained some signal advantages over the enemy. Not only the strong city of Barcelona, the capital of Catalonia, but Mount Joy, the fort by which it is defended, situated on a rocky mountain about a mile to the west of the city, has surrendered to the patriots under Gen. Reding. This success was followed by the immediate retreat of the French, not only from the whole of Catalonia, but from all the eastern provinces of the peninsula; and a solemn thanksgiving had in consequence been observed throughout the Spanish armies. In one of the neighboring provinces, in which the French had attempted to rally, report says, they were again attacked by the Spanish peasantry, who after three days’ hard fighting, had entirely annihilated the whole body.

House of Commons, March 27. Mr. Rose stated, from an account which had been presented to the House, of the general return of the Exports and Imports for the year ending the 5th of January, 1809 — that notwithstanding the embargoes, and other measures of the American government, the Exports of British manufactures the last year, exceeded that of the preceding year, by nearly a million and a half, and that it had been very nearly equal to the best years which the country had ever known. By the Protector, from Canton, we learn that an expedition fitted out at Bengal and Penang, under direction of Admiral Drury for the purpose of taking possession of Macao, arrived in Macao Roads on the 11th September last.

The object of this visit was to obtain an interview with the Viceroy, who haughtily refused to admit him into his presence, and treated him with contempt. On the 10th Nov. Admiral Drury ordered all the English subjects to quit Canton in 3 days, and repair on board the ships of their nation at Whampoa. Ten days after, he attempted another visit to Canton with the launches and other boats of the fleet strongly armed, but was driven back by the Chinese, who had stationed some Man of War Junks five or six miles below the city, where the boats were fired at and stopped. From this time till the 20th of December, all communication between Canton and the ships at Whampoa, and all supplies of provisions were strictly forbidden, and no Englishman was suffered to remain in Canton, or return to that city. One gentleman in attempting to get there by stealth, was discovered, carried into the city and there kept in confinement during the continuance of the difficulties. Finding that his expedients to induce the Chinese to connive at, or consent to his holding Macao, were ineffectual, the Admiral abandoned the enterprise, withdrew his troops and left Macao for Bengal about the first of January last. As this was a compliance with the conditions required by the Chinese, the trade with the English, was renewed. Washington, May 18.

Our democratic brethren sneeringly demand, if we will give Mr. Madison our support for President, the next four years? Washington, the "father of his country," found it impossible to obtain from the British government any concession on that ground; and Mr. Adams, his successor, after many well-directed efforts, was equally unfortunate. Since the presidency of Mr. Adams, Mr. Jefferson has, with zeal and ability, directed his attention to an abatement or removal of the grievance, but with no greater success. In January, 1804, Mr. Madison concludes an elaborate paper, addressed to Mr. Monroe, with intimations to withdraw from the court of London, unless he could obtain a treaty, otherwise agreeable, expressly relinquishing the right of searching our merchant ships for men. Did he withdraw? No, nor has he to this moment, although nearly four years have since elapsed. The truth is, and it cannot and ought not to be concealed, that great as the grievance, wrong as the practice is, not one man could have been found in the country, except some mad-cap, ready to go to war to redress it, had it not been for the indignation excited by the outrageous conduct of the Leander and the Leopard.

Mr. Quincy wished to know of the chairman of the committee, whether this money was to be appropriated exclusively to erect new fortifications, or to repair old ones, or for both. Mr. Blount said the sum of 750,000 dollars, was considered sufficient to complete such fortifications as have been erected on proper sites, and to erect such others as might be necessary in aid of gunboats. The secretary of the navy could not state the particular sum that each place would require. Past experience had shown that such express appropriation could not be made. It was the wish of the committee to afford to the President the power of applying these sums to such places as he should think best. Mr. Quincy wished to know whether the terms of the resolution expressed the intention. He conceived that this sum of money should be placed in the hands of the President of the United States, not only to erect new fortifications, but to repair old ones where necessary. As he understood the resolution, the President was to apply the whole sum to new fortifications, and could not appropriate it without misapplication to repair old ones.

All agreed that the ports and harbors of the U.S. should be better fortified than they were at present; in point he trusted there could be but one opinion: but unless a certain sum was named the people in the seaports would remain in the same state of doubt and uncertainty which they had experienced ever since the commencement of the session. He wished to come to the point which was most important to consider; he wished to know how much gentlemen would give towards the protection of our ports and harbors. If they were not so fully prepared to decide as they might perhaps hereafter be, he thought they might do much by entering into the discussion of the subject. For himself he could not readily assent to what had fallen from the Chairman of the committee; he could not comprehend the propriety of making a difference between the expense to be incurred in case the appearances of war should arise, and those estimated on a prospect of peace. He had heard nothing said that was calculated to change his uniform opinion on this subject, that a state of peace was the season for a nation which had so many valuable points to prepare for war, and place itself in a condition to repel attack.

In a state of war, and it seemed to be seriously approaching, it would be impossible to lay out money to so much advantage as in a state of peace. It was in the time of peace peculiarly that they could erect barriers against some of the most dreadful evils of war: He would here apply the maxim of Washington, quoted by a gentleman from Maryland some days since, "that to preserve peace, we should be prepared for war." Supposing it should happen, improbable as it was, that the country should remain at peace, were they on that account to relax in the fortification of our ports and harbors? How could they, acting in this way, expect ever to be prepared for war, when it should actually arrive? A country whose coasts were so much exposed, and whose cities were so rich, so valuable, and therefore so tempting, should never be unprepared; but if, said he, we should be persuaded to postpone the defense of the country, while we are waiting for new and hoping for peace, the enemy may be at our doors; our cities may be sacked, and nothing left in them, worth defending; it would be too late then, because it will be to no purpose to fortify, and the money we talk of appropriating may be saved, while our cities are destroyed and desolate.

At this time, when they saw approaching so nearly to them—when they saw almost realized that state of war, which they had so often been told might happen, and for which the people had been so often warned to prepare. Mr. G. hoped they would give up some of that tenacious hard-fistedness which had hitherto clinched their fingers so closely in the purse strings of the national treasury. It was their cities which called for protection—it was better to expend money in protecting those deposits of individual wealth, those sources of national revenue, than in buying unproductive wildernesses, or speculating in hotbeds of sedition and treason; better protect what they had than purchase that which might become a curse to them. They had better do something for what a gentleman of that House once called "the good old thirteen United States," and not let all their care and all their tenderness travel westward. Do something for us, said Mr. G. but do not think of satisfying us by merely pretending to do it; let us know what you mean to do. I feel myself authorized to demand that what we have asked shall be granted to us, or that we shall be told in direct terms that you will do nothing for us. At least deal plainly with us. When you come with your 300,000 or 750,000 dollars, what does it amount to?

Dark Day.—Thursday last, was the most remarkable dark day, that has ever been witnessed by the citizens of this place. The Darkness occasioned by the eclipse of the Sun in June 1806, was nothing in comparison to that of Thursday. The Court which was then sitting—tavern-keepers, and many private families, were obliged to light candles at 11 o’clock in the forenoon, and keep them burning for nearly two hours; the fowls went to roost, and everything had the appearance of night: Indeed it was the opinion of some, that the Court ought to have suspended “the business of the country,” as there was every appearance of a sudden termination of earthly affairs, and that they, as well as all others, would soon have to appear before a higher tribunal. The morning had been foggy and the atmosphere extremely cloudy, but whether that could have occasioned the darkness at noon, we cannot pretend to say. NEW-YORK, Dec. 3, 1807. I blush for the honor of my country, when I know that foreigners frequently hear these Legislators deal out for information and argument, the scraps they have picked up from newspapers; and which a horn-book school-boy’s judgment would have shown to have been false and contradictory—While men of real talents, and information of both parties, sit mute, and appear not only unable to check the delusion, but to be pleased with the deluders and deluded. One of these Legislators lately affirmed, that the British were instigating the Indians against us, on our frontiers; and this too after the falsehood of the report had been acknowledged, in the very papers which first gave circulation to it. Yet this same impartial Lawgiver forgot to say a word on an actual Indian War, waged on us by the very savages, on our “South-Western borders; though the slaughter of several of our countrymen had been officially announced; and strong suspicions entertained that the Indians were instigated by the Spaniards—But the Spaniards are the good friends and allies of France; and of course, according to some men’s creed, can do no wrong. It is such bold-faced partiality and falsehoods which have driven our country to its present situation; and a remedy will not be applied until the people are made to feel, as well as see, the iniquity of their blind guides.”

Libel Suit,—Yesterday came on for trial, at The Sittings before His Honor Judge Spencer, the cause of Maturin Livingston vs. James Chettham, for another libel, in charging the plaintiff with having been detected in cheating at Cards. The Judge, in his charge to the Jury, about 4 o’clock in the after noon, with perspicuity and strict im partiality, recapitulated the evidence, explained the law, and stated the grounds which ought to govern them in assessing the damages. On the last point, he observed, that they ought to have in view, not merely an atonement to the plaintiff, but an example for the benefit of the public. The Jury retired, and this morning came into Court with a sealed verdict for the plaintiff; damages, one thousand dollars. —o— Extract of a letter from an American gentleman residing in Great Britain, to his friend in New York: “The storm seems gathering over the heads of Britons and Americans. How extremely unwise to suffer the spirit of enmity between them to be blown up, by artful and mischievous men, who are the enemies of both countries! If there have been errors on both sides, is there no wisdom, no benevo lence strong enough, in the cabinets of both countries, to correct them, and prevent miseries a thousand times greater than the evils complained of?"

Here is the spirit of true religion, the love of our species, tenderness for the lives and happiness of our countrymen? I will yet indulge the consoling hope that Britain and America love each other, and themselves, too well, to become the sport of evil spirits and be driven by them towards each other's destruction. In this unnatural contest, it is difficult to say which party would be the greatest sufferer. One point is, however, certain, that the nation which manifests the most forbearance, the greater horror in entering on the conflict, will display the greatest magnanimity, the noblest proof of being influenced by the amicable and excellent spirit of Christianity. What a happy exemplary struggle for pre-eminence would this be!" All doubt is now vanished on the question, What course the British will adopt respecting British seamen found on board foreign vessels. They expressly disavow any right to search for them on board National Ships: But are determined to seize them whenever found on board Merchantmen. The point is now ascertained as it respects the United States and Great Britain. One or both must recede. Our government, it is said, has fixed it as a sine qua non, that the American flag, on board merchantmen, shall protect even British subjects sailing under it. The British government has proclaimed their determination to take their native-born seamen and mariners whenever they find them on board foreign merchantmen.

The two nations are thus at issue. And six weeks will not elapse before it will be seen, whether, or not, our Rulers are such "madcaps"—to use the phrase of a New York democratic pa- per—to go to War for the protection of foreign seamen.—Cent. The great, the important questions must soon be decided, Whether the United States will encounter all the horrors of War, to attempt to make American merchant ships an asylum for English, Scotch, and Irish runaway seamen, and marines? And whether, to give protection to such foreigners, who are taking the bread from the mouths of native born Americans, the American seamen, now navigating distant seas, shall be liable to all the calamities of war—to capture, imprisonment and confiscation of their hard earnings. This declaration, we think, settles the question of the attack on the Chesapeake, and amounts to an acknowledgement on the part of the British government that the attack was unauthorized. We see nothing to doubt that reasonable reparation will be made for the outrage. But it appears, England is determined to adhere to the principle of taking their men from private vessels at any hazard. Mr. Jefferson contends that the flag of the U.S. shall be a sufficient protection for every description of men sailing under it; this point will never be yielded on the part of Great Britain. In a few days, this diligence will probably be brought to an issue. In the meantime, it is a subject of the first importance for the consideration of the people of this part of the country, whether it would be either wise or prudent to engage in a war for the purpose of affording an asylum to British rejects, runaways, and deserters. That part of the community, the mercantile, who alone are interested in the measure would unanimously be in the negative. Dutch papers of October the 18th state that an alliance, offensive and defensive, has been made between France and Denmark. One of the Danish Generals, who signed the capitulation with the English, has been arrested by the Crown Prince.

Mr. Jefferson contends that the flag of the U.S. shall be a sufficient protection for every description of men sailing under it; this point will never be yielded on the part of Great Britain. In a few days, this diligence will probably be brought to an issue. In the meantime, it is a subject of the first importance for the consideration of the people of this part of the country, whether it would be either wise or prudent to engage in a war for the purpose of affording an asylum to British rejects, runaways, and deserters. That part of the community, the mercantile, who alone are interested in the measure would unanimously be in the negative. Dutch papers of October the 18th state that an alliance, offensive and defensive, has been made between France and Denmark. One of the Danish Generals, who signed the capitulation with the English, has been arrested by the Crown Prince.

The nominal King of Prussia has appointed a Court Martial, to inquire into the conduct of several officers during the late war with France. A serious misunderstanding continues between England and Russia, but there are no official accounts of hostilities having been commenced by either party. Mr. Monroe's Conge—After many contradictory reports concerning Mr. Monroe's leaving England, as to the terms on which he closed his official duties, from a paragraph in the National Intelligencer and several letters from Washington on that subject, we believe the following statement may be relied on as correct. That Mr. Monroe communicated to Mr. Canning his instructions to demand satisfaction for the attack on the Chesapeake, and a relinquishment of the right of impressment from American merchantmen. That Mr. Monroe was asked, whether he could not treat on one point without discussing the other. On his replying in the negative, he was informed that under such circumstances, further negotiation was impracticable, and that a special minister would be deputed to our government, to attempt an accommodation with respect to the affair of the Chesapeake. That Mr. Monroe having thus brought his business to a close, demanded his passports, and immediately prepared to return. The news of Mr. Monroe's arrival in this country may be very shortly expected.

We regret that the young poet has dared to mimic the lyric blast against the breast of our most excellent President; But, as the lines are a good specimen of the author’s powers, we cannot resist the temptation of quoting them, conscious that the first magistrate of this country, secure in the impenetrable armor of mature rectitude, “smiles at the drawn dagger, and defies its point.” When shall this land, some courteous angel say, Throw off a weak and erring ruler’s sway? Rise, injured people, vindicate your cause! And prove your love of Liberty and laws; Oh well, sole refuge of a sinking land, The scepter from the slave’s imbecile hand; Or ne’er consent, obsequious, to advance The views of imperious France! Correct that suffrage you misused before, And lift your voice above a congress’ roar! And thou, the scorn of every patriot name, Thy country’s ruin and her council’s shame! Poor servile thing, derision of the brave! Who erst from Tarleton fled to Carter’s cave; Thou, who, when menaced by perfidious Gaul, Didst prostrate to her whiskered minion fall; And when our cash her empty bags supplied.

On the third Tuesday of October, in the year of our Lord one thousand eight hundred and eight, HUMBLY shews—The Petition of Robert Stover, and Theophilus Stover, both of Portland aforesaid, Merchants, That they are seized in fee in common and undivided with Daniel Newman, of Portland aforesaid, and other persons to your petitioners unknown, of two undivided fifth parts of a certain lot of land, situate in said Portland; being the same lot of land which Thomas Newman, deceased, purchased of Ebenezer Mayo, deceased, by deed dated the twentieth day of March, in the year of our Lord one thousand seven hundred fifty-five; said lot lying on Federal-Street, between the land of Jeremiah Berry and the land of said Robert & Theophilus with all the buildings thereon standing. Wherefore your petitioners pray this Honourable Court that partition of the premises may be made, and that their two undivided fifth parts may be let off to them to hold in severalty, according to the statute in such case made and provided. And as in duty bound, shall ever pray. ROBERT STOVER, THEOPHILUS STOVER, By HOPKINS & MELLEN, their Attys. Commonwealth of Massachusetts. Cumberland, ss—At the Supreme Judicial Court, begun and holden at Portland, within the county of Cumberland, and for the counties of Cumberland and Oxford, on the third Tuesday of October, A. D. 1808.

Wherefore your petitioners pray this Honourable Court that partition of the premises may be made, and that their two undivided fifth parts may be let off to them to hold in severalty, according to the statute in such case made and provided. And as in duty bound, shall ever pray. ROBERT STOVER, THEOPHILUS STOVER, By HOPKINS & MELLEN, their Attys. Commonwealth of Massachusetts. Cumberland, ss—At the Supreme Judicial Court, begun and holden at Portland, within the county of Cumberland, and for the counties of Cumberland and Oxford, on the third Tuesday of October, A. Portland, Sept. 27, 1808. * (10.10) A FARM FOR SALE, IN the town of Falmouth, in the county of Cumberland, consisting of one hundred and five acres of land, of which thirty is Interval, and lying on Presumpscot River, and five miles from the town of Portland, and on the post road that leads from Portland to Augusta, and into many of the back towns. Said farm is conveniently situated for a Public House, with a large two-story House and Barn, with out-houses. The soil of said farm is inferior to none.

House of Representatives, TUESDAY FEB. 2. NATURALIZATION BILL. The Bill reported by Mr. Mitchell, on the 26th instant, for revising and amending the laws on Naturalization proposes several objects:— 1. To repeal the act passed in the year 1798, during a time when the United States were threatened with being involved in the European war. At that time a residence of fourteen years was required, before an alien could acquire the rights of citizenship. He was also subjected to a variety of forms and penalties, which have since the passing of that act, been disregarded both by aliens themselves and by the magistrates of the places in which they did reside. 2. To recur to the act of 1797, which requires a previous residence of five years before an alien can be admitted to citizenship; and to make that the rule governing the admission of aliens.
